cards.status_note: Musick’s 6 September 2026 preprint claims a polynomial-time solution. Its correctness has not been independently established in this review, so the card is not labelled either a settled theorem or an unqualified open problem. Established certificates and earlier algorithmic results are distinguished from this new claim. Checked through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: Status requires special care: Chad Musick’s preprint of 6 September 2026 claims a positive answer in Corollary 1. Its route is a polynomial-time construction of a locally minimal bridge presentation using compressed descriptions, followed by an existing characterization of bridge presentations of the unknot. I checked the claim and its main proof dependencies, but have not independently verified the local-minimality argument or compressed-update complexity. The card is therefore marked uncertain pending validation of this fresh claimed resolution.

The underlying task is deceptively simple: determine whether a closed loop can be untangled without cutting it or passing one strand through another. A diagram can contain many crossings that are artifacts of its projection. Looking complicated does not prove knottedness, while repeatedly removing visible twists can get stuck on a diagram that still represents the unknot. The input can be deliberately chosen to frustrate familiar simplification strategies.

The chosen representation makes the computational question independent of numerical geometry. Coordinates, thickness, physical forces and drawing quality do not enter the running time. Cyclic orders record the planar embedding, and the crossing data tell us which strand passes over the other. The task concerns the topology represented by those finite combinatorial data, not the visual complexity of a particular rendering.

Hass, Lagarias and Pippenger prove that unknot recognition belongs to NP using normal-surface techniques. Informally, an unknot bounds an embedded disk, and a suitable disk can be encoded compactly through its intersections with tetrahedra in a triangulation. Large counts are stored in binary. The existence of a polynomial-size verifiable certificate gives an upper bound on nondeterministic complexity, while finding such a certificate may still require substantial search.

Lackenby proves that knottedness also belongs to NP, so unknot recognition lies in coNP as well. This is an unconditional theorem, unlike earlier approaches that required the generalized Riemann hypothesis. It places the problem in NP∩coNP and makes ordinary NP-completeness unlikely: an NP-hard language in coNP would imply NP=coNP. Membership in both classes does not itself give a polynomial-time decision algorithm.

There is another strong certificate theorem. Lackenby proves that any n-crossing unknot diagram can be reduced to a crossing-free circle using at most (236n)¹¹ Reidemeister moves. These are local diagram changes preserving the knot type. The result bounds the length of a successful route; it does not identify which route to choose efficiently. Enumerating a branching collection of polynomial-length routes can still take exponential time.

In 2021, Lackenby announced an algorithm with quasipolynomial running time. The SoCG 2025 source still describes this as an announcement, and the checked author webpage lists talks on it. I retain that attribution rather than presenting a fully checked published proof. Quasipolynomial time, of the form exp((log N)^{O(1)}), can be much smaller than exponential time while remaining above a fixed polynomial bound.

Practical algorithms illustrate a different kind of progress. He, Sedgwick and Spreer’s SoCG 2025 paper builds knot factorisation machinery around edge-ideal triangulations and normal-surface crushing. Their introduction notes that Regina’s unknot-recognition implementation behaves polynomially in experiments but has an exponential worst-case bound. Strong performance on a census or on difficult examples is useful evidence for implementation design, without controlling every possible input diagram.

Lackenby’s July 2026 preprint gives a new algorithm through incompressible surfaces and hierarchies. For a nontrivial knot, the boundary of its exterior is incompressible; for the unknot it is compressible. This turns knot recognition into a question about surfaces in a 3-manifold. The paper’s Section 9 explicitly leaves key hierarchy-length and surface-complexity parameters unbounded in terms of the input, so it does not establish polynomial running time.

The central challenge is algorithmic control over global topology. A small diagram may hide the disk or decomposition that makes its type evident. Good certificates show that concise explanations exist; an efficient recognizer would show how to decide without searching an uncontrolled space of explanations. Any verified polynomial-time solution, including the new claimed one, would resolve a basic benchmark of computational topology and change how we understand this gap.

cards.title: Polynomial Hirsch conjecture for edge-path diameter
cards.formal: Do universal constants C>0 and k≥1 exist such that every nonempty pointed d-dimensional convex polyhedron with n facets has vertex-edge graph diameter at most C(n+d)^k?
cards.definitions: A polyhedron is an intersection of finitely many closed affine halfspaces over the real numbers. Work in its affine hull, identified with R^d, where d≥1, and require it to be pointed, meaning that it contains no affine line; this ensures that its vertices are present. Both bounded polyhedra, called polytopes, and unbounded pointed polyhedra are included. The number n counts distinct facets in an irredundant description, rather than repeated input inequalities. The graph G(P) has one vertex per geometric vertex of P and an undirected edge between u and v precisely when their segment is a bounded one-dimensional face of P. An unbounded ray is not an extra graph vertex or an edge to infinity. Graph distance counts edges, each at unit cost; diameter is the maximum distance between vertices and is zero for a one-vertex polyhedron. The constants C,k must be independent of dimension, facet count, coordinates, coefficient bit length and the choice of polyhedron. Real coordinates are allowed, and no simplicity or nondegeneracy assumption is made. Paths need not improve any objective function, and no algorithm for finding them is required.

cards.status_note: No polynomial upper bound or superpolynomial counterexample for the stated worst-case edge-diameter problem was found through 11 September 2026. Natura’s 2026 result resolves the circuit analogue and explicitly leaves the combinatorial problem open. The card includes bounded and pointed unbounded polyhedra, counts facets, and imposes neither monotonicity nor an efficient path-finding requirement.

context_blocks.text: The feasible region of a linear program is a polyhedron. Its vertices are candidate basic feasible solutions, and its edges describe elementary geometric moves between them. The diameter asks for the largest minimum number of such moves between any two vertices. It is therefore a question about the geometry of feasible solutions before one chooses a particular rule for navigating them.

The facet count is the relevant measure of description size here. A polyhedron described by a modest number of inequalities can have exponentially many vertices, so the trivial bound by the number of vertices is far too large. The d-dimensional cube illustrates the distinction: it has 2d facets and 2^d vertices, yet its diameter is only d because one can change differing coordinates one at a time.

Polynomial means a fixed exponent that works in every dimension. An n^d upper bound is polynomial in n when d is held fixed, but does not answer this question. Neither does a bound whose constant grows exponentially with d. The card includes pointed unbounded polyhedra, matching the saved formulation; pointedness removes polyhedra with no vertices, for which a vertex-graph diameter would not express the intended problem.

Hirsch originally proposed the much sharper n−d bound for bounded polytopes. Santos’s counterexample, announced in 2010 and published in 2012, has dimension 43 and 86 facets, with diameter exceeding 43. This refutes that linear expression, but it remains fully compatible with a bound such as Cn² or Cn¹⁰. The distinction between failure of one attractive formula and failure of every polynomial is the reason a major open question survived.

General upper bounds are quasipolynomial. Kalai and Kleitman’s 1992 argument gave n^{2+log₂d}; Todd improved it in 2014 to (n−d)^{log₂d}. For large d, Sukegawa’s later asymptotic refinement has the form (n−d)^{log₂d−log₂log d+O(1)}. The last exponent still grows with dimension. These are substantial structural bounds, but they do not reach one universal constant exponent.

The conjecture concerns shortest available paths, not the paths a chosen simplex pivot rule happens to take. A rule may visit exponentially many vertices even on a polytope whose graph has small diameter. Conversely, proving that short undirected paths exist would not tell a solver which edge to select efficiently, or ensure a short path that improves a specified linear objective at every step. Polynomial diameter is a geometric ingredient, not by itself a strongly polynomial linear-programming algorithm.

Recent complexity results make the distinction sharper. Wulf’s FOCS 2025 paper proves Π₂^p-hardness of computing the diameter of bipartite perfect-matching polytopes, and the corresponding decision problem is complete for that class. Such hardness is compatible with a polynomial upper bound on the value of the diameter. A small optimum can be difficult to compute exactly, just as short witnesses can be difficult to find.

Natura’s February 2026 paper proves a polynomial bound for a different geometric distance: circuit diameter. For a standard-form polyhedron {x∈R^N:Ax=b,x≥0}, with A having r rows, the stated bound is O(r²log r), and the construction also supplies monotone circuit walks. Circuit directions are support-minimal dependencies of A; a maximal feasible step in such a direction need not stay on an edge of the current polyhedron.

Every edge step is allowed among the circuit moves, but the converse fails. Consequently, a short circuit walk gives no automatic equally short edge walk: its intermediate points may lie inside higher-dimensional faces. The 2026 theorem settles the circuit analogue of the polynomial conjecture, while its introduction explicitly retains the ordinary combinatorial-diameter problem. The distinction is geometric, not a question of hiding logarithmic factors.

Other positive results exploit extra structure, such as totally unimodular constraint matrices or numerical bounds on subdeterminants. Those assumptions control features absent from the unrestricted statement. Random-polytope and smoothed analyses likewise describe particular distributions or perturbations; a worst-case theorem must include every allowed realization. This is why the model specifies arbitrary coefficients and requires constants independent of their encoding.

A positive resolution would reveal a universal short-route property of all polyhedral feasible regions, despite their potentially enormous vertex sets. A negative resolution would produce polyhedra on which every route between some vertices is intrinsically long. Both outcomes would identify a basic geometric limit underlying pivot-based optimization, independently of the performance of any individual implementation.

cards.title: Polynomial-time recognition of the 3-sphere
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm deciding whether a finite simplicial complex promised to triangulate a closed connected PL 3-manifold is PL-homeomorphic to the standard 3-sphere?
cards.definitions: Use uniform classical deterministic Turing computation, with no advice or oracle. Integers and rational numerators and denominators are encoded in binary; L denotes the total input bit length. A polynomial bound has constants independent of the input. The complex is represented by its vertex set and list of maximal tetrahedra, with all faces implicit. The promise requires each point of its realization to have a neighborhood PL-homeomorphic to ℝ³ and requires compactness, connectedness and no boundary. The standard PL 3-sphere is the boundary of a 4-simplex. PL-homeomorphism means that after finite subdivisions there is a simplicial isomorphism. Correctness is required on promised inputs; the time bound holds on all encodings.

cards.definitions: The input gives n≥0, V={1,…,n}, and two symmetric zero-diagonal n×n binary adjacency matrices, with total bit length N; each graph is promised planar. No drawing, vertex coordinates or embedding is supplied. The common graph is H=(V,E₁∩E₂), which may be disconnected and have isolated vertices. A drawing assigns distinct points p(v)∈ℝ² to vertices and to each edge uv a simple continuous arc with endpoints p(u),p(v), whose interior contains no vertex point. Planarity means that arcs for distinct edges of the same graph meet only at a common endpoint, if there is one. A simultaneous drawing uses the same p(v) in both graphs and exactly the same arc image for every edge in E₁∩E₂. Edges exclusive to different graphs may cross each other. Arcs may bend freely; no grid, edge-length, area or bend bound is imposed. The requested output is only YES or NO. Polynomial time means one always-correct deterministic Turing machine and constants C,c≥1 with at most C(N+1)^c bit steps on every promised input, with no oracle or advice. “Fixed edges” means shared drawings agree on their common edges, not that any geometry is fixed in the input.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that a polynomial-time decider exists for all promised pairs, or prove that none exists. A positive answer must cover arbitrary disconnected common graphs and freely chosen embeddings. A nonembeddable pair is a NO instance, not a refutation of polynomial decidability. Hardness for three input graphs, straight-line drawings or an additional optimization objective does not answer this question.

context_blocks.title: Two compatible views of the same objects
context_blocks.text: Think of two network diagrams whose vertices denote the same objects and whose edges describe two relations. Each view must be crossing-free on its own. Shared edges must stay in place when switching views. This is why drawing each graph independently can fail to meet the simultaneous requirement.

context_blocks.title: The union need not be planar
context_blocks.text: Take G₁ to be K₅ with one edge deleted and G₂ to contain just that missing edge on the same five vertices. G₁ is planar, and G₂ can use the same vertex positions with its edge crossing edges exclusive to G₁. This is a valid simultaneous drawing, even though the union is the nonplanar graph K₅. Testing the union’s planarity would therefore reject valid instances.

Allowing H to have multiple components introduces compatibility of their positions as well as choices of embeddings, and the unrestricted two-graph question remains open in those sources.

cards.definitions: A convex polyhedron here is a compact convex polytope K⊂ℝ³ with nonempty interior, whose boundary ∂K is a polyhedral sphere. Distances and angles are intrinsic to that boundary: neighboring faces may be unfolded into a plane along a shared edge. A simple closed curve is a continuous injective map γ:S¹→∂K, where S¹ is a circle; equivalently, a parametrization on [0,1] has equal endpoints and no other repetitions. The curve is nonconstant and locally polygonal. At a point away from a polyhedron vertex it must become a straight line after local unfolding. At a vertex on the curve, its two incident directions divide the total incident face angle into two surface angles, each required to be at most π. These angles are measured along the surface, not as angles of 3D chords. An ordinary geodesic has angle π on both sides everywhere; the relaxed condition allows a quasigeodesic to pass through a vertex with positive angular defect. The desired output is one curve satisfying all these conditions, not an approximate curve or an existence certificate without a specified curve. A doubled path that retraces itself is not injective and is excluded from this imported strict-simple target.
cards.answer_criterion: After the missing numerical and output conventions are fixed from the intended source model, exhibit one uniform algorithm with a polynomial worst-case bound in that model’s input size, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A finite but geometrically dependent exponential procedure, a possibly self-intersecting quasigeodesic or a weakly simple doubled path does not satisfy the stated strict polynomial-time target. The current card is not marked as a completed standalone computational formulation.

context_blocks.title: A straight route on a folded surface
context_blocks.text: A route can turn sharply in three-dimensional space when it crosses a polyhedron edge yet be straight after the two faces are unfolded. At an actual vertex, less than a full turn of surface may be available, so the two-sided angle condition replaces ordinary straightness. On a cube, the square loop halfway up the four vertical faces unfolds locally straight and is a simple closed geodesic.

context_blocks.title: Existence and finding a curve

Turning that existence statement into a fast construction requires controlling both the number of face segments and the exact geometry of their endpoints. A bound involving a ratio of geometric lengths can be enormous compared with the number of bits needed to describe those lengths.

cards.definitions: The input lists n≥0 distinct points (x_i,y_i), and B, with every rational written as a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator. Let N be the total bit length. A triangulation is a maximal plane straight-line graph with vertex set exactly S: edges are segments joining pairs of distinct input points, no edge interior contains another input point, and two edges meet only at a shared endpoint. Maximal means that no further admissible segment can be added while preserving these conditions. This definition permits collinear points; in the entirely collinear case the graph is the path through consecutive points, and with fewer than two points it has no edges. No new vertices are permitted. Hull-boundary edges are included in the weight W(T)=∑_{ {i,j}∈E(T) }√((x_i−x_j)²+(y_i−y_j)²). Lengths are exact nonnegative square roots, with no rounding or tolerance, and equality W(T)=B is accepted. Malformed encodings and lists with duplicate points are rejected. Membership in NP means that there are a polynomial q and one deterministic Turing-machine verifier V, running in time polynomial in |x|+|y|, such that for every encoded instance x, x is a yes instance if and only if V(x,y) accepts for some binary certificate y of length at most q(|x|). Certificates may include auxiliary information beyond a list of edges; no exact-real arithmetic primitive has unit cost.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove NP membership by establishing a polynomial-length, polynomial-bit-time-verifiable certificate system for precisely these yes instances, or prove that this language is not in NP. Showing that one proposed verifier fails does not prove nonmembership. The certificate need only establish some triangulation below the threshold, not optimality of that triangulation.

context_blocks.title: The geometry is small; the lengths need not be rational
context_blocks.text: A triangulation can be described by listing its edges. Even with integer coordinates, their lengths can be irrational: the three points (0,0), (1,0), (0,1) have a single triangular boundary of total length 2+√2. A rational threshold must be compared with that exact value. With many edges, many different radicals appear in the sum.

context_blocks.title: What a certificate would have to establish
context_blocks.text: The edge list and its geometric validity have polynomial-size descriptions and can be checked using rational-coordinate operations. The remaining numerical comparison is why merely saying “guess the triangulation” does not establish an NP upper bound. The definition of NP also permits other short auxiliary certificates, so difficulty with direct numerical evaluation is not a proof that membership is impossible.

context_blocks.title: Hardness is already known
context_blocks.text: Mulzer and Rote prove strong NP-hardness of minimum-weight triangulation. Their paper explicitly distinguishes this lower bound from NP membership for exact Euclidean costs. Its rounded-cost variant is NP-complete, but replacing lengths by rounded values changes the language and the thresholds.

context_blocks.title: The related arithmetic frontier
context_blocks.text: An edge-length sum is a sum of square roots of rational numbers. After a common rational scaling, the threshold comparison is an instance of square-root sum with integer data. A polynomial-time method, or suitable NP certificates, for that general arithmetic comparison would supply the missing numerical verification. The 2025 ICALP paper still identifies an unresolved NP bound for square-root sum; the reverse implication from this triangulation question is not asserted.

context_blocks.title: Large solved instances and worst-case guarantees
context_blocks.text: Haas reports practical methods that solve very large triangulation instances to optimality. This is useful computational progress, but it does not establish a polynomial bound on verification resources for every possible binary-encoded input. The card asks for that uniform complexity guarantee.

cards.definitions: The input consists of t abstract tetrahedra and a finite list of affine face identifications, each encoded by two tetrahedron indices, face indices and a permutation of the face vertices. Unpaired faces are permitted. Identifying these faces produces the quotient space M=|T|. The input is promised to be a PL-triangulation of a compact connected topological three-manifold, possibly with boundary; no orientability or irreducibility promise is imposed. Its encoding length |T| counts all bits in the explicit tetrahedron and face-pairing data, with binary indices. Closed means that M has empty boundary, since compactness is already promised. A hyperbolic metric means a Riemannian metric locally isometric to hyperbolic three-space H³; for example H³ is the upper half-space {(x,y,z)∈ℝ³:z>0} with metric ds²=(dx²+dy²+dz²)/z². Equivalently, the metric has constant sectional curvature −1. On closed M it is complete. The abstract tetrahedra in the input are topological data and are not supplied as geometric tetrahedra in that metric. V is one uniform deterministic Turing algorithm without advice or an oracle, and runs in time polynomial in |T|+|w| on all encoded inputs. Correctness is required on every promised manifold triangulation; no particular certificate format or method is prescribed. The polynomial certificate bound and verifier are fixed for the entire problem, not chosen separately for each manifold.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a polynomial certificate bound and a uniform polynomial-time verifier that accepts some bounded-length certificate for every closed hyperbolic input and accepts none for every other promised manifold input. Alternatively, prove that no such bound and verifier exist. A terminating recognition algorithm alone, or certificates for non-hyperbolicity, do not establish this NP membership.

context_blocks.title: Geometry from a finite gluing description
context_blocks.text: The input says which faces of finitely many tetrahedra are glued together. It determines a topological space, but does not hand the verifier a hyperbolic metric. The question asks whether existence of that global geometric structure always has a short, efficiently checkable witness.

context_blocks.title: The certificate must work for every triangulation
context_blocks.text: Two very different gluing descriptions can represent the same manifold. A successful verifier must accept every description of a closed hyperbolic manifold with some certificate polynomial in that description’s size. It cannot be limited to triangulations that visibly carry a convenient geometric structure.

context_blocks.title: Decidable versus efficiently certifiable
context_blocks.text: Schleimer’s 2024 report records decidability of hyperbolic recognition and separately asks for NP membership. Decidability guarantees eventual termination; NP requires a polynomial bound on both the witness size and verification work.

context_blocks.title: Boundary and answer direction both matter
context_blocks.text: Haraway and Hoffman study non-hyperbolicity certificates for orientable manifolds with torus boundary. Their results give coNP statements about hyperbolicity in that setting. The present question concerns positive certificates for closed hyperbolic manifolds, so it has both a different input class and a different answer direction.

cards.title: Does every VC class admit linear-size sample compression?
cards.formal: Is there a universal constant C such that every nonempty binary concept class H⊆{0,1}^X of finite VC dimension d≥1 admits a labeled sample compression scheme with kernel bound k and side-information bound b satisfying k+b≤Cd, in the model below? The same compressor and reconstructor must work for every finite H-realizable sample, independently of its size.
cards.definitions: The domain X is an arbitrary set, and a concept h∈H is a total function X→{0,1}. A finite set A⊆X is shattered if {h|_A:h∈H}={0,1}^A; d is the largest cardinality of a shattered set. A realizable sample is a finite set S⊆X×{0,1} agreeing with some h∈H. A scheme consists of deterministic maps κ and ρ, which may depend on H, and nonnegative integers k,b. For every realizable S, κ(S)=(T,z), where T⊆S is an unordered labeled subset with |T|≤k and z∈{0,1}^b. The reconstructor receives only T and z and produces a total predictor ρ(T,z):X→{0,1} agreeing with every pair in S. It does not receive S, its size, the omitted points, or their indices. The side string has fixed length b; padding shorter strings changes only constant-factor size conventions. Reconstruction need not lie in H, be stable under deleting unused examples, or have any prescribed computational complexity. No probability distribution, efficiency, or measurability condition is part of this combinatorial existence question. Dimension zero is harmless: a nonempty such class has one labeling and needs no stored examples.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A central question connecting the combinatorial complexity of prediction with how many observations suffice to represent all training decisions. Its universality across concept classes, and its links to learning, extremal set systems and graph geometry, make the linear-versus-exponential gap fundamental.

importance.reason: A longstanding general conjecture asking whether VC dimension controls sample representation up to a constant factor; it reaches far beyond any one learning algorithm or geometric example.

progress.text: The framework of Littlestone and Warmuth led to the conjecture that compression size can be linear in VC dimension; the general conjecture remains explicit in the 2025 survey of reductions.
Moran and Yehudayoff prove a general 2^{O(d)} bound for binary classes. The corrected arXiv v2 is the appropriate preprint; the journal version appeared in JACM in 2016.
Chase and coauthors prove an exponential dimension obstruction to embedding arbitrary VC classes in extremal classes, limiting a major proposed approach without refuting sample compression itself.
Bourneuf and coauthors obtain almost-linear proper compression in treewidth and cliquewidth for graph-ball classes, while retaining the general conjecture as open.

The latest version of arXiv:2603.23561, which had earlier claimed a compression breakthrough and later a no-clash teaching result, is withdrawn. Its authors identify an incorrect proof of Lemma 2. This is not a resolution.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The general linear bound remains open in the primary sources checked. The 2026 graph-ball theorems concern structured classes. The claimed breakthrough at arXiv:2603.23561 is withdrawn and is included only to document its status. This card fixes labeled, possibly improper, unordered-subset compression with all side bits counted.

context_blocks.text: The stored object is a small selection of examples that lets a fixed decoding rule recover every training label. It need not identify the unknown target function on points never observed. For example, consider indicators of closed intervals on the real line. Retain the leftmost and rightmost positive examples, or the empty set if there are no positives. Decode to the interval between those retained points, or to the all-zero function in the empty case. Realizability ensures that no negative example lies between the extreme positives. Thus an arbitrarily large sample can be represented by at most two examples.

The distinction between examples and bits is essential. A real-valued example may itself require arbitrarily many bits to describe; sample compression charges one unit for retaining it. Conversely, permitting an arbitrary uncharged side message would trivialize the problem, because that message could encode the whole sample. The fixed reconstructor and the explicit bound b prevent this loophole. The question concerns the combinatorial information carried by selected observations, rather than ordinary lossless compression of their numerical representations.

Moran and Yehudayoff proved that every finite-VC binary class has a scheme of size 2^{O(d)}, settling the earlier existence question. Their argument combines learning with an approximate minimax principle. More precisely, their bound also involves the dual VC dimension: this reverses the roles of domain points and concepts, treating each point as its pattern of membership across the concepts. Since the dual dimension can be exponential in d, that result leaves a substantial quantitative gap. Their corrected 2015 version retains the binary theorem while withdrawing an erroneous multiclass extension.

A studied auxiliary question asks whether each class embeds in an extremal class of comparable VC dimension. Chase and coauthors show that such embeddings can require an exponential increase in dimension. Their COLT 2024 result rules out that general route to a linear bound; it does not show that the original class itself needs exponential compression. A failed intermediate representation is different from a lower bound against every compressor.

The problem also has concrete graph instances. Fix a graph and label sampled vertices according to membership in an unknown metric ball. Bourneuf and coauthors give proper schemes of size O(t log(t+1)) when the graph has treewidth at most t, and an analogous bound for cliquewidth. Proper means that decoding produces another ball, a stronger requirement than this card imposes. Their April 2026 work supplies structured examples and explicitly leaves the general linear-VC conjecture open.

Attias, Hanneke, and Ramaswami show how binary compression results transfer to multiclass, regression, and robust-learning settings, with additional factors or additional requirements on the binary scheme. Consequently, a solution could have consequences beyond binary prediction, but those transfers have hypotheses. In particular, their Open Problem 28 is about adversarially robust compression; the standard conjecture used here appears in their introduction.

cards.title: Polynomial-time learning parity with constant random noise
cards.formal: For every fixed rational noise rate η with 0<η<1/2, does there exist a uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, for every n and every secret s∈{0,1}^n, recovers s with probability at least 2/3 from independent samples (a,⟨a,s⟩⊕e), where a is uniform in {0,1}^n and e is independently Bernoulli(η)?
cards.definitions: The inner product ⟨a,s⟩ is Σ_i a_i s_i modulo two, and ⊕ is addition modulo two. The unknown s is fixed throughout an execution. Each requested sample uses a fresh independent uniform vector a and an independent error bit e, with Pr[e=1]=η. The learner knows n and the fixed rate η, and receives only classical samples. It cannot choose a, request a noiseless label, identify which labels were corrupted, or make coherent quantum queries. For each fixed η the algorithm and its polynomial bound pη may depend on η, but they must be uniform in n, without advice. Every execution uses at most pη(n) bit operations and requests at most pη(n) samples; reading and storing samples is charged. Polynomially many stored bits and repeated access to stored samples are allowed. The success probability is over the example generator and the learner’s random coins, for each fixed s. The desired output is the entire secret vector, not merely a predictor with unspecified advantage. No sparsity promise is imposed on s or on a. The quantifier over fixed rational η does not demand a running-time bound uniform as η approaches 1/2 with n.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A canonical computational learning problem where a tiny amount of independent label noise defeats the obvious algebraic method, connecting efficient learning, random-code decoding and cryptographic hardness.

importance.reason: A fundamental boundary between information-theoretic learnability and efficient learning, with broad consequences for noise-tolerant algorithms and cryptographic assumptions.

cards.status_note: The primary literature checked through 11 September 2026 leaves classical polynomial-time learning at fixed constant noise open. The card asks for all fixed rational rates separately, allowing rate-dependent polynomial bounds. The September 2026 reduction is conditional; sparse, quantum-example and limited-memory models do not replace the specified problem.

context_blocks.text: A parity function is among the simplest algebraic classifiers: choose a hidden subset of coordinates and return their XOR. Without label noise, sufficiently many random examples give linear equations, and Gaussian elimination recovers the secret with high probability. Independent noise changes the task from solving a consistent system to identifying which apparent equations should be trusted. Ordinary elimination mixes error bits along with the equations, so its usual exactness argument no longer applies.

The difficulty is computational rather than a lack of information. For a fixed noise rate below one half, the true secret agrees with a fresh label with probability 1−η. Every other secret agrees with probability one half under the uniform distribution on inputs. With a sufficiently large constant multiple of n examples, concentration and a union bound over the 2^n candidates identify the true secret with high probability. Exhaustively testing those candidates takes exponential time, leaving open whether their search can be avoided.

At η=1/4, for example, the correct candidate has expected agreement 3/4, while every incorrect parity has expected agreement 1/2. A threshold strictly between these values separates them once enough independent samples have been collected. This simple gap explains why a polynomial sample bound alone is not the desired breakthrough. One must locate the exceptional candidate efficiently among exponentially many possibilities.

Writing the sample vectors as rows of a matrix A gives b=As+e over the binary field. The columns of A generate a random linear code, and the task becomes decoding a random noisy codeword. This connection explains the relevance to cryptography. It does not turn a worst-case NP-hardness theorem for decoding arbitrary codes into an average-case hardness theorem for the random distribution used here. Quantifiers over matrices, errors and sample counts have to survive the reduction.

Blum, Kalai and Wasserman give a 2^{O(n/log n)}-time algorithm using a comparable subexponential number of examples for constant noise. Combining examples cancels blocks of coordinates, while the analysis controls how the combined noise approaches a fair coin. Their work also separates noise-tolerant learning from the statistical-query framework in an appropriate restricted parity regime. Thus failure of statistical-query methods cannot simply be interpreted as failure of all algorithms with access to individual examples.

Lyubashevsky answers a different sample-efficiency question: subexponential computation is possible using only n^{1+ε} examples for each fixed ε>0. The resulting running time is 2^{O(n/log log n)}. This result is directly relevant to a learner that can collect only polynomially many samples, but its time bound is still superpolynomial. Keeping the two resources visible prevents the better exponent of the many-sample algorithm from being quoted as a polynomial-sample guarantee.

There are substantial unconditional lower bounds in restricted resource models. Garg, Kothari, Liu and Raz show that a streaming learner needs either Ω(n²/(1/2−η)) bits of memory or exponentially many samples, with a strong success-probability guarantee in their theorem. For fixed η, the memory alternative is quadratic, which is permitted by the polynomial-time question. This establishes a real storage cost without ruling out a general polynomial-time algorithm.

Aggarwal, Gupta and Zeyong’s May 2026 hardness amplification relates success on a small fraction of instances to success on almost all instances after changing the dimension and noise parameters. Aggarwal and coauthors’ September 8 revision gives low-noise LPN hardness under simultaneous worst-case assumptions concerning decoding a code and distinguishing noisy codewords of its dual. These strengthen the understanding of hardness assumptions; neither is an unconditional proof that this learner cannot exist.

The every-secret guarantee is not an artificial extra obstacle compared with a uniform random secret. A learner can choose a uniform mask r, replace each label b by b⊕⟨a,r⟩, learn the masked secret s⊕r and remove the mask. The transformed secret is uniform while the noise law is unchanged. The central uncertainty therefore persists even when randomness in the hidden parity itself is supplied for free.

cards.title: Learning decision trees from uniform random examples in polynomial time
cards.formal: Is there a uniform randomized learner which, for all n,s≥1 and rational ε∈(0,1), learns every size-at-most-s Boolean decision tree on n variables from uniform random labeled examples in time poly(n,s,1/ε), with error at most ε and success probability at least 2/3?
cards.definitions: A decision tree has internal nodes querying one input coordinate, two outgoing edges labeled zero and one, and leaves labeled zero or one. Size counts all nodes. Samples are independent uniform x∈{0,1}^n labeled by the unknown target f. The learner receives n,s,ε and may draw samples but cannot request labels at chosen inputs. It outputs a Boolean circuit h of polynomial size, with Pr_{x uniform}[h(x)≠f(x)]≤ε on at least two thirds of runs. All sampling, computation, circuit writing and evaluation costs use classical bit operations; the total worst-case learning time has one polynomial bound.

context_blocks.text: Decision trees are an elementary representation for Boolean classification. Uniform data removes distributional pathologies but still leaves open whether random examples suffice for fully polynomial learning.

Kalai and Teng contrast the unresolved uniform-distribution problem with their positive result for most perturbed product distributions. Chosen-input queries can provide information unavailable from examples alone. The existing proper-learning card allows membership queries and requires a tree output. This target permits improper output but removes that query access.

cards.title: Efficient learning for stochastic linear Bellman-complete MDPs
cards.formal: Can online episodic reinforcement learning find an ε-optimal policy in every stochastic-transition linear Bellman-complete MDP with sample and computation complexity polynomial in feature dimension d, horizon H, action count A and 1/ε, without an oracle that supplies exploratory state-action coverage?
cards.definitions: The learner knows feature maps φ_h(x,a)∈ℝ^d and interacts through episodes of H steps; transition probabilities are unknown and may be stochastic. Rewards lie in [0,1], their means are linear in the features, ||φ_h(x,a)||₂≤1, and the instantaneous reward coefficient has norm at most √d. Linear Bellman completeness means that taking the expected maximum over next-step actions of a bounded linear feature function gives a linear function of the current features. No norm bound on arbitrary Q-function coefficients is silently imposed. Success means returning a policy within ε of optimal expected total reward with probability at least 2/3. Finite action sets are used; exact feature/state representation and arithmetic cost still need to be fixed.

context_blocks.text: Linear Bellman completeness is a fundamental assumption for value-function approximation, broader than the standard linear-transition MDP model. Polynomial statistical complexity is known, while efficient exploration and computation remain problematic in the general setting.

The March 2026 result makes the deterministic-transition case efficient. It explicitly leaves stochastic transitions as the major remaining extension. Algorithms exponential in the number of actions do not satisfy the requested polynomial dependence.

cards.why: A central computational-statistical gap in reinforcement learning with function approximation, rather than a tuning question for a particular algorithm.

cards.title: Statistically optimal sparse robust Gaussian mean estimation in polynomial time
cards.formal: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm for ε-contaminated N(μ,I_d) samples, with k-sparse μ, achieving Euclidean error O(ε) from Õ(k log d/ε²) samples?
cards.definitions: The clean samples are independent draws from a d-dimensional Gaussian with identity covariance; at most an ε fraction may be replaced adversarially after observing them. A k-sparse mean has at most k nonzero coordinates. Success is intended with probability at least 2/3 over clean samples and algorithm coins for every such contamination. Runtime must be polynomial jointly in d,k and 1/ε, rather than having an exponent depending on k.

context_blocks.text: Sparsity reduces the number of samples statistically needed to estimate a high-dimensional mean. Adversarial corruption creates a gap between that sample advantage and the guarantees of polynomial-time estimators.

The cited work develops sum-of-squares algorithms and lower-bound evidence for this gap. Their resource tradeoffs do not establish a universal polynomial-time algorithm at the stated statistical scale. The goal is distributional robustness, not a particular estimator or proof technique.

cards.title: The Statistical Query Complexity of Learning Sparse Halfspaces
cards.formal: Do there exist absolute constants C≥2 and a,b>0 such that, for every n≥2 and 1≤r≤n, SQ-DIM(Hn,r, 1/[C(r log₂ n)^a])≤C n^b, where Hn,r is the class of r-sparse halfspaces on {0,1}ⁿ and SQ-DIM is the distribution-worst-case correlation parameter defined below?
cards.why: Clarifies whether a statistical-query learner can exploit sparsity while tolerating coarse, sample-efficient estimates. The problem isolates an informational obstruction from the cost of reading many irrelevant coordinates, without assuming a favorable data distribution.

cards.definitions: A member of Hn,r is a function h:{0,1}ⁿ→{−1,+1} of the form h(x)=+1 if ∑j wⱼxⱼ≥θ and h(x)=−1 otherwise, where w∈ℝⁿ has at most r nonzero coordinates and θ∈ℝ. Different weight representations of the same function define one member. For any probability distribution D on the finite cube and 0<γ<1, SQ-DIM(Hn,r,D,γ) is the largest integer d for which there are d distinct functions h₁,…,hd in Hn,r satisfying |∑x D(x)hᵢ(x)hⱼ(x)|≤γ whenever i≠j. Then SQ-DIM(Hn,r,γ) is the maximum of this integer over all D, without any uniformity, product-distribution or margin promise. These maxima exist because the Boolean function class is finite and each feasible correlation condition is a closed constraint on the finite probability simplex. The constants C,a,b must work simultaneously for all n,r and all distributions. This is exactly the polynomial-versus-superpolynomial parameter question in source Problem 3, with its O(1) exponents made explicit. It asks for an upper bound on this dimension, not polynomial time to enumerate the functions or evaluate real weights.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed universal polynomial bound for some fixed C,a,b, or prove its negation: for every choice of such constants there are n,r and a distribution supporting a family larger than Cn^b with pairwise absolute correlations at most 1/[C(r log₂ n)^a]. The target is this source-defined parameter statement, not a guarantee restricted to one distribution or to halfspaces with large margin.

context_blocks.title: Learning with many irrelevant coordinates
context_blocks.text: A sparse halfspace uses at most r of n coordinates, even though the learner does not know which ones matter. For example, a rule depending only on x₇ is one-sparse regardless of how many other features are supplied. Attribute efficiency asks whether learning can benefit from this sparsity without requiring labeled information proportional to every coordinate.

context_blocks.title: What a statistical query reveals
context_blocks.text: An SQ learner asks for an approximate expectation of a bounded function φ(x,h(x))∈[−1,1]. A tolerance τ allows any answer within τ of the true expectation. Smaller tolerance requires more precise information. The source relates inverse-polynomial tolerance in r log n to attribute-efficient use of labeled examples.

context_blocks.title: Why nearly uncorrelated functions appear
context_blocks.text: Under the uniform distribution, the one-sparse rules 2x₁−1 and 2x₂−1 have correlation zero: they agree as often as they disagree. SQ-DIM asks how many candidate halfspaces can be almost uncorrelated at once under the same distribution. It then takes the worst distribution, which need not be uniform.

context_blocks.title: The two polynomial requirements differ
context_blocks.text: The allowed correlation scale is inverse-polynomial in r log n, while the required bound on the number of nearly uncorrelated functions is polynomial in n. Replacing the latter with a polynomial in r log n would ask for a stronger statement. Allowing inverse-polynomial tolerance in n instead would change the intended attribute-efficiency regime.

context_blocks.title: What the source result establishes
context_blocks.text: The source gives bounds connecting this correlation parameter to weak SQ learning. Its discussion of converting weak learning to high accuracy additionally allows unlabeled samples. The exact Problem 3 dimension question keeps those access models distinct.

cards.title: Can Local Regularization Learn All Multiclass Problems?
cards.formal: Does every realizably PAC-learnable multiclass hypothesis class H admit a fixed local regularizer ψ:H×X→ℝ≥0 such that every learner induced by ψ, under the pointwise minimum-score rule below, PAC learns H? This is the existence part of the source question; optimal sample complexity is a separate refinement.
cards.why: Tests whether a fixed preference over hypotheses at each prediction point is a general principle for multiclass learning. A negative answer would identify a limit of regularization even when improper prediction is allowed; a positive answer would give a common template for all learnable multiclass classes.
cards.status_note: As of 11 September 2026, two checked preprints claim a negative resolution. Their theorem statements and local-regularization/PAC definitions match the main target, but the full impossibility proofs were not independently audited and no accepted publication was verified. Retained as uncertain rather than certified open or resolved.

cards.definitions: Let X be an instance space, Y a label space that may be infinite, and H⊆Y^X a nonempty class of predictors h:X→Y. A distribution D on labeled examples X×Y is realizable by H if some h*∈H satisfies PrD[h*(x)≠y]=0. The risk of a predictor g is LD(g)=PrD[g(x)≠y]. A learner A maps a finite labeled sample S to a predictor A(S), which need not belong to H. It PAC learns H if, for every ε,δ∈(0,1), there is mA(ε,δ)<∞ such that for every H-realizable D and every m≥mA(ε,δ), a sample S of m independent draws from D satisfies Pr[LD(A(S))>ε]≤δ. Probability spaces, predictors and learners are understood with measurable error events, so these probabilities are defined. There is no running-time requirement. For a nonempty realizable sample S, the version space H[S] consists of all h∈H agreeing with every labeled example in S. A local regularizer assigns each pair (h,x) a nonnegative real score ψ(h,x), fixed before observing S. It is admissible only if a minimum score on H[S] is attained at every test point x and the induced prediction rules are well-defined; an empty argmin cannot make the claim vacuously true. A learner is induced by ψ when A(S)(x) belongs to {h(x): h∈argmin g∈H[S] ψ(g,x)} for every such S,x. On empty or unrealizable samples its behavior is unrestricted. The quantifier “every induced learner” includes every valid tie-breaking rule; its sample bound may depend on that learner. The regularizer can depend on H and x, but not on S, its size, its unlabeled points, D, ε or δ.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every realizably PAC-learnable H has such an admissible regularizer, or give a PAC-learnable class H and prove that every admissible local regularizer induces at least one learner that is not PAC consistent in the stated distribution-independent sense. A favorable tie-breaking rule alone is insufficient. Neither a transductive separation nor failure of proper learning alone settles this PAC question.

context_blocks.title: A different preference at each test point
context_blocks.text: A regularizer expresses which hypotheses the learning rule prefers. Local regularization lets that preference depend on the new point being classified. After training, only hypotheses that fit the sample remain eligible, and the rule predicts using a least-scored eligible hypothesis at that point.

context_blocks.title: Why the prediction can be outside the class
context_blocks.text: One hypothesis might be preferred in one region of X and another in a different region. The resulting predictor can combine their labels without being a single hypothesis from H. This flexibility matters because some multiclass problems are learnable only by allowing such improper output.

context_blocks.title: Ties carry a real quantifier
context_blocks.text: The source asks the regularizer to succeed for every induced tie-breaking learner. If all scores are zero, the rule imposes no preference among sample-consistent hypotheses. Selecting one specially chosen successful learner from those ties would not show that the regularizer itself learns the class. Likewise, score minima must exist for the prediction rule to be meaningful.

context_blocks.title: Sample-dependent regularization is a different model
context_blocks.text: The source reports a general positive result when a local regularizer may first use the unlabeled training points. Here the score function is fixed independently of the sample. The question tests whether that extra sample information is necessary for a general multiclass learning rule.

context_blocks.title: Two 2026 claims of a negative resolution
context_blocks.text: Hou’s July preprint claims a countable learnable class beyond all local regularizers. The August preprint by Asilis and coauthors independently claims a PAC counterexample under the same worst-case tie convention and acknowledges Hou’s work. The checked statements match the main question, but their full lower-bound proofs have not been independently verified in this review. The card therefore records a claimed negative resolution with uncertain status.

cards.title: Does P≠NP imply the existence of one-way functions?
cards.formal: Does P≠NP imply that there exists a deterministic polynomial-time computable function f:{0,1}*→{0,1}* such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm I and every constant c>0, all sufficiently large n satisfy $\Pr_{x\sim U_n,\,I}[\,|z|=n\ \land\ f(z)=f(x)\,]\le n^{-c}$, where $z\leftarrow I(1^n,f(x))$?
cards.definitions: Uₙ is the uniform distribution on n-bit strings. The function f is computed by one deterministic Turing machine in worst-case polynomial time; in particular its output length is polynomially bounded in n. The inverter receives n in unary and the output f(x), uses independent unbiased random bits, and runs in worst-case polynomial time in the length of its input on every random tape. Its output may be an n-bit candidate or failure. Finding any n-bit preimage counts as success, not only recovering the original x. The probability includes both the choice of x and the inverter’s coins. Formally, for every fixed inverter I and real c>0 there exists N(I,c) such that the inequality holds for every n≥N(I,c). This is eventual negligible inversion probability, not security only at infinitely many lengths. Algorithms have no oracle, nonuniform advice, trapdoor, or quantum computation. The premise P≠NP concerns ordinary uniform deterministic polynomial-time decision versus polynomial-time verification. The task is an existence implication and does not require a black-box construction or a particular proof method.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A positive answer would base fundamental cryptographic hardness on the best-known general conjecture about efficient computation. A negative answer would demonstrate that efficient verification and worst-case intractability can coexist without this basic form of usable secrecy. The problem identifies the gap between computational difficulty and adversarial security.

importance.reason: A foundational question about the weakest assumptions supporting cryptography, linking NP hardness, average-case complexity, inversion, and pseudorandomness.

progress.text: The theory of computational cryptography develops reductions from one-way functions. Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin, and Luby establish equivalence between existence of one-way functions and pseudorandom generators.
Bogdanov and Trevisan give a nonadaptive oracle-reduction barrier to basing average-case NP hardness or one-way security on NP-complete worst-case hardness, unless PH collapses.

Wigderson’s Open Problem 4.9 explicitly asks whether P≠NP implies one-way functions, and separately asks about stronger average-case premises and trapdoor conclusions. This card fixes the basic one-way-function implication.

Liu and Pass strengthen characterizations using boundary hardness of randomized time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity. Their ordinary deterministic K^t consequence assumes exponential circuit hardness for derandomization; it does not derive one-way functions from P≠NP alone.

cards.status_note: Explicitly open in the original source. Primary literature was checked through 10 September 2026; no derivation of eventually secure classical one-way functions from P≠NP alone was located. The security quantifiers are stronger than an infinitely-often one-wayness target.

context_blocks.text: If P=NP, an inverter can search for a preimage one bit at a time. At each step, it asks whether the current prefix can be extended to an n-bit string mapping to the given output. That is an NP question because a full preimage is a short efficiently checked certificate. Thus one-way functions imply P≠NP. The missing direction is whether worst-case difficulty alone supplies the required average-case inversion hardness.

A hard instance somewhere is insufficient for security. A polynomial-time inverter might succeed on nearly every output generated from a uniform input and fail only on an extremely rare set. One-wayness must rule out even inverse-polynomial overall success. The distribution is induced by evaluating f on uniform x; requiring hardness on uniformly random output strings would be a different condition, particularly when f has uneven preimage sizes.

One-way functions have unusually broad consequences despite their simple definition. Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin, and Luby prove that they suffice for pseudorandom generators, with the converse also holding. This makes the question a foundation for computational pseudorandomness and basic cryptographic constructions. Public-key encryption or a trapdoor for inversion would impose additional requirements beyond the target here.

Known barriers constrain certain attempts to turn an arbitrary NP-hard problem into a secure function by oracle reductions. They do not rule out constructions that use more structure or different proof methods. Separating a limitation of a reduction from a negative answer to the mathematical implication is essential.

The 2026 work of Liu and Pass relates one-way functions to boundary hardness of time-bounded description complexity. For the ordinary deterministic description-length formulation, their characterization retains an exponential circuit-hardness derandomization assumption. This is progress on specific sources of cryptographic hardness, but the premise is not merely P≠NP.

cards.title: Can every perfect secret-sharing access structure use shares below exponent one half?
cards.formal: Do there exist real constants K>0 and 0<c<1/2 such that, for every n≥1 and every monotone access structure Γ on [n] with ∅∉Γ and [n]∈Γ, there exists a perfect secret-sharing scheme for a uniform one-bit secret with max_i log₂|S_i|≤K·2^(cn), where S_i is the finite alphabet of participant i’s share?

cards.definitions: [n]={1,…,n}. An access structure Γ⊆2^[n] is monotone when A∈Γ and A⊆B⊆[n] imply B∈Γ. A scheme is a joint probability distribution of a secret B uniform on {0,1} and shares X_i∈S_i, where each S_i is a finite nonempty set. For each A∈Γ there is a deterministic map r_A:∏_{i∈A}S_i→{0,1} such that r_A((X_i)_{i∈A})=B with probability one. For each A∉Γ, the conditional distributions of (X_i)_{i∈A} given B=0 and B=1 are identical. This is exact reconstruction and perfect information-theoretic privacy, with arbitrary collusion within A. Share size is the base-two logarithm of its alphabet cardinality, not its Shannon entropy or the sum over participants. It is normalized by the secret size of one bit. There is no linearity, field, threshold, computation-time or uniform construction requirement. The scheme may depend on the whole finite access structure. K,c must be universal. Rounding log₂|S_i| up to an integer encoding length changes K only by an absolute factor.
cards.answer_criterion: Establish universal K>0 and 0<c<1/2 with the stated guarantee for every n and every monotone access structure, or prove that no such constants exist. A refutation must rule out all permitted schemes, including nonlinear ones. An upper bound with exponent exactly 1/2 or a lower bound confined to linear schemes does not resolve the target.

context_blocks.text: Status update: Nir’s August 2026 preprint states a directly matching positive result. Theorem 1.5 gives every n-party access structure a scheme for a one-bit secret with maximal share size 2^{0.496n+o(n)}. Taking any fixed c between 0.496 and 1/2 absorbs the sublinear exponent for large n; a universal K covers the finitely many smaller sizes. The proof has not been independently verified here, so the card records an uncertain claimed resolution.

An access structure describes which groups may reconstruct a secret. It need not depend only on group size: a designated participant may be essential, or several different combinations may be authorized. Monotonicity means that an authorized group stays authorized when more participants join. Perfect privacy requires even an unlimited observer holding every share of an unauthorized group to see the same distribution for either secret value.

For example, suppose participant 1 together with either participant 2 or participant 3 may reconstruct a bit B. Choose an independent uniform bit R and give shares R, B XOR R, B XOR R respectively. Either authorized pair recovers B by XOR. Participants 2 and 3 together see two copies of a uniform masked bit and learn nothing about B; participant 1 alone sees independent randomness. This simple access structure needs only one bit per share, but arbitrary patterns can be much harder.

The question concerns the largest participant’s stored alphabet, measured in bits. A share with M possible values costs log₂ M, even if its probability distribution has smaller entropy. The total share size is between the largest share and n times that share; these measures have the same leading exponential rate. None of these conventions permits replacing perfect privacy by computational secrecy or small statistical leakage.

The classical construction treats authorized sets separately and can use exponentially large shares. Successive results reduced the exponent; Applebaum and Nir’s 2021 bound is 1.5^{n+o(n)}, equivalently 2^{0.58496…n+o(n)}. This remains above the half exponent requested in the seminar question. The seminar list prints a different earlier upper exponent; the primary construction is used for the historical bound recorded here.

Linearity is a real restriction: shares are linear combinations of the secret and random field elements. Known exponential lower bounds for linear schemes do not apply to all joint distributions allowed in this card. Likewise, lower bounds for particular reconstruction degrees or graph access structures need their own hypotheses. A general upper bound must handle every monotone authorized-group pattern, with one universal exponent.

The same 2026 preprint gives a half-exponent linear construction and a strictly smaller nonlinear exponent. Its nonlinear theorem is the part relevant to this card; the linear theorem alone would not satisfy c<1/2.

cards.title: Do classical one-way functions exist?
cards.formal: Does there exist a total deterministic polynomial-time computable function f:{0,1}*→{0,1}* such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm I and every integer d≥1, there is n₀ with Pr[f(I(1ⁿ,f(X)))=f(X)]≤n⁻ᵈ for all n≥n₀, where X is uniform on {0,1}ⁿ and the probability also includes the independent random coins of I?
cards.why: Asks for the unconditional existence of the basic computational asymmetry underlying much of modern cryptography.

cards.definitions: The security parameter n≥1 is given in unary as 1ⁿ. A single deterministic Turing machine computes f on every finite binary string in time polynomial in its input length. Each inverter I is one classical randomized Turing machine with a worst-case polynomial running-time bound; its input contains 1ⁿ, so its running time and output length are polynomial in n. It receives f(X), not X, and has no advice, oracle or secret information. An output Y succeeds exactly when f(Y)=f(X); any preimage is accepted, even one of a different length from X. An explicit failure output is unsuccessful. No injectivity, permutation property or length preservation is imposed. A probability function is negligible if it is eventually at most n⁻ᵈ for each integer d≥1. The threshold n₀ can depend on I and d. Security is averaged over the uniformly sampled input and the inverter’s coins, and must hold for all sufficiently large n, not merely an infinite subsequence.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves, without an unproved computational hardness assumption, that at least one f satisfies the stated efficiency and inversion bound. A negative resolution proves that every polynomial-time f has a polynomial-time inverter whose success is non-negligible: for some d≥1 it exceeds n⁻ᵈ for infinitely many n. A conditional construction or a failure of one particular candidate does not decide existence.

context_blocks.title: What must be hard
context_blocks.text: Computing an output and finding an input that produces it are different tasks. The experiment first generates an ordinary random input, computes its image, and asks an efficient algorithm for any matching input. The difficulty must survive every polynomial-time inverter on this distribution. A few exceptional hard inputs, or a single unsuccessful attack, do not establish this average-case guarantee.

context_blocks.title: Forgetting information is not enough
context_blocks.text: Suppose f keeps the first ⌈n/2⌉ bits of an n-bit input and discards the rest. Recovering the exact original random string would usually be impossible because the discarded bits are missing. Inversion as defined here is easy: append enough zero bits to obtain an n-bit string with the given prefix. Its image is the required value. This example explains why the success condition accepts any preimage and why simple information loss is not cryptographic hardness.

context_blocks.title: How strong is negligible success?
context_blocks.text: An inverter that succeeds with probability 1/n¹⁰ still violates the requirement. A probability such as 2⁻ⁿ is negligible, while 1/n¹⁰ is not. The quantifiers allow a different eventual threshold for each algorithm and each requested exponent. They do not ask for a single finite input length at which every conceivable polynomial-time program is already defeated. The forward computation and all adversaries here are classical; a quantum primitive with different inputs or outputs is a separate model.

context_blocks.title: Relation to other open questions
context_blocks.text: One-way functions would imply P≠NP, since P=NP would permit efficient search for a polynomial-length preimage. Whether P≠NP alone implies their existence is separately recorded in TCS-0022. One-way functions are equivalent to several basic cryptographic primitives, including pseudorandom generators and suitable private-key encryption, but it is not known whether they suffice for public-key encryption; that implication is TCS-6545. The present question assumes neither P≠NP nor any candidate’s hardness.

context_blocks.title: What the existing theorems establish
context_blocks.text: Levin gives a concrete complete function whose one-wayness follows if any one-way function exists. Completeness identifies a universal candidate; it does not establish the premise. Liu and Pass characterize existence through an average-case hardness property of time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity, the length of a shortest program producing a string within a time bound. Their equivalence does not prove that hardness property. Hirahara and Nanashima’s June 2026 revision characterizes Pessiland, the hypothetical situation with average-case hard problems but no one-way functions. This is another structural theorem, not evidence that either hypothetical world actually occurs. The checked sources do not resolve unconditional existence.

cards.definitions: For security parameter n≥1, Gen(1ⁿ) samples a public key pk and a secret key sk. Enc(1ⁿ,pk,m) takes a bit m∈{0,1} and fresh independent coins and outputs a binary ciphertext; Dec(1ⁿ,sk,c) returns a bit or failure. All three algorithms have worst-case polynomial running time in their input length. Correctness means that max over m∈{0,1} of Pr[Dec(1ⁿ,sk,Enc(1ⁿ,pk,m))≠m] is negligible in n, with probability over key generation, encryption and any decryption coins. For IND-CPA, Gen runs first, and a uniform PPT adversary A₁ receives (1ⁿ,pk) and outputs bits m₀,m₁ and a state z. Independently choose a uniform bit b, generate c=Enc(1ⁿ,pk,m_b), and give (1ⁿ,pk,z,c) to its second stage A₂, which outputs a bit b′. For every pair (A₁,A₂), |Pr[b′=b]−1/2| must be negligible. A function η(n) is negligible if, for every integer d≥1, η(n)≤n⁻ᵈ for all sufficiently large n. Adversaries may run the public encryption algorithm themselves polynomially many times before and after seeing c; there is no decryption oracle. The model has no trusted correlated setup, ideal oracle, secret advice or quantum algorithms. The receiver’s public key is given authentically; its replacement by an active attacker is outside this confidentiality experiment. One-bit message space fixes an equivalent existence question: independent bit encryptions and the standard hybrid argument extend IND-CPA security to every polynomial message length.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves existence of a scheme satisfying the stated correctness and computational indistinguishability bounds with no unproved computational assumption. A negative resolution proves that every efficient correct scheme fails that security requirement. An assumed-hardness construction, experimental resistance to attacks, or an impossibility theorem only for unbounded attackers does not settle this question.

context_blocks.title: Public information, private recovery
context_blocks.text: A sender receives the public key and can encrypt a message without knowing the secret key. The receiver can decrypt with that secret key. An observer has the same public encryption capability as the sender, so secrecy must come from a limitation on computation rather than from hiding the encryption algorithm. The question asks whether such a limitation can be proved to exist for some efficient scheme.

context_blocks.title: Why the challenge compares two messages
context_blocks.text: The adversary chooses two messages after seeing the public key, then receives an encryption of a fair random choice between them. Guessing always gives success 1/2. Security requires every efficient adversary’s additional advantage to be negligible. This is stronger than merely failing to recover a long message exactly: learning one distinguishing bit can already violate the requirement. Restricting the displayed experiment to message bits keeps the existence question concrete without requiring a particular practical ciphertext format.

context_blocks.title: A simple failure of deterministic encryption
context_blocks.text: Imagine that encryption uses no fresh randomness and the two possible messages are 0 and 1. Anyone with the public key can compute both ciphertexts and compare the challenge with them. On keys for which both messages decrypt correctly, the two ciphertexts must differ, so the comparison reveals the challenge bit. Randomized encryption avoids this immediate comparison attack, but randomness by itself is not a proof of security.

context_blocks.title: Which assumptions are still missing?
context_blocks.text: Regev’s lattice-based construction gives classical public-key encryption from learning-with-errors hardness. This is a theorem relating two computational tasks; it does not prove the assumed task hard. In March 2026, Lu, Poremba, Quek and Ramkumar gave another conditional route based on average-case hardness of quantum stabilizer decoding, with classical cryptographic algorithms. A new candidate assumption broadens the foundations available for constructions while leaving unconditional existence unresolved. The word quantum in the underlying decoding problem does not itself make the encryption algorithms quantum.

context_blocks.title: The boundary of the question
context_blocks.text: Secure public-key encryption implies one-way functions and hence P≠NP. The converse implication from arbitrary one-way functions is a separate open question, TCS-6545; proving that implication alone would still leave their existence unproved. Computational security here permits an unbounded adversary to succeed. Consequently, the impossibility of information-theoretic secrecy from only public information does not answer the present question. Chosen-ciphertext security adds access to a decryption oracle and is also a different requirement. The requested theorem concerns precisely efficient classical attackers in the stated chosen-plaintext experiment.

cards.title: Exponential lower bounds for unrestricted perfect secret sharing
cards.formal: Do constants c>0 and n₀ exist such that, for every n≥n₀, some monotone access structure Γ on [n] requires max_i log₂|S_i|/log₂|S|≥2^(cn) in every perfect secret-sharing scheme for a uniform secret in an arbitrary finite alphabet S with |S|≥2?
cards.definitions: Γ⊆2^[n] is upward closed, excludes ∅ and includes [n]. A scheme is a joint distribution of a uniformly distributed secret over a finite alphabet S and shares X_i in finite alphabets S_i. For every A∈Γ a deterministic function of (X_i)_{i∈A} equals S with probability one. For every A∉Γ the share vector (X_i)_{i∈A} is statistically independent of S. There is no linearity, efficiency or restriction on reconstruction functions. Share size counts the logarithm of its alphabet size, not its entropy or the total size of all shares. The structure may depend on n and need not be explicitly constructed.

cards.title: Does perfect zero knowledge equal statistical zero knowledge?
cards.formal: Does PZK=SZK for classical single-prover interactive proofs of promise problems, with polynomial-time verifiers and simulators, negligible proof error, and zero knowledge against every polynomial-time verifier?
cards.definitions: A promise problem is a pair (Y,N) of disjoint sets of finite binary strings. An interactive proof consists of a computationally unbounded prover P and a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time verifier V exchanging polynomially many bits on common input x. There is a negligible function ε such that on x∈Y the honest interaction accepts with probability at least 1−ε(|x|), and on x∈N every prover strategy is accepted with probability at most ε(|x|). Negligible means smaller than |x|^{−d} for every fixed d>0 at all sufficiently large lengths. No condition is imposed outside Y∪N. The view of a verifier consists of its random bits and exchanged messages. SZK requires that for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time verifier V* there is a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time simulator S* which, on x alone, produces a distribution within negligible total variation distance of the view of (P,V*)(x), for every x∈Y. Total variation distance is one half of the sum of absolute probability differences over possible views. PZK instead permits S* to output a failure symbol ⊥ with probability at most 1/2; conditioned on nonfailure, its output distribution must equal that view exactly. Every runtime bound is a strict polynomial bound over all random outcomes, with a polynomial allowed to depend on the fixed verifier or simulator. This is the ordinary input-only simulation convention of the cited definitions, without a shared random string, an oracle, a setup assumption, or a restriction to honest verifiers.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every promise problem admitting the stated statistical proof also admits a perfect one in this model, or exhibit a promise problem in SZK and prove that it has no PZK proof. The protocol may change completely in a positive result. An oracle separation, a failure of one proposed compiler, a perfect-zero-knowledge PCP, or an honest-verifier-only theorem does not resolve this unrelativized class equality.

context_blocks.text: Zero knowledge formalizes the idea that a verifier can reproduce what it sees without receiving help from the prover. Statistical simulation permits a negligible discrepancy between distributions. Perfect simulation requires exact agreement after the allowed failure event. Goldreich’s textbook asks whether this difference changes which statements can be proved.

The failure convention is part of the model. A strict polynomial-time perfect simulator that never fails is a different requirement, often called super-perfect zero knowledge. Allowing an expected polynomial runtime is also a separate definitional issue discussed in the source. Neither convention is silently substituted here.

PZK is contained in SZK: repeat the bounded-failure perfect simulator polynomially many times until it succeeds, and use an arbitrary output if every attempt fails. The remaining probability of failure is negligible, while successful outputs retain the exact distribution. The open direction asks whether negligible simulation error can always be eliminated by some proof system.

Bouland, Chen, Holden, Thaler and Vasudevan construct an oracle relative to which SZK is not contained in PZK. This supplies evidence against equality and rules out a proof that relativizes in the corresponding way. It does not separate the classes in the ordinary model specified here.

Gur, O’Connor and Spooner explicitly retain PZK versus SZK as open in their 2024 paper. Their perfect-zero-knowledge construction is for probabilistically checkable proofs, where a verifier queries a proof oracle. That achievement concerns a different access model from ordinary interactive proofs and leaves this equality unresolved.

The target asks for a class equality, not a quantitative improvement in a particular cryptographic protocol. Its resolution would determine whether exact distributional privacy has an intrinsic expressive cost. TCS-1929 instead concerns zero knowledge for streaming interactive proofs with a memory restriction.

cards.title: Does worst-case Nearest Codeword hardness imply low-noise LPN hardness?
cards.formal: Does the following implication hold? If binary Nearest Codeword is not in BPP, then no uniform probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher D has advantage at least $n^{-c}$, for any fixed $c>0$ and all sufficiently large square n, between $(A,As+e)$ and $(A,u)$. Here $A\in\mathbb F_2^{n^2\times n}$, $s\in\mathbb F_2^n$, and $u\in\mathbb F_2^{n^2}$ are independent uniform random variables, and the coordinates of e are independent Bernoulli variables with rate $1/\sqrt n$. Advantage is the absolute difference of D’s acceptance probabilities in the two experiments.
cards.why: A basic security assumption would obtain an explanation through independently studied hardness. The extra assumption in the new reduction makes the remaining target concrete.

progress.text: The revision gives a reduction for $\eta=n^{-\alpha}$, any constant $\alpha<1$, from simultaneous worst-case hardness of two tasks on a code and its dual. This advances beyond earlier near-half-noise reductions; the single-assumption target remains stronger.
