references.locator: Revision 1, 8 September 2026

cards.status_note: Literature checked on 10 September 2026; dates and review scope are recorded below.
cards.review_note: Editorial specialization of the NCP-only direction in Section 1.2 of the September 2026 revision. It fixes the starting problem, decision-LPN distribution, sample count, noise, uniformity, and asymptotic advantage, replacing the vague phrase natural worst-case problem. The source does not state this exact parameter specialization as a numbered conjecture.

context_blocks.text: LWE has strong connections to worst-case lattice problems. Establishing comparable foundations for LPN at cryptographically useful noise rates is more difficult.

Without noise, enough independent parity equations reveal the secret by linear algebra. Flipping some answers breaks that direct procedure: the learner must cope with equations whose right-hand sides may be wrong. At a low noise rate, most equations remain correct, which makes the precise source of hardness especially important.

A worst-case-to-average-case reduction would start with an arbitrary hard coding instance and turn it into the random samples used by LPN. It must preserve a usable noise regime and show how an LPN solver would solve the original task. Requiring two different coding tasks to be hard simultaneously is a stronger premise than deriving the guarantee from one standard worst-case problem.

cards.definitions: Binary Nearest Codeword receives a binary matrix G, a binary target y with the same number of rows, and an integer t, and asks whether $\min_z\operatorname{wt}(Gz-y)\le t$, with arithmetic over F_2 and Hamming weight wt. BPP means a uniform randomized polynomial-time decider correct with probability at least 2/3 on every instance. The LPN side here is a decision problem with n-squared samples, random secret, and inverse-square-root noise. Restricting n to squares makes the noise parameter an exact rational; this is an explicit specialization of the source’s broader low-noise direction.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed complexity-theoretic implication, for example by a reduction turning such an LPN distinguisher into a BPP algorithm for Nearest Codeword, or prove that the implication is false. Invoking simultaneous hardness of an additional problem on the dual code does not establish this implication.

importance.reason: Would connect worst-case coding hardness to a central average-case cryptographic assumption in a concrete low-noise regime.

cards.title: Do arbitrary one-way functions imply one-way functions in NC⁰?
cards.formal: Does the existence of a classical one-way function imply the existence of a classical one-way function computed by a polynomial-time uniform NC⁰ circuit family?
cards.definitions: The security parameter λ is supplied in unary. Algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time machines; security is against nonuniform polynomial-size classical circuit families. A function ν(λ) is negligible if for every c>0, ν(λ)≤λ^(−c) for all sufficiently large λ. Probabilities include setup, algorithm and adversary coins. No ideal oracle or additional trusted setup is supplied unless explicitly stated; arbitrary non-black-box implications are allowed. A one-way function is a deterministic polynomial-time map f:{0,1}*→{0,1}* of polynomially bounded, length-dependent output size, such that every allowed inverter on (1^n,f(U_n)) finds any n-bit preimage with negligible probability, for uniform U_n. A polynomial-time uniform NC⁰ family is generated from 1^n in poly(n) time, has polynomial size and a universal constant depth, and uses fan-in-two AND/OR and unary NOT gates. Inversion security quantifies over all polynomial-size adversaries, not just shallow ones.

context_blocks.text: Local evaluation and global inversion difficulty are strikingly different requirements. An NC⁰ one-way function has each output bit depend on only a constant number of input bits, while inverting the full output must defeat every polynomial-size adversary.

Known locality transformations start from stronger assumptions such as one-way functions in NC¹. Those constructions establish plausible NC⁰ cryptography, but they do not derive it from an arbitrary sequentially computable one-way function. The implication therefore asks whether cryptographic hardness can always be made local.

cards.why: Identify whether extreme locality is inherent in minimal cryptographic hardness or requires a stronger assumption.

sentences: Pseudorandom generators expand a short random seed into a longer string that efficient observers cannot distinguish from uniform randomness.
General one-way functions are known to imply such generators, but the quantitative loss in seed length can be substantial.
This problem asks for a fully explicit construction whose seed is only linear in the input length of the underlying one-way function while retaining the specified security dependence.
The source contrasts arbitrary one-way functions with one-way permutations, where the desired kind of construction is already available.
A tighter reduction would preserve much more of the original function's hardness when converting it into pseudorandomness.

sentences: Cryptographic hardness must occur on instances that honest users can efficiently generate, rather than only on a difficult exceptional input.
The cited question asks whether P ≠ NP, or a suitable average-case separation between distributional classes, already implies one-way functions.
It also asks about the stronger possibility of trapdoor functions, where secret information enables inversion that remains hard publicly.
These targets add progressively more structure to a bare claim that efficient algorithms cannot solve everything.
Establishing the implications would connect cryptographic foundations to broad complexity assumptions instead of relying on individual number-theoretic or algebraic candidates.

cards.title: Quantum PCP: a constant promise gap for local Hamiltonians
cards.formal: Do there exist integers k,d≥1 and a rational constant ε∈(0,1) such that the following promise problem is QMA-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Input is a list of m≤(n+1)^d k-local Hermitian terms H_i on n≥1 qubits and rational a<b in [0,1], with 0⪯H_i⪯I and b−a≥ε. For H=(1/m)Σ_i H_i, distinguish λ_min(H)≤a from λ_min(H)≥b.
cards.why: This asks whether approximating a quantum system’s energy captures the full difficulty of quantum witness verification. It connects complexity, quantum codes, and local testing.

progress.text: The survey develops the Hamiltonian conjecture and obstacles to quantum PCP constructions.

Bafna–Vyas explicitly describe the general conjecture as open. Their classical private PCP uses $O(\sqrt n)$ queries; stronger parameters depend on a product-expansion conjecture. This does not prove Quantum PCP.

context_blocks.text: The classical PCP theorem replaces full verification by inspecting a small part of a proof with a constant gap. Entanglement and local indistinguishability obstruct a direct quantum analogue.

Normalization makes the target meaningful. Multiplying a Hamiltonian by a large number could enlarge its energy gap, but would also violate the bound on individual terms. The conjecture asks for a constant gap in average local energy while every constraint retains bounded strength.

A useful way to read the two cases is that one input admits a low-energy global state, while in the other every state has appreciably higher average energy. The challenge is to preserve computational hardness at that coarse resolution. Checking a few local terms can detect a constant average discrepancy, but constructing a reduction with that discrepancy is the unresolved step.

cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.definitions: Here 1≤m; each term is specified by at most k distinct qubit indices and the complete matrix on those qubits, with rational real and imaginary parts encoded by signed binary numerators and positive denominators. It is tensored with identity on the other qubits. n is written in unary, thresholds in binary rational notation; N counts every supplied bit. λ_min is the smallest eigenvalue. M⪯N means that N−M is positive semidefinite, equivalently z*(N−M)z≥0 for every complex vector z. Inputs violating the matrix promises or with a<λ_min(H)<b are outside the promise. QMA consists of disjoint pairs (Y,N₀) of sets of binary strings with a polynomial-time uniform quantum verifier: on x it uses polynomially many qubits and gates over {H,T,CNOT}, an arbitrary polynomial-qubit witness, and auxiliary qubits initialized to |0⟩. H=2^(−1/2)((1,1),(1,−1)) is the Hadamard matrix, T=diag(1,exp(iπ/4)), and CNOT flips its target when its control is 1. A designated final qubit is measured. For x∈Y some witness gives acceptance probability ≥2/3; for x∈N₀ every witness gives probability ≤1/3. A deterministic machine produces the verifier circuit from x in polynomial time. QMA-hard means that for every such pair there is a deterministic polynomial-time map sending Y into the low-energy case and N₀ into the high-energy case, always producing legal instances on promised inputs. Constants k,d,ε are shared by the target problem; reduction polynomials may depend on the source promise problem.

cards.title: Does BPP differ from BQP?
cards.formal: Is $\mathrm{BPP}\subsetneq\mathrm{BQP}$? Equivalently, is there a total decision language L⊆{0,1}* with a uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm that is correct with probability at least 2/3 on every input, but no uniform probabilistic polynomial-time classical algorithm with the same per-input correctness guarantee?
cards.definitions: BPP uses a single classical probabilistic Turing machine with independent unbiased coins, worst-case time C(n+1)^k on n-bit inputs, and error probability at most 1/3 separately for every input. BQP uses a polynomial-time uniform family of polynomial-size quantum circuits: a deterministic classical machine on 1ⁿ generates the circuit description in polynomial time. Fix gates H, T, and CNOT, where H is the Hadamard gate, T=diag(1,exp(iπ/4)), and CNOT is controlled bit-flip. Gates may act on any addressed qubits. The input register starts in |x⟩, polynomially many auxiliary qubits start in |0⟩, and one designated qubit is measured in the computational basis at the end. Its output must equal the membership bit with probability at least 2/3 for every x. The family has no advice, oracle gates, postselection, or arbitrary real-number gate parameters. Size and register bounds use fixed polynomial exponents independent of n. Equivalent standard uniform quantum-machine definitions give the same class. The problem concerns one-bit decisions on all binary strings, with no promise on the input. It does not ask for exact amplitudes, full output distributions, or a separation restricted to shallow classical circuits.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This is the basic complexity-theoretic question of whether quantum computation expands the set of efficiently decidable problems beyond classical randomization. It gives a precise target behind the broader phrase quantum advantage and distinguishes unrestricted computational power from experimentally or structurally restricted demonstrations.

importance.reason: A central foundational separation between classical and quantum efficient computation, with consequences for algorithms, simulation, and the computational interpretation of quantum mechanics.

progress.text: Uniform bounded-error quantum computation is formalized, with BPP⊆BQP. Wigderson’s Definition 11.1 and Theorem 11.2 state the model and inclusion.
Shor gives polynomial-time quantum algorithms for prime factorization and discrete logarithms. No unconditional classical polynomial-time lower bound for those tasks follows.
Raz and Tal prove an oracle separation BQP⊄PH. This also separates BQP from BPP relative to that oracle, but not in ordinary unrelativized computation.
Bene Watts and Parham publish an unconditional shallow-circuit sampling separation. Its classical resource restrictions and sampling output differ from the unrestricted decision model fixed here.

cards.status_note: Wigderson’s Conjecture 11.4 explicitly asks for strict containment. Primary literature was checked through 10 September 2026; no unrelativized separation of these bounded-error decision classes was located. Oracle and shallow-circuit sampling advantages are recorded with their model restrictions.

context_blocks.text: Quantum computation uses interference between amplitudes, while a randomized classical algorithm evolves a probability distribution. Both models on this card ultimately output one ordinary bit with bounded error. Efficient classical random computation can be embedded in a quantum circuit, so the question is whether interference provides a strict advantage for some decision problem when both sides receive unrestricted polynomial time.

Shor’s algorithms give polynomial-time quantum factoring and discrete logarithms. They are compelling candidate advantages because efficient classical algorithms for these tasks are not known. Their classical intractability has not been proved, so the quantum algorithms alone do not separate BPP from BQP. Moreover, these are naturally function problems; a class separation still needs an appropriate decision language and a classical lower bound.

Oracle results demonstrate a stronger separation in a different setting. Raz and Tal construct an oracle relative to which BQP is not contained even in the polynomial hierarchy. In that model, an oracle call accesses a specially chosen function at unit cost, including coherently for the quantum machine. Replacing that oracle by an explicit efficiently implemented input computation is an additional requirement, not part of the oracle theorem.

There are also unconditional advantages against restricted classical circuits. Bene Watts and Parham’s August 2026 publication separates constant-depth quantum sampling from specified bounded-fan-in classical sampling models, including a restriction on available random inputs in its uniform result. This establishes an actual lower bound in that model. It leaves open arbitrary-depth polynomial-time classical decision procedures.

Even the equality BPP=BQP would assert efficient simulation only of the decision tasks defining these classes. A demand to reproduce every quantum output distribution or calculate every amplitude to high precision can be computationally stronger. Keeping the output requirement explicit prevents those simulation problems from being mistaken for this one.

cards.title: Information-theoretic classical verification of quantum computation
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform interactive protocol (P,V) for the following promise problem? Input is an explicit quantum circuit C over {H,T,CNOT}, starting on all-zero qubits, with one designated output bit and binary description length N. Let p(C) be the probability of output 1. YES instances have p(C)≥2/3 and NO instances have p(C)≤1/3. V is a classical probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm and the honest P is a quantum polynomial-time algorithm; they exchange only classical messages. On every YES instance, Pr[V accepts after interacting with P]≥2/3. On every NO instance, for every computationally unbounded cheating prover P*, Pr[V accepts after interacting with P*]≤1/3. Both honest running times, the number of rounds and total communication must be polynomial in N.
cards.definitions: H is the Hadamard gate, T=diag(1,exp(iπ/4)), and CNOT is controlled NOT. The circuit explicitly specifies its qubits and gates, with at most N qubits. The promise excludes intermediate acceptance probabilities; no answer is required there. The two parties know C. The verifier may use private classical random coins, but has no trusted quantum memory, operations or measurements. The honest prover starts without an input-dependent advice state and uses a uniform polynomial-size quantum computation with classical control. All communication is through a single classical interface to one prover. Soundness quantifies over arbitrary adaptive response strategies with no computational bound; probabilities include the verifier’s coins and any prover randomness or measurements. There is no trusted setup, shared secret, second noncommunicating prover or cryptographic assumption. Fixed constant completeness and soundness gaps are the target; no constant-round requirement is imposed. This circuit promise problem expresses verification for arbitrary BQP computations. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This asks whether efficient quantum computation has an equally efficient, purely classical way to establish trust without computational hardness assumptions or isolated extra devices. A resolution would identify a basic boundary between producing quantum answers and certifying them.

importance.reason: A central quantum-complexity question connecting interactive proofs, delegation and the minimum resources needed to verify computations beyond classical simulation.

progress.text: Shamir proves IP=PSPACE. Combined with BQP⊆PSPACE this gives interactive proofs, without guaranteeing quantum-polynomial-time honest provers.

Aharonov, Ben-Or, Eban and Mahadev release the completed treatment of interactive proofs with a verifier holding a few qubits; the original work dates to 2008.

Kalai, Khurana and Raizes construct witness-preserving classical verification with negligible errors under post-quantum LWE.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The April 2026 primary paper explicitly leaves this single-prover, information-theoretic question open. The May 2026 trusted-gate result changes verifier resources, and the February 2026 witness-preserving protocol retains LWE. Neither meets this card’s classical-verifier and unbounded-cheater requirements.

context_blocks.text: A user who can run only classical computations would like to check the answer returned by a quantum computer. Repeating the same claimed computation on the same untrusted device gives no independent reason to trust it. Interactive verification instead lets the user issue challenges whose answers constrain whether the reported result is correct. The survey by Gheorghiu, Kapourniotis and Kashefi organizes approaches according to what the verifier can do and which resources or assumptions establish trust. This card fixes the most restrictive physical verifier: entirely classical.

The usual inclusion BQP⊆IP does not settle the question. Since quantum polynomial time is contained in polynomial space, Shamir’s IP=PSPACE theorem supplies a classical interactive proof with an unrestricted prover. However, a proof system whose honest prover must carry out much harder auxiliary computations cannot be implemented merely by running the quantum computation being certified. Requiring the honest prover to be quantum polynomial time is therefore substantive.

Aharonov, Ben-Or, Eban and Mahadev show that a verifier with a small quantum register can verify arbitrary efficient quantum computations. Quantum authentication lets a weak client protect data while delegating its processing. This demonstrates that a very limited quantum capability can be enough, but its communication and trusted operations do not satisfy the all-classical interface specified here. Their 2017 paper supplies the completed journal treatment of work first reported in 2008.

Reichardt, Unger and Vazirani provide another route: a classical verifier interacts with separated quantum devices sharing entanglement. Correlations in nonlocal games can force the devices to implement the required states and measurements. Isolation is crucial because it prevents the devices from coordinating arbitrary answers during the test. Combining both devices into one freely communicating prover removes that constraint, so the multiprover result cannot simply be reused for this card.

Mahadev’s 2018 breakthrough gives classical verification with one efficient quantum prover under the hardness of Learning With Errors for quantum algorithms. Cryptographic structure conceals information needed to cheat in the measurement tests. Its soundness is computational: the theorem protects against efficiently implementable attacks under the assumption. The present question deliberately quantifies over unbounded cheating strategies, which may break the underlying cryptography.

Recent work continues to refine these neighboring models. Kalai, Khurana and Raizes’s February 2026 construction verifies computations using one reusable QMA witness without destroying it, with negligible errors under post-quantum LWE. This is useful when the input quantum state cannot be copied. It retains the computational soundness assumption and therefore does not supply an unconditional protocol for the simpler BQP target here.

Kashefi, Leichtle, Music and Ollivier’s May 2026 journal article achieves information-theoretic verification without trusted state preparations or measurements. Its client still applies trusted quantum gates: one construction uses single-qubit Z rotations and bit flips. Removing two particular hardware requirements is meaningful progress, but a client performing these gates is not a purely classical verifier.

Aaronson, Natarajan, Tal and Villányi explicitly retain the single-prover question in April 2026. They prove BQP^O⊆MIP^O for every classical oracle O using an exponentially long classical proof queried in polynomially many locations. Their theorem concerns multiple classical provers and does not establish efficient honest provers. Relativization is proposed as a way to investigate the difficulty, rather than as an equivalence that resolves it.

cards.title: NP outside BQP
cards.formal: Is NP⊈BQP? Equivalently, is there no uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm that decides satisfiability of every Boolean 3-CNF formula with error probability at most 1/3 on each input?
cards.definitions: NP is the class of languages L⊆{0,1}* for which there exist a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and a polynomial p such that x∈L exactly when some binary string y of length at most p(|x|) satisfies V(x,y)=1. BQP consists of languages decided by polynomial-size quantum circuit families {C_n} that a deterministic classical algorithm generates from 1ⁿ in polynomial time. The circuits use a fixed finite universal gate set, for example Hadamard, T and controlled-NOT, polynomially many qubits initialized with the input x and zero ancillas, and a final measured output bit. Acceptance probability is at least 2/3 when x∈L and at most 1/3 when x∉L. The size bound counts all elementary gates, not only calls to a selected subroutine. There is no advice, postselection, oracle or supplied witness. A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most three literals, with a literal being a variable or its negation. The input length is the length of a conventional explicit binary encoding; malformed encodings are rejected. NP⊈BQP asserts the existence of at least one language in NP outside BQP, rather than merely inequality of the two classes.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove an unconditional separation NP⊈BQP, or refute it by establishing NP⊆BQP. By NP-completeness and closure under classical polynomial-time reductions, the latter is equivalent to putting 3-SAT in BQP. An oracle separation, a lower bound only on unstructured search, an algorithm for a restricted family of formulas, or a conditional hardness statement does not settle the question. A separation from BQP must exclude every uniform polynomial-size circuit family, not just a particular quantum algorithm or architecture.
cards.why: Determine whether efficient classical verification always leads to efficient quantum solution, a central limit on what quantum computation can achieve.

importance.reason: A foundational relation between quantum algorithms and NP-completeness; a noncontainment proof would also separate P from NP.

progress.text: Shor gives polynomial-time quantum factoring and discrete-logarithm algorithms, establishing major structured algorithmic successes without solving an NP-complete problem.
Grover obtains a quadratic speedup for unstructured search, which yields an exponential-time generic approach to searching SAT assignments.
Bennett–Bernstein–Brassard–Vazirani prove quantum search lower bounds and NP-versus-quantum separations relative to random oracles.
Wigderson explicitly records NP⊈BQP as Conjecture 11.5, distinct from BPP≠BQP.
Cifuentes reduces NP hardness to detecting a large Pauli coefficient, deriving quantum algorithmic hardness under NP⊈BQP rather than resolving the assumption.

cards.status_note: No unconditional separation or general quantum polynomial-time SAT algorithm found through 11 September 2026. Black-box lower bounds do not establish the ordinary language-class separation. June 2026 work continues to use NP⊈BQP explicitly as an unproved hardness hypothesis.

context_blocks.text: An NP witness gives a short, classically checkable reason for a yes answer. For satisfiability, that witness is an assignment to the variables. The question is whether the existence of such a witness can always be decided efficiently using quantum computation, even when the witness itself is not supplied. Wigderson lists the noncontainment as Conjecture 11.5 in the inherited 2018 draft.

The distinction between verification and discovery is essential. A quantum computer can certainly evaluate a Boolean formula on a proposed assignment. It can also place assignments into superposition. But a measurement does not reveal a list of the values computed on every assignment. An efficient algorithm must arrange interference so that the eventual measurement supplies the desired decision with bounded error.

Shor’s factoring and discrete-logarithm algorithms show that quantum computation can exploit special mathematical structure to solve important problems in polynomial time. Their speed comes from extracting periodic information, not from a general procedure for every efficiently checkable witness relation. Factoring is not known to be NP-complete, so its quantum algorithm does not imply that 3-SAT or all of NP belongs to BQP.

Grover’s search algorithm gives a different kind of advantage: a quadratic improvement for an unstructured search space. Applied to N Boolean variables, the space has 2ᴺ assignments, so the generic search scale becomes 2^{N/2}, with additional polynomial work to evaluate the formula. This is a substantial speedup and remains exponential in N. The distinction is about asymptotic resources, even if that reduction could be valuable on concrete instances.

Bennett, Bernstein, Brassard and Vazirani prove a matching black-box obstruction and an oracle separation of NP from quantum polynomial time. Their result excludes a universal shortcut that treats the witness verifier only as an unknown function. An explicit formula reveals more than black-box evaluations: an algorithm can inspect shared variables, clauses and every feature of its encoding. Thus the oracle theorem does not establish the unrelativized separation asked for here.

There is a useful elementary implication. Since deterministic polynomial-time computation is contained in BQP, P=NP would put all of NP in BQP. Therefore a positive answer to this card would also prove P≠NP. The converse implication is unavailable: P≠NP alone does not rule out quantum polynomial-time algorithms for NP-complete problems. This helps explain why proving an unrestricted quantum lower bound is such an ambitious target.

The decision version already captures efficient witness finding for SAT. If a bounded-error quantum SAT decider existed, one could repeatedly fix a variable, ask whether the remaining formula is satisfiable, and retain a satisfiable branch. Amplifying the decision success probability makes the probability of any mistake across the polynomially many calls small. Finally, the resulting assignment can be checked classically. This is a consequence of SAT’s self-reduction, not an assumption that a quantum algorithm hands over all possible witnesses at once.

The conjecture also supports hardness results for tasks whose inputs and outputs are intrinsically quantum. In June 2026, Cifuentes proves that an efficient quantum algorithm for detecting a large nonidentity Pauli coefficient of a circuit-prepared state would imply NP⊆BQP. The reduction holds even for pure states and a constant threshold with a promised gap. It transfers the conjecture to a tomography-related task; it does not prove the conjecture itself.

Several nearby questions should remain distinct. BPP versus BQP asks whether quantum computation adds power beyond classical randomization. NP versus BQP asks whether quantum computation can solve every classically verifiable decision problem. Allowing a quantum witness changes the verifier class again, to QMA. Establishing a separation or a speedup involving one pair does not automatically establish the relation between the others.

A resolution would locate a fundamental boundary of quantum computation. If NP⊆BQP, quantum algorithms would provide a universal efficient route to classical constraint satisfaction and its many reductions. If NP⊈BQP, some efficiently verifiable problems would resist even ideal fault-tolerant quantum computers. Neither answer is about today’s hardware capacity: the model already grants arbitrarily scalable, accurate quantum computation with polynomial resources.

cards.title: Does a quantum witness have more power than a classical witness?
cards.formal: Is $\mathrm{QMA}=\mathrm{QCMA}$? Both classes have a polynomial-time quantum verifier and bounded error. QMA permits a polynomial-size quantum witness; QCMA permits only a polynomial-length classical string. The question concerns the standard classes without an oracle.
cards.why: This identifies what kind of information might be intrinsically necessary for efficient verification.

context_blocks.text: A quantum state may encode a proof that has no short classical description. Oracle separations test this idea but do not separate the standard classes.

The same quantum verifier is used on both sides of the comparison. What changes is the proof supplied by a prover: either a classical string or a quantum state. A classical proof is still allowed to instruct the verifier to perform a sophisticated quantum computation, so this is not simply a comparison between classical and quantum algorithms.

To prove a separation, one needs a verification task whose positive instances admit useful quantum proofs but no comparably short classical proofs for any efficient quantum verifier. Observing that a particular state has a long classical description is not sufficient: a different classical argument might certify the same claim without describing that state.

cards.definitions: Use uniform polynomial-time quantum verification, completeness at least 2/3 and soundness at most 1/3, with no shared advice or oracle. Classes here contain promise problems; the witness may depend on the whole input.

cards.formal: Does there exist a classical Boolean oracle A and a language L⊆{0,1}* such that L∈BQP^A but L∉IP^A?

cards.definitions: An oracle is an arbitrary fixed Boolean function A:{0,1}*→{0,1}; it need not be computable. All languages are subsets of {0,1}*, and n is the input length. A classical oracle call supplies one string z and returns A(z). Quantum access uses the unitary |z,b⟩↦|z,b⊕A(z)⟩, extended linearly to superpositions of strings of a given length. Query registers and the work required to prepare them count toward the computation bound. No quantum-valued oracle, advice string or promise on inputs is supplied. BQP^A consists of languages decided by one uniform quantum algorithm with polynomial total running time, oracle calls and qubits. On every yes input it accepts with probability at least 2/3, and on every no input with probability at most 1/3. One standard machine convention uses Hadamard H=(1/√2)[[1,1],[1,−1]], T=diag(1,e^(iπ/4)) and CNOT |a,b⟩↦|a,a⊕b⟩ gates, zero-initialized auxiliary qubits, computational-basis measurements and polynomial-time classical control. Circuit descriptions are generated uniformly in polynomial time; there is no nonuniform advice. Probabilities are over measurements and any internal random bits. An IP^A protocol has one classical probabilistic polynomial-time verifier and one prover, exchanging only classical bit strings. The verifier has private fair random bits and classical access to A. Its total computation, random bits, communication and number of rounds are bounded by a polynomial in n, with no predetermined universal degree. Completeness requires one honest prover strategy that makes the verifier accept with probability at least 2/3 on every yes input. Soundness requires acceptance probability at most 1/3 on every no input against every prover strategy, including computationally unbounded strategies. The prover knows the common input and oracle but not the verifier’s unrevealed private coins; its messages can depend on its conversation history. There is no trusted setup or shared entanglement. Prover efficiency is unrestricted in IP^A. Probabilities include verifier randomness and any randomness or measurements of the prover.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of one oracle A and language L with the stated separation, ruling out every polynomial-time classical interactive proof for L relative to A. Alternatively, prove BQP^A⊆IP^A for every classical Boolean oracle A. A lower bound for a fixed round limit does not by itself exclude all polynomial-round protocols.

context_blocks.title: Can a classical verifier trust a quantum computation?
context_blocks.text: A quantum computer might efficiently decide a language while a classical computer cannot directly reproduce its calculation. An interactive proof lets the verifier ask questions and test the answers. This card asks whether even an all-powerful helper can always make the quantum answer classically checkable when both sides must use a supplied oracle through its query interface.

context_blocks.title: The same function, different query access
context_blocks.text: The quantum computation may query a superposition, whereas the verifier queries one ordinary string at a time. The oracle function itself is identical for both. Some oracle languages are easy for both: for L={x:A(x)=1}, the verifier simply queries x. The question requires a language whose quantum computation cannot be certified by the stated interaction.

context_blocks.title: Two distinct single-prover questions
context_blocks.text: For every oracle, IP_BQP^A⊆BQP^A and IP_BQP^A⊆IP^A by definition. An oracle separation of BQP from unrestricted-prover IP therefore also separates BQP from IP_BQP. The efficient-honest-prover separation is a weaker demand: an unrestricted prover might still verify that language. The two cards record this implication without identifying the targets.

context_blocks.title: Unbounded cheating is part of the guarantee
context_blocks.text: The prover can lie in any computationally possible way, even with unlimited computation. Restricting only a dishonest prover to efficient strategies would instead describe a computationally sound argument. Cryptographic verification protocols with that guarantee do not establish the information-theoretic IP containment requested here.

context_blocks.title: What the 2026 multiple-prover result changes
context_blocks.text: Aaronson, Natarajan, Tal and Villányi state BQP^A⊆MIP^A for every classical oracle. MIP permits several separated provers who cannot communicate during the protocol; the stated result uses classical provers without shared entanglement. The source still identifies the single-prover oracle question as open and does not supply a polynomial-time quantum honest prover for its MIP result.

cards.title: Oracle separation of BQP from efficient-prover interactive proofs
cards.formal: Does there exist a classical Boolean oracle A and a language L⊆{0,1}* such that L∈BQP^A but L∉IP_BQP^A, where IP_BQP^A requires a polynomial-time quantum honest prover and classical interaction with a polynomial-time classical verifier?
cards.why: Distinguishes the existence of a classical interactive proof from the ability of an efficient quantum device to carry out its honest strategy. It tests whether verification can match the computational resources of the device while retaining soundness against all cheating provers.
cards.status_note: Source Problems 7–8 and the April 2026 paper checked; subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026 located no resolution of the stated oracle question. cards.definitions: An oracle is an arbitrary fixed Boolean function A:{0,1}*→{0,1}; it need not be computable. All languages are subsets of {0,1}*, and n is the input length. A classical oracle call supplies one string z and returns A(z). Quantum access uses the unitary |z,b⟩↦|z,b⊕A(z)⟩, extended linearly to superpositions of strings of a given length. Query registers and the work required to prepare them count toward the computation bound. No quantum-valued oracle, advice string or promise on inputs is supplied. BQP^A consists of languages decided by one uniform quantum algorithm with polynomial total running time, oracle calls and qubits. On every yes input it accepts with probability at least 2/3, and on every no input with probability at most 1/3. One standard machine convention uses Hadamard H=(1/√2)[[1,1],[1,−1]], T=diag(1,e^(iπ/4)) and CNOT |a,b⟩↦|a,a⊕b⟩ gates, zero-initialized auxiliary qubits, computational-basis measurements and polynomial-time classical control. Circuit descriptions are generated uniformly in polynomial time; there is no nonuniform advice. Probabilities are over measurements and any internal random bits. An IP^A protocol has one classical probabilistic polynomial-time verifier and one prover, exchanging only classical bit strings. The verifier has private fair random bits and classical access to A. Its total computation, random bits, communication and number of rounds are bounded by a polynomial in n, with no predetermined universal degree. Completeness requires one honest prover strategy that makes the verifier accept with probability at least 2/3 on every yes input. Soundness requires acceptance probability at most 1/3 on every no input against every prover strategy, including computationally unbounded strategies. The prover knows the common input and oracle but not the verifier’s unrevealed private coins; its messages can depend on its conversation history. There is no trusted setup or shared entanglement. Prover efficiency is unrestricted in IP^A. Probabilities include verifier randomness and any randomness or measurements of the prover. IP_BQP^A is the subclass of BQP^A whose languages admit such an IP^A protocol with one uniform quantum polynomial-time oracle algorithm as the honest prover. Its total local work and oracle queries across all rounds are polynomial in n, under the same quantum access convention as BQP^A. Only the honest prover is restricted: soundness still quantifies over all computationally unbounded cheating strategies. Polynomial bounds and machines may depend on A and the language, but must work for all input lengths; they cannot depend on the particular input through advice.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of one oracle A and BQP^A language L for which no classical interactive proof has an honest quantum polynomial-time oracle prover. Alternatively, prove BQP^A=IP_BQP^A for every classical Boolean oracle A. All negative instances must rule out arbitrary polynomial bounds on rounds and honest-prover work, and the positive alternative must retain soundness against unbounded cheating provers.

context_blocks.title: Can a classical verifier trust a quantum computation?
context_blocks.text: A proof of a quantum answer is useful for verification by a classical computer only if the honest quantum device can actually provide it. An interactive proof with an unrestricted prover does not guarantee this. This card asks whether some oracle world separates efficient quantum computation from verification with an efficient quantum honest prover.

context_blocks.title: The same function, different query access
context_blocks.text: The quantum computation may query a superposition, whereas the verifier queries one ordinary string at a time. The oracle function itself is identical for both. Some oracle languages are easy for both: for L={x:A(x)=1}, the verifier simply queries x. The question requires a language whose quantum computation cannot be certified by the stated interaction.

context_blocks.title: Two distinct single-prover questions
context_blocks.text: For every oracle, IP_BQP^A⊆BQP^A and IP_BQP^A⊆IP^A by definition. An oracle separation of BQP from unrestricted-prover IP therefore also separates BQP from IP_BQP. The efficient-honest-prover separation is a weaker demand: an unrestricted prover might still verify that language. The two cards record this implication without identifying the targets.

context_blocks.title: Unbounded cheating is part of the guarantee
context_blocks.text: The prover can lie in any computationally possible way, even with unlimited computation. Restricting only a dishonest prover to efficient strategies would instead describe a computationally sound argument. Cryptographic verification protocols with that guarantee do not establish the information-theoretic IP containment requested here.

context_blocks.title: What the 2026 multiple-prover result changes
context_blocks.text: Aaronson, Natarajan, Tal and Villányi state BQP^A⊆MIP^A for every classical oracle. MIP permits several separated provers who cannot communicate during the protocol; the stated result uses classical provers without shared entanglement. The source still identifies the single-prover oracle question as open and does not supply a polynomial-time quantum honest prover for its MIP result.

sentences: The source compares two versions of transfinite recursion and two forms of analytic choice.
ATR₂ may return a jump hierarchy for a whole linear order or an infinite decreasing sequence, while ATR₂′ permits a hierarchy on a sufficiently large initial segment.
The first question asks whether those two tasks are equivalent using arithmetical transformations.
The second asks whether hyperarithmetical transformations reduce choice of an infinite sequence to countably many analytic choices of natural numbers.
The inherited record still bundles these distinct targets, and a proved separation for ordinary computable transformations does not resolve the stronger comparison.

cards.definitions: A countable linear order L may be encoded by its domain D⊆ℕ and order relation <_L. It is well-founded when it has no infinite strictly decreasing sequence. Its well-founded part is its largest well-founded initial segment. In the cited preprint, a jump hierarchy is a sequence of sets H_p⊆ℕ satisfying H_p=⊕_{q<_L p}H_q′, where A′ is the halting set for machines with oracle A and ⊕ codes a sequence of sets as one set using pairs of natural numbers. ATR₂ takes a countable linear order and may output either a jump hierarchy on all of it or an infinite decreasing sequence. ATR₂′ permits the hierarchy to be restricted to an initial segment containing the whole well-founded part; it still permits a decreasing sequence instead. Baire space ℕ^ℕ is the space of infinite sequences of natural numbers, and Cantor space 2^ℕ consists of binary sequences. Analytic choice takes a code for a nonempty analytic set A and returns a member of A; analytic means a projection of a closed set with an auxiliary Baire-space coordinate. Countably parallel choice on ℕ receives a sequence of nonempty coded analytic subsets A_i⊆ℕ and returns a sequence (a_i) with a_i∈A_i. An ordinary Weihrauch reduction from f to g uses one uniform computable transformation K of an input x into a valid g-instance and another H that turns (x,y) into an f-solution for every y∈g(K(x)). Arithmetical reducibility permits fixed finite-level arithmetic transformations instead. Q2 permits the broader hyperarithmetical transformations, involving effective transfinite rather than merely finite arithmetic computation; their precise uniform representation remains part of the unfinished final formulation.
cards.answer_criterion: For Q1, establish both arithmetical reductions or prove a failed direction. For Q2, establish the stated hyperarithmetical reduction or its failure. Resolving one does not automatically resolve the other. The record still needs a choice of primary benchmark target and complete conventions for that target; an ordinary computable nonreduction alone does not refute a reduction with stronger preprocessing and postprocessing.

context_blocks.title: Recursion with a second possible output
context_blocks.text: Transfinite recursion usually takes a well-order as a promise. ATR₂ accepts a linear order without that promise and allows an infinite descent as an alternative output. A hierarchy can sometimes exist even on an ill-founded order, so the output is not required to classify the input as well-founded or ill-founded.

context_blocks.title: Full order versus a large initial segment
context_blocks.text: ATR₂′ weakens one output option by allowing a hierarchy on a suitable initial segment. On a well-order, that segment must be the entire order. The distinction therefore lies in ill-founded inputs and how much of their order structure the hierarchy must cover.

context_blocks.title: Independent choices versus a whole infinite object
context_blocks.text: Parallel choice on ℕ selects one number from each separately specified set. Analytic choice on Baire space selects a whole infinite sequence subject to a single analytic condition, which can couple its coordinates. The second question asks whether stronger effective transformations remove the gap between these tasks.

cards.definitions: Fix an optimal plain conditional universal machine U. Define C(u|v)=min{|p|:U(p,v) halts with output u}; there is no prefix-free restriction or time bound on programs p. Set C(u)=C(u|ε), where ε is the empty string. Use the computable, uniquely decodable pairing ⟨x,y⟩=1^|x|0xy, and write C(x,y)=C(⟨x,y⟩) and C(u|x,y)=C(u|⟨x,y⟩). The integer n bounds joint description length, not the bit lengths of x or y; z has no length or complexity bound. The single constant a may depend on U and the fixed encoding, but not on n,x,y,z. cards.definitions: A countable linear order is a strict total order on a subset of ℕ, presented by codes for its domain and comparison relation. It is a well-order if it has no infinite decreasing sequence. An order embedding f from L into M is an injective map satisfying x<_L y exactly when f(x)<_M f(y). For well-orders, weak comparison asks for an embedding in one direction; initial-segment comparison additionally requires the image to be an initial segment of the target. The ordinal sum β+γ places a copy of γ after a copy of β. A nonzero ordinal α is additively indecomposable when β+γ<α for all β,γ<α; examples include ω and ω². The source mentions weak comparability of indecomposable well-orders, preservation of well-foundedness under α↦ω^α, and expressing an indecomposable α as ω^β. It does not fix the computational presentations and outputs for these alternative tasks. For represented multivalued tasks f,g, f≤W g means that computable transformations K,H uniformly produce a valid g-instance K(x) and convert every y∈g(K(x)) into an f-solution H(x,y). Weihrauch equivalence means reducibility in both directions; the actual f and g remain to be selected here.
cards.answer_criterion: Specify one of the source’s ordinal tasks, its represented inputs and outputs, and an exact proposed degree comparison or complete classification target; then prove that comparison or its negation. cards.title: Do some tautologies require superpolynomial Extended Frege proofs?
cards.formal: Is Extended Frege not polynomially bounded? Precisely, for every constants C>0 and c≥1, is there a propositional tautology φ whose shortest Extended Frege proof has bit length greater than C(|φ|+2)ᶜ? Here |φ| is the bit length of the explicitly written formula.
cards.definitions: Fix Boolean formulas over ¬ and →, with → interpreted as material implication and variable indices encoded in binary. Use the Frege axiom schemes A→(B→A), (A→(B→C))→((A→B)→(A→C)), and (¬B→¬A)→(A→B), together with modus ponens from A and A→B to B. An Extended Frege proof of φ may additionally introduce an abbreviation variable e by the two extension axioms e→θ and θ→e. Here e is fresh, absent from φ, θ, and every preceding line; θ uses original variables of φ and previously introduced extension variables. Extensions are thus acyclic definitions. Other proof lines are axiom instances or applications of modus ponens, and the last line must be φ, with no extension variables. Lines may cite and reuse earlier lines arbitrarily: proofs are not required to be trees. Proof size is the full binary encoding length of all explicitly written formulas, extension definitions, and inference references; there is no depth or per-line-size restriction. A tautology is true under every assignment to its variables. This fixed presentation is polynomially equivalent to the usual Extended Frege systems, so changing a standard finite Frege basis does not change polynomial boundedness. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Extended Frege captures a powerful form of efficient propositional reasoning with reusable definitions. A superpolynomial lower bound would cross one of the central barriers in proof complexity and clarify whether a standard, highly expressive certificate language necessarily fails on some short true statements.

importance.reason: A defining open lower-bound problem for strong propositional reasoning, closely connected to bounded arithmetic, circuit complexity, and the limits of efficiently checkable certificates.

progress.text: Cook and Reckhow formalize propositional proof systems, polynomial simulation, and Extended Frege, proving robustness under the choice of standard rules and connectives.
Strong lower bounds emerge for weaker systems, while even unrestricted Frege lower bounds remain open. EF adds the ability to abbreviate and share formulas.

Pich and Santhanam establish conditional routes from EF proof lower bounds to P≠NP. The assumptions include formally provable computational statements; the result is not an unconditional EF lower bound.
Hsieh, Jain, Li, and Mathialagan obtain SNARGs for NP from derandomization, LWE, SXDH, and a bounded-arithmetic unprovability assumption concerning certificates of EF-hard tautologies.

Alekseev’s journal paper proves an exponential bit-size lower bound for algebraic Binary Value Principle refutations in extended polynomial calculus with a square-root rule. Its Section 1 explicitly distinguishes this from propositional Frege and EF lower bounds.

Research through 10 September 2026 found no unconditional resolution for unrestricted Extended Frege. The algebraic and conditional results cited here retain their stated scope.

context_blocks.text: Extension variables let a proof name a formula once and reuse its name. This can represent shared computations economically, as a Boolean circuit shares intermediate gates. Expanding all abbreviations into formula trees can cause an exponential increase in length, so a lower bound that counts only ordinary Frege proofs does not automatically survive the extension rule.

The question concerns the existence of short certificates, not the time required to discover them. A particular proof search method might take exponential time even though another method could find a short proof; conversely, a proof-size lower bound would constrain every method that outputs an EF derivation. The input length is the final tautology’s actual encoding length, so a lower bound exponential in a smaller hidden parameter may still be only polynomial in the input.

If NP≠coNP, every polynomial-time verifiable propositional proof system has hard tautologies, including EF. The converse for this particular system is unknown: showing that EF is inefficient does not rule out a different proof system that gives short certificates for all tautologies. This is why an EF lower bound would be a major advance without automatically constituting a proof of NP≠coNP.

Recent algebraic lower bounds illustrate an encoding issue. Alekseev proves exponential bit-size lower bounds for an extension of polynomial calculus that can simulate EF on suitable propositional translations. The hard Binary Value Principle instance is not the corresponding translation of a polynomial-size CNF. The paper explicitly explains that its result therefore does not yield a Frege or EF lower bound.

Pich and Santhanam give implications from EF lower bounds to P≠NP under additional bounded-arithmetic assumptions. This explores the consequences of proof-complexity hypotheses without proving an unconditional EF lower bound.

Hsieh and coauthors construct succinct arguments under derandomization, cryptographic, and formal unprovability assumptions. Their result connects the difficulty of certifying hard tautologies to cryptography; it does not establish the unconditional size lower bound asked for here.

cards.title: Does Frege simulate Extended Frege with polynomial proof size?
cards.formal: Do there exist constants C>0 and k≥1 such that every Extended Frege proof π of a propositional tautology φ has some ordinary Frege proof ρ of the same formula with |ρ|≤C(|π|+2)ᵏ? Equivalently, if sF(φ) and sEF(φ) are the minimum proof sizes in the two systems, is sF(φ) polynomially bounded in sEF(φ), uniformly over all tautologies?
cards.definitions: Fix formulas over negation ¬ and material implication →, with binary-encoded variable indices. Ordinary Frege uses the axiom schemes A→(B→A), (A→(B→C))→((A→B)→(A→C)), and (¬B→¬A)→(A→B), and modus ponens: infer B from A and A→B. A proof is a finite sequence ending with φ; earlier lines may be cited and reused without restriction. Extended Frege adds acyclic definitions, introducing the pair e→θ and θ→e, where e is a new variable absent from φ, θ and all preceding lines. θ may use variables of φ and earlier extension variables. The final formula contains no extension variables. Proof size is the complete binary encoding length of every explicitly written line, definition and inference reference. No formula-depth, proof-depth or tree-shape bound is imposed. These presentations are polynomially equivalent to the usual finite-basis Frege and Extended Frege systems. The target is existence of short translated proofs: it does not require a polynomial-time function that finds ρ from π. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This asks whether reusable definitions fundamentally shorten mathematical proofs, beyond any polynomial factor. It is one of the central comparisons between strong propositional proof systems and captures the difficulty of reasoning with shared circuits versus explicit formulas.

importance.reason: A canonical strong-system simulation problem, directly tied to Frege lower bounds, finite consistency and circuit-based reasoning.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No polynomial size simulation or superpolynomial separation of unrestricted Frege and EF was found in the primary literature. The newest checked simulation, TR26-166, concerns a restricted algebraic formula system and has quasipolynomial overhead.

context_blocks.text: The extension rule gives reusable names to intermediate computations. If a subformula is used many times, ordinary formula syntax writes out each occurrence; Extended Frege can define it once and refer to its name. A network of such definitions represents a Boolean circuit with shared gates. The rule does not permit a false final theorem: every assignment to the original variables uniquely extends through the definitions, and the conclusion uses only original variables.

Repeated substitution eliminates definitions, but can create exponentially large formula trees. This explains why the obvious simulation is expensive; it does not prove that all ordinary Frege proofs must be expensive. The challenge is to compare the shortest proofs, not one syntactic expansion procedure.

The distinction between proof size and proof-search time is essential. The quantifiers are “for every EF proof there exists a short Frege proof.” They do not supply an algorithm for locating that proof. The stronger notion usually called p-simulation requires a polynomial-time transformation. A size simulation alone can hold even if the available methods for finding the translated proof are much slower.

Buss connects the comparison to finite consistency statements. Frege has polynomial-size proofs of its own partial consistency, meaning the corresponding finite statements that no contradiction has a proof up to a specified length. His theorem characterizes Frege simulation of EF by polynomial-size Frege proofs of the analogous partial consistency statements for EF. This turns a comparison of all proofs into a canonical family of propositional statements; it is not a general proof of the desired simulation.

For example, Aisenberg and coauthors give polynomial-size EF proofs and quasipolynomial-size Frege proofs of propositional Kneser–Lovász coloring principles. That upper bound constrains possible lower bounds for the family, but it does not demonstrate a separation and does not rule out a polynomial Frege upper bound. Quasipolynomial and polynomial must remain distinct in this problem.

Krajíček’s June 2026 paper gives a circuit-rewriting description of EF reasoning. An EF proof of circuit equivalence yields a polynomially long chain of equivalence-preserving rewrites; each rewrite adds at most seven gates and may delete gates. This is a normal-form result about circuit reasoning. The intermediate objects still retain circuit sharing, so it does not turn an arbitrary EF proof into a polynomial-size formula-based Frege proof.

A September 2026 preprint by Chatterjee, Chatterjee, Ghosal and Mukhopadhyay proves a quasipolynomial Frege simulation of a partially commutative formula version of the Ideal Proof System over GF(2). Variables lie in two groups: they commute across groups but not within a group. The proof formalizes an identity-testing algorithm inside Frege. The restrictions on the algebraic certificates, and the quasipolynomial overhead, both matter; the theorem is not the full EF simulation asked for here.

A negative answer would establish a concrete benefit of reusable definitions for strong propositional reasoning. It would also imply superpolynomial Frege lower bounds, since the final formula is part of every EF proof. By contrast, proving that Frege has some hard tautologies, or assuming NP≠coNP, does not automatically separate it from EF: those same tautologies might require equally long EF proofs. The separate question of whether EF itself is polynomially bounded asks about a different comparison.

cards.title: Superpolynomial AC⁰[p]-Frege lower bounds
cards.formal: For every fixed prime p, does there exist a family of propositional tautologies (τ_{p,n})_{n≥1}, constructible in time polynomial in n, whose encoded lengths lie between n and n^O(1), such that each τ_{p,n} is a DNF and, for every fixed proof-line depth d and every constant r>0, infinitely many n have the following property: every depth-at-most-d Frege proof with MOD_p connectives of τ_{p,n} has total encoded size greater than n^r? The proof system and depth convention are specified below; the family may depend on p but not on d or r.
cards.definitions: A tautology evaluates to true on every Boolean assignment. A DNF is a disjunction of conjunctions of literals, with a literal being a variable or its negation. Fix a conventional sound, implicationally complete finite Frege calculus F over constants 0,1 and connectives NOT, AND, OR. A proof is a sequence of formulas, each a substitution instance of an axiom or obtained from earlier lines by a rule of F; earlier lines may be reused arbitrarily. Extend the language and rules as F(MOD_p) in Krajíček §5: MOD_{p,j}(A_1,…,A_t) is true precisely when the number of true arguments is j modulo p, for 0≤j<p. Besides F’s rules with formulas from this language, permit the empty-list axioms MOD_{p,0}() and NOT MOD_{p,j}() for j≠0, and all instances of MOD_{p,j}(Γ,A) ↔ [(MOD_{p,j}(Γ) AND NOT A) OR (MOD_{p,j−1}(Γ) AND A)], with j−1 taken modulo p and Γ any list of formulas. Constants and variables have depth zero; NOT and MOD increase depth by one, while consecutive ANDs, or consecutive ORs, are flattened and together count as one layer. Every line, including instantiated axioms, obeys the bound d. Proof size counts all symbols and encoded variable indices across all lines, together with rule annotations. Proofs are ordinary Frege proofs, without extension-variable definition axioms; they need not be tree-like or have bounded derivation-graph depth. Standard choices of F give equivalent systems up to polynomial overhead and a constant depth adjustment, immaterial when every fixed d is quantified.
cards.answer_criterion: Exhibit the uniform tautology families and prove the stated superpolynomial proof-size lower bounds, or refute their existence. The tautology condition must itself be established: a formula that has no short proof because it is false is not a hard tautology. A lower bound only for bounded derivation depth, regular proofs, a restricted algebraic subsystem or Boolean circuits alone does not settle this question. A result for one prime is a major partial answer; this single card groups the full fixed-prime frontier rather than duplicating it for each modulus.
cards.why: A central frontier in propositional proof complexity: current methods can handle ordinary bounded-depth reasoning but still cannot establish explicit superpolynomial lower bounds once modular counting is available. The problem tests how circuit lower-bound ideas can constrain entire deductions.

importance.reason: A classical next step beyond the strongest broadly established bounded-depth Frege lower bounds, with direct connections to algebraic proof systems and a persistent gap between circuit and proof complexity.

progress.text: Ajtai establishes superpolynomial bounded-depth Frege lower bounds for the pigeonhole principle; Pitassi, Beame and Impagliazzo’s 1993 paper gives exponential improvements. These systems lack MOD_p gates.
Krajíček develops extended Nullstellensatz systems and explains their connection to modular Frege lower bounds; §5 fixes the proof-system presentation used here.
Efremenko and Itsykson publish amortized-closure lifting and stronger size-versus-derivation-depth results for resolution over parities.
Lu, Santhanam and Tzameret publish their no-short-proof result for candidate DNFs, first posted in September 2025; unconditional tautologicity remains open.
Itsykson, Podolskii and Shekhovtsov give near-quadratic-depth lifting and a quadratic unconditional size lower bound for parity resolution. These do not settle general modular Frege.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The 2026 primary sources retain modular Frege lower bounds as open. ITCS 2026.99 does not prove that its hard-to-prove candidates are tautologies. ECCC TR26-018 restricts derivation depth or proves a polynomial size bound; TR26-070 treats a restricted algebraic certificate representation. None establishes the fully specified tautology families and unrestricted derivation size lower bounds requested here.

context_blocks.text: Proof complexity measures how long a formal explanation of a tautology must be. A short conclusion can require a much longer sequence of intermediate deductions. Restricting the depth of each intermediate formula limits the expressive power of individual statements while still allowing a long derivation and arbitrary reuse of earlier facts. Modular gates add compact statements about counts modulo p, such as parity when p=2. Krajíček gives the explicit modular axiom presentation used in this card.

The corresponding problem without modular gates has been solved. Ajtai’s work gives superpolynomial lower bounds for the pigeonhole principle in bounded-depth Frege, and Pitassi, Beame and Impagliazzo strengthen these to exponential bounds. Their argument uses restrictions adapted to the combinatorics of partial matchings. Permitting modular counting defeats the direct extension of that approach: a short parity statement can remain meaningful after many ordinary variables have been fixed.

Circuit complexity provides an analogy but not a solution. Razborov and Smolensky establish lower bounds for constant-depth Boolean circuits with prime modular gates. A proof, however, is a sequence of related formulas, and every tautology itself computes the constant true function. Showing that some nonconstant function requires a large circuit therefore does not directly force long proofs of tautologies. The February 2026 work of Itsykson, Podolskii and Shekhovtsov explicitly identifies this remaining gap between circuit and proof lower bounds.

Resolution over parities is a much weaker subsystem whose lines are disjunctions of linear equations modulo two. Efremenko and Itsykson’s CCC 2025 work develops amortized closure and strengthens lifting lower bounds for restricted-depth parity-resolution refutations. The restriction there concerns the number of inference steps along a path in the derivation graph. That is different from the constant logical depth of each formula in AC⁰[p]-Frege. A long chain of shallow formulas remains allowed in the present question.

Itsykson, Podolskii and Shekhovtsov’s February 2026 lifting theorem gives derivation depth Ω(w²/log S) for size-S parity-resolution proofs when the underlying CNF needs resolution width w. It also gives a pure quadratic size lower bound. These are meaningful advances, but a quadratic bound is polynomial, and a tradeoff requiring sufficiently deep proofs still permits polynomial-size proofs with large derivation depth. Neither gives the superpolynomial unrestricted proof-size target here.

Lu, Santhanam and Tzameret’s ITCS 2026 result studies explicit DNF formulas expressing the difficulty of proving certain algebraic circuit lower bounds. They show that these formulas do not all have polynomial-size AC⁰[p]-Frege proofs. The unresolved point is whether the formulas are tautologies: the theorem leaves open the possibility that some are simply false. They provide a conditional route to tautologicity through hardness of proving properties related to tensor rank. This separates two obligations that a completed lower-bound construction must satisfy.

Algebraic proof systems offer another route, but their representation restrictions matter. Hakoniemi, Limaye and Tzameret’s May 2026 work gives hard CNF instances for a fragment of the Ideal Proof System represented by read-once oblivious algebraic branching programs. It overcomes the obstacle that earlier lower bounds in that line concerned purely algebraic, non-Boolean instances. It does not remove the restricted representation of certificates or establish lower bounds for full modular Frege.

The quantifiers exclude a fixed-degree lower bound such as n¹⁰ and require failure of every polynomial size bound at every fixed line depth. They also keep the target formulas short and efficiently constructible, so hardness cannot come from writing an exponentially large conclusion or searching indefinitely for an unnamed formula. Resolving this frontier would extend lower-bound methods to formal reasoning that can perform modular counting, an ability missing from ordinary bounded-depth Frege.

cards.title: Superpolynomial lower bounds for unrestricted Frege proofs
cards.formal: Is the Frege proof system not polynomially bounded? Precisely, for every C>0 and c≥1, does some propositional tautology φ have shortest Frege proof size s_F(φ)>C(|φ|+2)ᶜ?
cards.definitions: Use explicitly written Boolean formulas over propositional variables, negation ¬ and material implication →. Fix the axiom schemes A→(B→A), (A→(B→C))→((A→B)→(A→C)), and (¬B→¬A)→(A→B), where A,B,C may be replaced uniformly within an instance by any formulas. A proof is a finite sequence of formulas, each either an instance of one of these schemes or inferred from two earlier lines A and A→B by modus ponens. Its last line is φ. There are no undischarged assumptions and no extension rule introducing abbreviations for other formulas. Previously derived lines may be reused arbitrarily. Intermediate formulas may have arbitrary depth and length; there is no independent cap on a line’s size. Variables not occurring in φ may occur in ordinary axiom instances and inference lines. A tautology is a formula true under every Boolean assignment. Fix a standard binary encoding with variable indices in binary and explicitly encoded connectives, delimiters and inference references. The input size |φ| and the proof size are their full bit lengths, including every repeated formula occurrence. The minimum over all such proofs is s_F(φ). Standard finite Frege presentations are polynomially equivalent, so polynomial boundedness is independent of this choice of basis. The question concerns existence of proofs, without a uniform algorithm to generate either the hard tautologies or their shortest proofs.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that no one polynomial bounds the minimum Frege proof size of every tautology, or refute this by proving a universal bound s_F(φ)≤C(|φ|+2)ᶜ for fixed C,c. A fixed-degree lower bound, a lower bound for a restricted subsystem, or hardness of searching for proofs is not a complete affirmative answer. An explicit efficiently generated hard family would be a stronger form of a positive solution, but is not required by the quantified statement.
cards.why: A defining lower-bound problem for formal reasoning. It asks whether an elementary, robust and powerful language of efficiently checkable proofs necessarily fails to certify some short tautologies with polynomial-size derivations.

importance.reason: A central unresolved step in the Cook–Reckhow program, beyond the systems for which current general lower-bound methods succeed.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No unconditional superpolynomial lower bound for unrestricted Frege proof size was found in the checked primary sources. The April 2026 tree-like result has a line-size cap, the formalization result concerns bounded-depth proofs, and the June 2026 algebraic result does not translate into the required propositional lower bound.

context_blocks.text: Frege systems formalize ordinary propositional deduction with finitely many rule patterns. A proof may introduce a useful intermediate lemma, combine it with other lemmas and reuse it later. Each step is easy to check syntactically. The open question asks whether this familiar form of deduction must sometimes produce certificates whose size exceeds every polynomial in the statement being proved.

The distinction between the size of a statement and the number of its variables matters. A formula on n variables may itself have exponential length in n. An exponential lower bound expressed only in n can therefore be small relative to the actual input. This card compares the complete proof encoding directly with |φ|, and counts the sizes of all lines rather than treating a very large intermediate formula as a single unit of cost.

Cook and Reckhow placed these questions in a general theory of efficiently checkable proof systems. There exists some polynomially bounded propositional proof system if and only if NP=coNP. Consequently, NP≠coNP would imply a positive answer here. The reverse implication is not established: proving that this particular proof language is inefficient would leave open the possibility that a different language provides short certificates for every tautology.

Short certificates and efficient discovery are separate issues. A failed search through proofs of length at most a million says nothing about all longer proofs, and exponential running time for one search strategy does not establish a lower bound on the shortest proof. Even a universal polynomial size bound would be an existence theorem; it would not by itself supply a polynomial-time algorithm that finds those proofs.

The pigeonhole principle explains why lower bounds for weaker systems have not directly extended to Frege. Its propositional encoding asserts that n+1 pigeons cannot be injected into n holes. Although the familiar encoding requires exponentially large resolution refutations, Buss proved in 1987 that it has polynomial-size Frege proofs. The stronger system can organize counting arguments that clause-by-clause resolution cannot express economically.

Wigderson’s textbook records the unrestricted lower bound as Open Problem 6.10, after surveying systems that already admit strong lower bounds. Frege permits arbitrary Boolean formulas as intermediate assertions. Removing a fixed-depth restriction therefore changes the available reasoning, even if the final tautologies are shallow. A theorem about bounded-depth Frege must control all proofs allowed by its depth bound; it does not control proofs that use deeper intermediate lemmas.

A substantial 2026 result by de Rezende, Engström, Ghannane and Risse gives superpolynomial refutation-length lower bounds for tree-like Frege with bounded line size, including a stronger semantic version. Their explicit families contain formulas for which almost every sampled instance is hard under the prescribed cap. The result is useful because the restricted systems can still efficiently handle several standard combinatorial benchmarks.

The line cap is essential to interpreting that theorem. Without such a cap, ordinary tree-like Frege polynomially simulates general Frege. The usual simulation can enlarge intermediate formulas, however, so it does not preserve the restriction used by the new lower bound. In the semantic setting, sufficiently large lines can even package a whole inconsistent input at once. The paper explicitly explains this obstruction to transferring its theorem to unrestricted Frege.

Davis and Robere’s April 2026 work studies another layer: short proofs of statements asserting that certain bounded-depth proofs must be long. They show that a relatively weak system, Res(log), can formalize strong bounded-depth Frege lower bounds in the specified parameter regime. This is progress on the complexity of proving lower bounds themselves, while the underlying lower-bound target retains restrictions on depth and line size.

Alekseev’s June 2026 journal paper gives exponential bit-size lower bounds for a powerful algebraic system with extension variables. It emphasizes that its Binary Value Principle input is not the corresponding translation of a polynomial-size propositional CNF. Thus the algebraic theorem does not establish the propositional Frege lower bound, despite the strength of the algebraic proof system on suitable translations.

Extended Frege is a separate, stronger target elsewhere in the catalogue: it adds variables naming previously written computations. A lower bound for Extended Frege would imply one for Frege, whereas a Frege lower bound need not survive those abbreviations. The present question is already a central obstacle because it asks for a limitation on broad propositional reasoning with unrestricted intermediate formulas and unrestricted reuse of lemmas.

cards.title: Do p-optimal propositional proof systems exist?
cards.formal: Does there exist a Cook–Reckhow proof system P for propositional tautologies such that, for every Cook–Reckhow proof system Q for the same tautologies, there is a deterministic polynomial-time translation t_Q satisfying P(t_Q(π))=Q(π) for every finite binary proof string π?
cards.why: Asks whether one efficiently checkable proof formalism can efficiently absorb every other such formalism.
