cards.title: Optimal explicit pseudorandom generators for read-once branching programs
cards.formal: Do there exist absolute constants C,D and a uniform family of generators G_{n,w,p}:{0,1}^s→{0,1}^n, for all integers n,w≥2 and p≥1, with s≤C(log_2 n+log_2 w+p), such that |Pr_{u uniform in {0,1}^s}[B(G_{n,w,p}(u))=1]−Pr_{z uniform in {0,1}^n}[B(z)=1]|≤2^(−p) for every length-n, width-at-most-w ordered read-once branching program B? Require a single deterministic algorithm that, given n,w,p,u and an output position i, computes G_{n,w,p}(u)_i using at most D(log_2 n+log_2 w+p) work bits and time (nw·2^p)^D.
cards.definitions: An ordered read-once branching program has layers V_0,…,V_n, each containing at most w states, a designated initial state in V_0, and an accepting subset of V_n. For each layer i−1, each state has one outgoing edge labeled 0 and one labeled 1 to V_i. On input z, the program follows the edge labeled z_i at step i and accepts exactly when the final state is accepting. Different edges may merge; neither regularity nor permutation transitions are required. The order is the fixed order z_1,…,z_n. Programs may be arbitrary nonuniform objects, but the generator cannot inspect their descriptions. The parameters and seed are read-only inputs to the generator algorithm, and the output bit is written separately; all work space, counters and intermediate storage are counted. Seed length is a computable function of the parameters within the stated resources. Uniform seeds induce an ordinary probability distribution, without signed or externally assigned weights. Set ε=2^(−p); this dyadic formulation gives the usual O(log(nw/ε)) target for arbitrary positive error by rounding down to a smaller dyadic tolerance.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: An optimal generator would remove randomness from logarithmic-space computation and identify how little entropy suffices to fool every small-memory streaming computation. The question joins explicit constructions, space complexity and the gap between real distributions and useful signed approximations.

importance.reason: A central constructive route to L=BPL, with optimal nonconstructive seed length known and a persistent gap for uniform space-efficient generators despite advances in restricted and weighted models.

Cheng and Hoza show that suitable logspace hitting sets imply L=BPL and analyze stronger reductions toward ordinary PRGs; the journal version appears on 20 September 2022.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. ECCC TR26-064 revision 3 explicitly retains the optimal general PRG target and the log-squared barrier. Its new generator is weighted; the July TR26-123 result is restricted to permutation programs. This card requires one ordinary, program-independent distribution family and optimal seed length as well as optimal work space.

context_blocks.text: The program processes a long stream while remembering only its current state. Width w corresponds to about log_2 w bits of memory; length n is the number of random bits it can inspect. A pseudorandom generator replaces that long random stream with the deterministic expansion of a much shorter genuinely random seed. The requirement is simultaneous: the same generated distribution must fool every permitted program, even though their transition tables may be entirely different.

There is no information-theoretic obstacle to the seed-length target. After padding to w states, the number of programs is at most w·2^w·w^(2nw). Choose a list of independent uniform n-bit strings and use a uniformly chosen list position as the seed. A concentration bound and union bound show that a list of O(ε^(−2)(nw log w+w)) strings suffices to approximate every acceptance probability. Indexing that list takes O(log n+log w+log(1/ε)) bits. The argument does not tell us how to generate its entries in the tiny workspace required here.

The computational payoff is direct. Fix an input to a bounded-error logarithmic-space randomized machine and view its evolution on random bits as a polynomial-length, polynomial-width branching program. A logarithmic seed permits enumeration of all seeds, regeneration of individual pseudorandom bits and counting accepting runs within logarithmic space. With constant error small enough to preserve the acceptance gap, this would prove L=BPL. The card asks for a uniform generator, which is a particular strong route to that complexity-class equality.

Nisan’s construction gives seed length O(log n·log(nw/ε)). For polynomial width and constant error this is O(log²n), so reaching the target would remove an entire logarithmic factor. The difficulty is generating a universally useful sample space in little space, rather than merely showing that some sample space exists. Even considerable improvements for simpler transition structures need not survive arbitrary merging of states.

Weighted pseudorandom generators relax the distribution requirement. They approximate acceptance by a weighted sum of program evaluations, with weights that may be negative. Hoza’s RANDOM 2021 construction attains seed length O(log²n+log(1/ε)) for width-n, length-n programs, improving the dependence on small error. Such weighted estimates can support deterministic simulation, but negative mass cannot be sampled as an ordinary probability distribution over the generated strings.

Cheng and Wu’s SODA 2026 work improves weighted generators across width and error regimes. Chen, Cohen, Doron, Khaskelberg and Ta-Shma’s May 2026 revision improves error reduction and the dependence on the input alphabet. It still constructs a weighted object. Its discussion credits Cheng and Hoza’s earlier reduction showing that sufficiently good ordinary-generator dependence on alphabet size and error would break the log-squared barrier. That implication does not turn the newly constructed weighted generator into an ordinary one.

The role of hitting sets provides another useful distinction. A hitting set ensures that an accepting string is included when the accepting fraction is sufficiently large; it does not directly approximate that fraction. Cheng and Hoza prove that sufficiently strong logspace hitting sets nevertheless imply two-sided logspace derandomization through a more involved reduction. Their results explain why a derandomization theorem need not arrive packaged as the universal probability distribution requested here.

Cohen, Doron and Goldgraber’s July 2026 paper gives an ordinary generator for permutation programs with seed O((log w+log(1/ε))log n), by a new analysis of the INW generator. In this subclass each symbol acts bijectively on the states between layers. The result has optimal logarithmic dependence on length when width and error are fixed, but the permutation promise excludes the arbitrary state merging allowed in this card.

cards.title: Does deterministic logarithmic space equal bounded-error randomized logarithmic space?
cards.formal: Is L=BPL? Equivalently, for every language S⊆{0,1}* decided with two-sided error at most 1/3 by a uniform randomized Turing machine using O(log(n+2)) work space and polynomial time on inputs of length n, is there a uniform deterministic Turing machine deciding S with O(log(n+2)) work space?
cards.definitions: The machines have a finite description, a read-only two-way input tape, and a fixed finite number of work tapes over a fixed finite alphabet. Space counts all visited work-tape cells; the input tape is excluded. A randomized machine receives independent fair coin outcomes one at a time, without a freely rereadable random tape: an outcome must be stored in counted work space to be remembered. It halts with ACCEPT or REJECT on every input and every random tape within K(n+2)^c steps and uses at most K log_2(n+2) work cells, for some constants K,c depending only on the machine. For each input x, acceptance probability is at least 2/3 if x∈S and at most 1/3 if x∉S. This is a language problem with no promise excluding intermediate-probability inputs. A deterministic decider must halt and give the correct answer on every input; any halting deterministic logarithmic-space decider has polynomially many configurations and hence polynomial running time. Both classes are uniform and have no advice. The deterministic machine and its space constant may depend on S. The equality does not demand a computable compiler transforming arbitrary machine descriptions, nor a particular pseudorandom-generator construction.

context_blocks.text: A logarithmic-space computation can maintain indices and counters while remembering only a small part of the input. Randomness lets it explore many possible choices without storing all of them. The equality asks whether this apparent extra power disappears when the required output is only a bounded-error decision about the input.

The memory convention is central. Fresh random outcomes can be read once; a machine cannot revisit an arbitrarily long random string without paying for its storage or reconstructing it. Conversely, the deterministic simulator is allowed a different constant in its logarithmic-space bound. The question concerns equality of language classes, not identical execution traces.

Saks and Zhou gave a deterministic simulation using O(log^(3/2) n) space. Hoza improved the bound to O(log^(3/2) n / sqrt(log log n)), with the expression understood asymptotically. These bounds are substantially below squared logarithmic space but remain above a constant multiple of log n.

The 2026 work of Chen, Cohen, Doron, Khaskelberg and Ta-Shma improves error reduction for weighted pseudorandom generators. Its revised account distinguishes weighted generators from ordinary generators and attributes the relevant arity/error connection to Cheng and Hoza. Those parameter improvements do not establish the equality of classes asked here.

The catalogue separately contains a concrete optimal-generator problem for read-once branching programs. Such a construction can have consequences for logarithmic-space derandomization, but the language-class equality does not prescribe that particular construction. This completed card retains the original TCS-0026 identity and Wigderson reference while making the computation and error models explicit.

cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with the stated model, domains, promises and quantifiers. A conditional theorem settles only its conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof matching the full target.

importance.reason: A central derandomization question with a resource regime and known techniques distinct from P=BPP. Specialist work on space-bounded pseudorandomness, including 2026 weighted-generator results, documents continuing interest. The class equality merits a full card even alongside a more specific generator-construction target.

cards.title: Optimal deterministic restricted-isometry matrices
cards.formal: Do there exist universal constants C,B,b>0 and a deterministic algorithm which, for every pair of integers N≥2 and 2≤s≤N, outputs in at most B N^b bit operations a rational m×N matrix A, with m≤C s ln(eN/s), such that (2/3)‖x‖₂²≤‖Ax‖₂²≤(4/3)‖x‖₂² for every real vector x∈ℝ^N with at most s nonzero coordinates?
cards.definitions: The input consists of N and s in binary. The output is an explicit list of all entries of A, each encoded as a signed integer numerator and positive integer denominator in binary. Its total encoding length must also be at most B N^b. Time is ordinary deterministic Turing-machine bit complexity, polynomial in N; randomness, advice and unit-cost exact real arithmetic are unavailable. The row count m is a positive integer chosen by the algorithm. The same constants and algorithm work for all allowed pairs N,s. The norm is Euclidean, and the displayed inequalities concern squared norms. They define restricted isometry of order s and distortion δ=1/3. The condition must hold simultaneously for every support of size at most s and every real choice of coefficients on that support. No probability over supports or signals is permitted. The natural logarithm and the factor e ensure a nonzero expression when s is close to N. The omitted case s=1 is trivial and can be handled by a single row of ones.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a deterministic algorithm satisfying all the uniform dimension, encoding, time and restricted-isometry requirements, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A negative result conditional on a complexity assumption must state it. An existence proof, a construction using random bits, success for most sparse signals, or a deterministic construction with a larger asymptotic row count does not settle the stated question.
cards.why: A central gap between random existence and efficient explicit construction, with direct consequences for uniform sparse recovery and for how pseudorandomness controls exponentially many spectral constraints.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No polynomial-time deterministic construction with the required uniform optimal row bound was found in the checked sources. Optimal randomized row counts, restricted parameter regimes and coherence guarantees are recorded as partial progress.

context_blocks.text: Suppose an unknown vector has N coordinates but only s of them matter. A measurement matrix replaces the vector by m linear measurements. Sparsity allows m to be much smaller than N, but the matrix must preserve every possible sparse direction if the measuring device is to work uniformly. The question asks whether a short, guaranteed measurement design can be computed without random choices.

The restricted-isometry requirement has a concrete spectral interpretation. For every set S of at most s column indices, all eigenvalues of A_SᵀA_S must lie between 2/3 and 4/3. Thus columns must behave almost orthogonally in every small group. Checking only individual column lengths, only pairs of columns, or a large collection of sampled test vectors leaves many of these simultaneous constraints untested.

This condition supports stable sparse recovery. If a matrix has restricted isometry of order 2t with distortion 1/3, then two different t-sparse signals cannot have identical measurements: their difference has at most 2t nonzero coordinates. Standard recovery theorems also give robust reconstruction by ℓ₁ minimization. The distinction between order t and order 2t is necessary; injectivity for t-sparse differences alone would not compare arbitrary t-sparse signals.

Random independent Bernoulli or Gaussian matrices attain m=O(s log(eN/s)) for fixed distortion, and matching row lower bounds make this the optimal order for s≥2. Rao’s paper summarizes this benchmark and improves the amount of randomness needed to attain it. The unresolved resource in the card is therefore deterministic construction time, rather than whether matrices with the desired geometric property exist.

Requiring rational output does not destroy the random benchmark. For example, choose the number of rows to be a perfect square t² within a constant factor of a sufficiently large target value, and use independent entries ±1/t. This keeps the usual normalized Bernoulli construction while giving an exact, short binary description of every entry. The real difficulty is choosing all the signs deterministically with a proof that every sparse direction is preserved.

One basic deterministic analysis bounds the coherence μ, the largest absolute inner product between two unit columns. Gershgorin’s theorem then gives restricted-isometry constant at most (s−1)μ. When μ is about 1/√m, this argument certifies only s on the order of √m. This is a limitation of that sufficient-condition analysis, commonly called the square-root bottleneck, rather than an impossibility theorem for deterministic matrices.

Bourgain, Dilworth, Ford, Konyagin and Kutzarova broke that bottleneck in a restricted parameter regime. Their explicit construction uses additive-combinatorial and exponential-sum estimates to control interactions beyond pairwise coherence. It is a major proof that deterministic analysis can go further, but its small exponent improvement does not reach the optimal s log(eN/s) row count uniformly in N and s.

Rao’s construction achieves the optimal row order with O(s log(N/s) log s) random bits in the sparse parameter regime discussed in the paper. Its proof extends the Hanson–Wright inequality to biased distributions. Reducing the seed length makes progress toward explicit construction, but enumerating all seeds can still take far more than polynomial time, and recognizing a successful seed is a separate issue.

The inherited 2025 paper of Fickus and Lake studies highly symmetric equiangular tight frames, which minimize coherence. It analyzes their minimal dependent column sets through regular simplices and designs. Such structure is informative in both directions: a dependent set of r columns immediately prevents restricted isometry of order r with distortion less than one. Optimal pairwise geometry alone does not guarantee the higher-order property.

cards.context:
Suppose an unknown vector has N coordinates but only s of them matter. A measurement matrix replaces the vector by m linear measurements. Sparsity allows m to be much smaller than N, but the matrix must preserve every possible sparse direction if the measuring device is to work uniformly. The question asks whether a short, guaranteed measurement design can be computed without random choices.

The restricted-isometry requirement has a concrete spectral interpretation. For every set S of at most s column indices, all eigenvalues of A_SᵀA_S must lie between 2/3 and 4/3. Thus columns must behave almost orthogonally in every small group. Checking only individual column lengths, only pairs of columns, or a large collection of sampled test vectors leaves many of these simultaneous constraints untested.

This condition supports stable sparse recovery. If a matrix has restricted isometry of order 2t with distortion 1/3, then two different t-sparse signals cannot have identical measurements: their difference has at most 2t nonzero coordinates. Standard recovery theorems also give robust reconstruction by ℓ₁ minimization. The distinction between order t and order 2t is necessary; injectivity for t-sparse differences alone would not compare arbitrary t-sparse signals.

Random independent Bernoulli or Gaussian matrices attain m=O(s log(eN/s)) for fixed distortion, and matching row lower bounds make this the optimal order for s≥2. Rao’s paper summarizes this benchmark and improves the amount of randomness needed to attain it. The unresolved resource in the card is therefore deterministic construction time, rather than whether matrices with the desired geometric property exist.

Requiring rational output does not destroy the random benchmark. For example, choose the number of rows to be a perfect square t² within a constant factor of a sufficiently large target value, and use independent entries ±1/t. This keeps the usual normalized Bernoulli construction while giving an exact, short binary description of every entry. The real difficulty is choosing all the signs deterministically with a proof that every sparse direction is preserved.

One basic deterministic analysis bounds the coherence μ, the largest absolute inner product between two unit columns. Gershgorin’s theorem then gives restricted-isometry constant at most (s−1)μ. When μ is about 1/√m, this argument certifies only s on the order of √m. This is a limitation of that sufficient-condition analysis, commonly called the square-root bottleneck, rather than an impossibility theorem for deterministic matrices.

Bourgain, Dilworth, Ford, Konyagin and Kutzarova broke that bottleneck in a restricted parameter regime. Their explicit construction uses additive-combinatorial and exponential-sum estimates to control interactions beyond pairwise coherence. It is a major proof that deterministic analysis can go further, but its small exponent improvement does not reach the optimal s log(eN/s) row count uniformly in N and s.

Rao’s construction achieves the optimal row order with O(s log(N/s) log s) random bits in the sparse parameter regime discussed in the paper. Its proof extends the Hanson–Wright inequality to biased distributions. Reducing the seed length makes progress toward explicit construction, but enumerating all seeds can still take far more than polynomial time, and recognizing a successful seed is a separate issue.

The inherited 2025 paper of Fickus and Lake studies highly symmetric equiangular tight frames, which minimize coherence. It analyzes their minimal dependent column sets through regular simplices and designs. Such structure is informative in both directions: a dependent set of r columns immediately prevents restricted isometry of order r with distortion less than one. Optimal pairwise geometry alone does not guarantee the higher-order property.

For a simple illustration, the m+1 unit vertices of a regular simplex in ℝ^m have small and equal pairwise inner products, yet their sum is zero. Their coefficient vector of all ones is therefore a nonzero sparse kernel vector. The example explains why an attractive frame construction must be accompanied by control over all relevant column subsets, not just a calculation of coherence.

The all-parameter formulation also matters. The identity matrix handles s comparable to N, while many explicit algebraic constructions work only along particular dimension sequences or for specified sparsity ranges. A resolution must cover the intermediate sparse regimes with one polynomial-time procedure. Likewise, statistical recovery guarantees and ℓ₁-norm versions of restricted isometry answer different geometric questions.

cards.title: Two-source extraction at log n plus constant entropy
cards.formal: Do a constant C and a deterministic algorithm running in poly(n) time exist that compute E_n:{0,1}^n×{0,1}^n→{0,1} with |Pr[E_n(X,Y)=1]−1/2|≤0.01 for every pair of independent sources X,Y of min-entropy at least log₂n+C?
cards.definitions: The algorithm receives n and the two n-bit strings, and defines one function for every n≥1. A source is any probability distribution on {0,1}^n; its min-entropy is −log₂(max_x Pr[X=x]). Independence means the joint law is the product of the two marginal distributions. For n where the entropy threshold exceeds n there are no eligible sources. No auxiliary uniform seed, advice or distribution description is supplied. The constants and time polynomial are universal.

context_blocks.text: Two independent weak sources can contain much randomness while neither source by itself yields even one predictably unbiased bit. The target reaches the entropy threshold permitted by a random truth table with a polynomial-time evaluable function.

cards.definitions: A generator G takes the output-length parameter 1ⁿ and a uniformly random seed s∈{0,1}^{ℓ(n)}, and deterministically outputs G(1ⁿ,s)∈{0,1}ⁿ. For a Boolean test circuit D:{0,1}ⁿ→{0,1}, its distinguishing advantage is |Pr_s[D(G(1ⁿ,s))=1]−Pr_r[D(r)=1]|, where r is uniform in {0,1}ⁿ and the two probabilities use independent uniform experiments. To fool a class means this advantage is bounded by a specified error for every test in that class. The source’s target has ℓ(n) on the n^ε scale, generator running time on the n^(1+ε) scale, and linear-size Boolean circuits as tests; constants may depend on the fixed ε. The algorithm generates the entire n-bit output, so merely writing it already costs Ω(n) in a bit-output model. Non-uniform tests may have unrelated circuit descriptions at different lengths. Cryptographic hypotheses here include the existence of one-way functions: efficiently computable functions whose random outputs are hard to invert with significant success. The source excludes replacing them by hardness against non-uniform nondeterministic or Merlin–Arthur computation, but does not enumerate all allowed other assumptions. Its general Definition 2.1 makes error a parameter; the paragraph specifying this ingredient does not supply its final value.
cards.answer_criterion: A completed target must state an independent permitted hardness hypothesis, precise generator and test models, distinguishing error and uniform resource bounds, then establish the construction or a matching impossibility statement. A construction assuming one-way functions does not answer the assumption-removal request. Unconditional existence and either full derandomization conclusion are not silently substituted for the inherited PRG ingredient.

context_blocks.title: Nearly the cost of writing the output
context_blocks.text: A short seed supplies much less randomness than the n output bits suggest. The generator’s output must nevertheless look random to every linear-size test. As ε approaches zero, the requested n^(1+ε) generation time approaches the linear cost of producing those bits.

context_blocks.title: Why the tests matter
context_blocks.text: A generator whose final output bit is always zero is detected by a test that reads that bit: the acceptance probabilities differ by 1/2. A valid generator must avoid every test allowed by its circuit class, not just match the frequency of zeros and ones across the output.

cards.title: Is k-Clique fixed-parameter tractable, equivalently FPT=W[1]?
cards.formal: Do there exist a total computable function f:ℕ→ℕ, a constant c, and one deterministic algorithm that decides whether an n-vertex graph contains a k-clique in time at most f(k)(n+2)ᶜ on every input? Equivalently, is FPT=W[1]?
cards.definitions: An instance is a finite simple undirected graph G on [n], encoded by its adjacency matrix, and an integer k with 0≤k≤n, encoded in binary. A k-clique is a set of k distinct vertices for which every pair is an edge; k=0 is a yes-instance. Inputs with k>n are rejected immediately, and other malformed inputs are rejected. The parameter is k, not treewidth, degree, or the size of a supplied decomposition. Running time counts deterministic Turing-machine steps on the full input. Constants and the function f may be arbitrary but must be fixed independently of n; the exponent c must also be independent of k. FPT comprises parameterized decision problems solvable in f(k)Nᶜ time, where N is their input encoding length. One equivalent definition of W[1] is the class of parameterized problems reducible to k-Clique by a deterministic f(k)Nᶜ-time many-one reduction whose output parameter is bounded by a computable function of k alone. This is the standard parameterized reduction convention under which Clique is W[1]-complete. No randomness, advice, or promise about G is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This is the principal boundary question for algorithms whose exponential difficulty is confined to a small parameter. It determines the force of thousands of parameterized hardness reductions and separates efficient small-solution search from algorithms whose input-size exponent grows with the solution size.

importance.reason: The defining unresolved tractability separation of parameterized complexity, with Clique as a precise and widely used complete problem.

progress.text: Downey and Fellows develop the W-hierarchy and the completeness framework that makes parameterized Clique a canonical target for the FPT-versus-W[1] question.
ETH-based reductions establish the stronger conditional obstruction to f(k)n^{o(k)} Clique algorithms; the textbook develops this in its parameterized lower-bound chapters.
Bottesch studies structural and relativization evidence concerning FPT and W[1], explicitly distinguishing this conjecture from P≠NP. No unrelativized separation is proved.
Lin proves constant-factor FPT approximation of Clique W[1]-hard, transferring the same central assumption to approximate search.
Chen, Feng, Laekhanukit, and Liu give a simpler combinatorial construction for the k^{o(1)} parameterized Clique inapproximability bound.
Abboud, Fischer, and Shechter improve combinatorial fixed-k Clique running times by logarithmic factors. The Algorithmica publication of 22 May 2026 retains dependence on k in the exponent of n.

cards.status_note: Explicitly presented as the central open conjecture in Bottesch’s primary paper and the parameterized-algorithms textbook. Research through 10 September 2026 located no proof of equality or separation. Conditional lower bounds and improved fixed-k algorithms are recorded with their distinct quantifiers.

context_blocks.text: For each fixed k, exhaustive search over vertex subsets decides Clique in polynomial time. The exponent grows with k, so this observation gives a different kind of tractability: increasing the target clique size can increase the power of n in the running time. The question asks whether all dependence on k can instead be moved into one multiplicative function. For example, 2^{2^k}n³ meets the requested form, while n^{k/10} does not.

The unrestricted Clique problem is NP-complete, but this alone cannot rule out fixed-parameter tractability. The permitted function f can grow much faster than any polynomial when k grows with n. If P=NP then Clique is certainly FPT; the converse implication is not known. Thus FPT≠W[1] is a stronger separation conjecture than P≠NP in the direction currently proved.

Parameterized reductions keep the output parameter controlled solely by the original parameter. Since Clique is complete under these reductions, an FPT Clique algorithm would solve every W[1] problem in FPT time. This is why a W[1]-hardness proof is useful evidence against a parameterized algorithm for another problem. The evidence is conditional on the separation being true, even when the reduction theorem itself is unconditional.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis supplies a stronger quantitative barrier: it rules out f(k)n^{o(k)} algorithms for Clique. That conclusion excludes FPT, but uses an assumption that is itself open. Matrix-multiplication methods and improved combinatorial methods accelerate Clique for fixed k while leaving an exponent that grows with the parameter. Their progress does not eliminate the central gap.

Approximation has become another way to measure the reach of the conjecture. Lin proves that even fixed-factor parameterized approximation of Clique is W[1]-hard. Later constructions strengthen the factor and simplify the reductions. These results enlarge the consequences of a separation; they do not prove FPT≠W[1].

cards.title: Does deterministic 3-SAT have a positive optimal exponential rate?
cards.formal: Is there a constant c>0 such that, for every deterministic algorithm A that correctly decides every 3-CNF satisfiability instance, and every constant d≥0, A does not have worst-case running time O(2^{cn}L^d)? Here n is the number of variables and L is the full binary input length. This is the deterministic Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH).
cards.definitions: A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of explicitly listed clauses, each containing at most three literals xᵢ or ¬xᵢ. Satisfiability means existence of a Boolean assignment satisfying all clauses. Variables are relabeled consecutively; n counts the distinct variables actually present, and L includes all literal indices, signs, delimiters, and repetitions. An empty clause is unsatisfiable and an empty conjunction is satisfiable. Algorithms are uniform deterministic Turing machines with no advice or oracles; they must halt and answer exactly on all inputs, with no promise about density, solution count, or distribution. Define s₃=inf{α≥0 : some such algorithm runs in O(2^{αn}L^d) for a fixed d}. ETH asserts s₃>0. The excluded exponent c is a single constant independent of the algorithm. The polynomial exponent and hidden constant may depend on the algorithm, but not the instance. Polynomial input factors allow the complete formula to be read even if clauses are repeated many times. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: ETH is the central hypothesis for ruling out subexponential exact algorithms and many fixed-parameter speedups. It turns the qualitative P versus NP question into a quantitative claim that can be transferred through carefully sized reductions.

importance.reason: A foundational quantitative hardness hypothesis underlying exact, parameterized, graph, and geometric algorithm lower bounds.

progress.text: Impagliazzo and Paturi formalize the exponential rates of k-SAT and study their relations. These rates remain conjectural lower bounds against unrestricted algorithms.
The authors’ IPEC survey describes how exact satisfiability complexity connects to parameterized complexity, circuit lower bounds, and data structures.
The parameterized-algorithms textbook states ETH as a positive infimum, develops sparsification, and derives consequences including FPT≠W[1]. It distinguishes randomized variants.
Liu gives a deterministic 3-SAT upper bound with base 1.32793 using branching and generalized covering codes. The saving leaves a positive exponential rate.

Aggarwal, Gupta, Morolia, and Zhang obtain new lattice approximation hardness from ETH or randomized ETH, depending on the target problem and reduction. Their ICALP paper continues to treat these as hypotheses and separates them from Gap-ETH.

cards.status_note: The cited foundational and 2026 conference sources treat ETH as an open hypothesis. Checked through 10 September 2026. This formulation is uniform, deterministic, and a positive-infimum assertion; randomized, nonuniform, gap, and stronger all-width hypotheses are distinct.

context_blocks.text: NP-completeness describes the possibility of polynomial-time algorithms and does not itself impose a positive exponential rate. Even if P differs from NP, a running time such as 2^{√n} remains possible for 3-SAT. ETH asks for a stronger obstruction: some fixed amount of exponential work must remain unavoidable when complexity is measured by the number of Boolean choices.

That parameter must be preserved carefully by a reduction. An ordinary polynomial-time reduction may turn an n-variable formula into an instance of size n³, which can destroy a claimed exponential lower bound in the new parameter. Sparsification supplies a controlled disjunction of bounded-density formulas, allowing variables and clauses to be related without an arbitrary polynomial blowup. This is a main reason ETH can support sharp bounds across many problems.

The infimum over all algorithms matters. Excluding one 2^{o(n)} algorithm is the common informal wording, but the textbook explicitly keeps the stronger positive-infimum statement because the converse is unclear. ETH would be false if arbitrarily small constant exponents were attainable, even if the known algorithms depended on the desired exponent. A card that omitted this distinction would change the quantified question.

There are substantial deterministic improvements over trying all 2ⁿ assignments. Liu combines branching with derandomized local search to obtain a 1.32793ⁿ bound for 3-SAT, up to polynomial factors. Such an algorithm decreases an upper bound on s₃ while leaving it positive. Empirical solver success, promises of many solutions, and bounded-occurrence restrictions do not address worst-case unrestricted formulas.

ETH is weaker than SETH, whose optimal rates approach one as the fixed clause width grows. It also differs from randomized ETH and from Gap-ETH, which asks for hardness of distinguishing fully satisfiable formulas from formulas with a constant unsatisfied fraction. Recent lattice reductions illustrate the value of tracking these distinctions: some approximation hardness can be obtained from deterministic ETH, while other results use randomized ETH. They extend the consequences of assumptions without proving the assumptions.

cards.title: Unique Games: is near-satisfiability NP-hard to distinguish from low value?
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: For every pair of rational constants ε,δ>0 with ε+δ<1, does there exist an integer q≥2 such that it is NP-hard to distinguish Unique Games instances with $\operatorname{val}(G)\ge1-\varepsilon$ from instances with $\operatorname{val}(G)\le\delta$? Here q is the alphabet size, fixed independently of the input graph, and val(G) is the largest fraction of constraints simultaneously satisfied by any labeling.
cards.definitions: An instance has finitely many vertices and a nonempty explicit list E of directed edges between distinct vertices; repeated edges are allowed and counted separately. Every vertex receives a label in [q]={1,…,q}. An edge e=(u,v) carries an explicitly given permutation π_e:[q]→[q] and is satisfied exactly when π_e(ℓ(u))=ℓ(v). Thus val(G)=max_ℓ |{e satisfied by ℓ}|/|E|. There are no graph expansion or degree promises. NP-hardness means a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction from 3SAT mapping every satisfiable formula into the ≥1−ε case and every unsatisfiable formula into the ≤δ case. The reduction, its running-time exponent, and q may depend on ε,δ. Inputs with value strictly between the thresholds are outside the promise. The question is the NP-hardness proposition itself; P≠NP is needed when drawing the usual conclusion that no polynomial-time distinguishing algorithm exists. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: UGC would turn many conditional approximation thresholds into NP-hardness theorems and explain the optimality of a general SDP framework. Its very simple permutation constraints isolate a fundamental boundary between exact consistency, approximate consistency, and hardness amplification.

importance.reason: An organizing conjecture for approximation thresholds, with consequences for whole families of constraint satisfaction problems and strong connections to SDP algorithms, PCPs, and analysis.

progress.text: Khot proposes the conjecture. Perfect satisfiability is polynomial-time decidable; the conjectured hard regime has positive completeness error and an alphabet depending on both gap parameters.

Raghavendra gives a general SDP and rounding framework for fixed finite-domain CSPs and transfers SDP integrality gaps to Unique-Games-based hardness. Under UGC, its achievable thresholds are optimal up to any fixed accuracy, unless P=NP.

Arora, Barak, and Steurer give, for an absolute α>0, an exp(q n^(ε^α))-time algorithm finding a (1−ε^α)-satisfying labeling in a (1−ε)-satisfiable q-label instance on n vertices. In the small fixed-ε regime this is subexponential, but not polynomial.

The line of work proving the 2-to-2 Games Theorem yields NP-hardness of Unique Games at completeness 1/2 and arbitrarily small soundness. Khot’s exposition states this explicitly as Theorem 2.20; it leaves the near-one completeness of UGC unresolved.

The journal version of Dinur, Khot, Kindler, Minzer, and Safra’s second installment documents its role in the proof sequence, while retaining the full Unique Games statement as Conjecture 1.4. Its publication is not a new proof of full UGC.

context_blocks.text: Each constraint is locally simple: fixing either endpoint label determines exactly one compatible label at the other endpoint. Exact satisfiability of all constraints is decidable in polynomial time. Allowing a small fraction of constraints to fail changes the question sharply.

The conjecture says that an instance admitting an almost perfect assignment can nevertheless be hard to distinguish from one where every assignment fails almost everywhere. These are two promised regimes, rather than a request to compute the exact optimum. The alphabet is allowed to grow as the desired gap becomes more demanding. Indeed, a uniformly random labeling satisfies a 1/q fraction in expectation, so a soundness threshold below 1/q is impossible.

Raghavendra’s theorem connects such reductions to a general semidefinite-programming framework: under UGC, that framework achieves the approximation thresholds of fixed finite-domain constraint satisfaction problems, to arbitrary constant accuracy.

The strongest relevant hardness milestone must be read with its completeness parameter. The 2-to-2 Games Theorem implies hardness for Unique Games with value at least one half versus arbitrarily small value. It does not make the yes instances almost perfectly satisfiable. Raising completeness from one half to arbitrarily close to one is precisely a remaining gap relevant to this card.

Algorithmic progress also matters even when it is slower than polynomial time. Subexponential algorithms exploit spectral decompositions of the constraint graph, limiting what quantitative hardness reductions could establish. Because a polynomial reduction can enlarge the instance by a parameter-dependent power, these algorithms coexist with the NP-hardness conjecture.

cards.definitions: Use finite simple undirected d-regular graphs G=([n],E), n≥2 and d≥1, given explicitly by their adjacency matrices. Regular means that every vertex has exactly d neighbours; d is not a fixed constant or an extra promise. For nonempty S, ∂_G S is the set of edges with exactly one endpoint in S, and Φ_G(S)=|∂_G S|/(d|S|). Internal edges contribute twice to d|S| and zero to the boundary. This is normalized edge expansion, not the number of outside neighbours. The graph has no promised connectivity, geometry or spectral gap. The constants η,δ are chosen before the input; they are not parameters tending to zero with n. For δ=a/b in lowest terms, inputs have n a positive multiple of b, so exact set size has no rounding ambiguity. The YES and NO cases are disjoint since η<1/2; inputs meeting neither case have no required decision answer. NP-hardness means that for every language L with polynomially checkable witnesses, a deterministic polynomial-time map sends each x∈L to a YES graph and each x∉L to a NO graph. Equivalently, it suffices to supply such a reduction from Boolean satisfiability. Reduction constants and the polynomial exponent may depend on η and its chosen δ. The card fixes the unweighted regular-graph, exact-cardinality version of the imported question; weighted-volume, randomized-hardness and size-interval versions must be identified when cited.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves the stated NP-hardness for every η by choosing δ and giving a valid promise-preserving reduction. A negative resolution refutes this quantified hardness statement for some fixed η. Polynomial-time algorithms for every fixed δ at that η would refute the hardness claim under P≠NP; an algorithm alone must not be called an unconditional disproof of NP-hardness. Results restricted to special graph classes or allowing a different output set size do not automatically settle this formulation.

context_blocks.title: What expansion measures
context_blocks.text: Choose a vertex uniformly from S, then choose one of its neighbours uniformly. The probability of leaving S is exactly Φ_G(S). A set with expansion near zero is a group whose connections mostly remain inside it. Expansion near one means that almost every connection goes out. The promise asks whether one unusually insulated set exists at the specified size, or whether every set of that size is almost completely exposed.

context_blocks.title: Small means a fixed fraction
context_blocks.text: If δ=1/1000, the target has one thousand vertices in a million-vertex graph and one million vertices in a billion-vertex graph. Its size still grows linearly with n. Enumerating all sets of a fixed number of vertices therefore does not give a polynomial-time algorithm for the question. The order of constants also matters: δ may depend on the desired expansion gap η, and an algorithm for one convenient pair of constants would not refute the full hypothesis.

context_blocks.title: A sparse large cut can miss the issue
context_blocks.text: Take the disjoint union of two complete graphs on 50 vertices. Either whole component has expansion zero. Yet a two-vertex set contained in one component has expansion 48/49, and a two-vertex set split between the components has expansion one. Thus every set of the specified small size expands very well even though a larger zero-expansion cut exists. Optimizing over all sets up to half the graph can answer a different question from the exact small-size promise.

context_blocks.text: For a proposed set, its size and edge boundary are easy to count. The universal NO condition ranges over all sets of that size. The hypothesis asserts hardness even though YES and NO graphs are separated by a wide gap, with many intermediate graphs excluded by the promise. A graph expansion construction, a bound on one spectral parameter, or an algorithm with an uncontrolled change in set size is not automatically a distinguisher for this promise.

context_blocks.title: Connections and current boundary
context_blocks.text: Raghavendra and Steurer reduce small-set expansion to Unique Games, making this hypothesis a sufficient foundation for Unique Games hardness. Raghavendra, Steurer and Tulsiani relate it to a version of Unique Games with an additional expansion requirement and derive conditional hardness for graph partitioning and arrangement problems. This does not establish equivalence to unrestricted Unique Games in both directions. In August 2026, Lin, Mirrokni and Woodruff use a randomized, weighted, exact-volume variant to prove a sparse least-squares hardness result. Such an application assumes an SSE statement; it does not prove the statement itself, and its modeling conventions should not be silently transferred to this card. The checked sources leave the hypothesis unresolved.

cards.title: A constant improvement over factor 2 for unrelated-machine makespan
cards.formal: Does there exist a constant ε with 0<ε<1 and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm which, for every unrelated-machine scheduling instance, assigns all jobs to machines with makespan at most (2−ε)OPT?
cards.definitions: An instance consists of m≥1 machines, n≥0 independent jobs, and an explicitly given m×n matrix of processing times pᵢⱼ in the nonnegative rationals or ∞. Rational numerators and denominators are binary encoded; ∞ forbids an assignment. Every job has at least one finite processing time. A schedule is a function σ:{1,…,n}→{1,…,m} with p_{σ(j),j}<∞. Its makespan is Cmax(σ)=maxᵢ Σ_{j:σ(j)=i} pᵢⱼ, and OPT is the minimum of this quantity over all feasible schedules. Jobs are available at time zero, indivisible and processed without interruption on one machine; there are no precedence constraints or communication costs. Jobs assigned to one machine can run consecutively in any order. The algorithm must output σ, not merely an estimate of OPT. Its bit running time is polynomial in the entire input length. ε and the polynomial are independent of m, n and all processing times; no predictions or promises on matrix structure are supplied. Empty or zero-optimum instances require makespan zero. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A defining unresolved approximation barrier in scheduling. Beating two by any fixed constant would also imply a constant approximation for general Santa Claus allocation, while known relaxation gaps rule out a large family of straightforward proofs.

importance.reason: A decades-old central scheduling problem with a large hardness gap, robust LP barriers and formal consequences for fair allocation.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The full worst-case constant-improvement question remains open in the checked primary literature. The known 2−1/m ratio and prediction-assisted results have different quantifiers from the fixed-ε target. The 3/2 hardness is conditional on P≠NP.

context_blocks.text: Each job can have a completely different processing time on each machine. There need not be a single ranking from fastest to slowest machines, as in the related-machine model. The challenge is to balance total load while respecting which assignments are expensive or forbidden. Even when every job has an individually attractive machine, sending all jobs to their favorite machines can create a severe bottleneck.

Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos obtain a polynomial-time factor-2 approximation by rounding a fractional assignment. For a candidate makespan T, assignments with pᵢⱼ>T are forbidden; the relaxation divides each job fractionally among the remaining machines while bounding each machine’s fractional load by T. Their rounding can charge the overload to at most one additional job per machine. Since every eligible job fits individually within T, the resulting schedule has load at most 2T.

The same foundational work establishes NP-hardness of approximation below 3/2. This leaves a genuine gap: the known hardness is compatible with an algorithm of ratio 1.9, 1.75 or 1.5. Moreover, Shchepin and Vakhania improve the general guarantee to 2−1/m. That is strictly less than two for each finite number of machines, but it approaches two as m grows. The ε in this question must be one fixed positive constant, so this refinement is not a resolution.

A stronger relaxation uses configurations: a variable represents an entire subset of jobs that fits on one machine within T. This remembers much more local packing structure than individual fractional assignments. Nevertheless, Verschae and Wiese construct an integrality gap approaching two even when each job is eligible on at most two machines. Thus rounding this relaxation solely against its own optimum cannot prove a universal constant improvement. This is a limitation of the relaxation, not a hardness theorem for all algorithms.

Restricted assignment is a special case in which job j has one processing time pⱼ on all eligible machines. It is substantially more structured than arbitrary unrelated processing times. Bamas and coauthors obtain a polynomial-time (1.75+δ)-approximation for the further restriction to two finite job sizes. Their general two-value unrelated-machine result instead gives 2−1/nᵟ for fixed δ>0, whose improvement still depends on instance size. Neither guarantee extends to the full target here.

The same SODA 2024 paper gives a formal connection to the Santa Claus allocation problem, where indivisible resources must be distributed to maximize the least satisfied player’s additive value. A (2−1/α)-approximation for makespan, for constant α≥2, would yield an (α+δ)-approximation for general Santa Claus for any fixed δ>0. Thus even a small fixed improvement here would also resolve a major constant-factor approximation question in fair allocation.

Baba, Bampis and Mitropoulos’ June 2026 preprint studies predictions of assignments for heavy jobs. For accurate predictions their algorithm approaches factor one, while its worst-case guarantee with arbitrary prediction error remains two. This identifies valuable information that helps scheduling, but the classical question supplies no such information. A worst-case proof cannot assume that a learned assignment resembles an optimal schedule.

The fundamental issue is whether indivisibility forces an approximation barrier at two, or whether a stronger global argument can control the interactions that fractional rounding loses. Progress would clarify both the power of optimization relaxations and the complexity of balancing heterogeneous resources.

sentences: Unrelated-machine scheduling allows each job to have a different processing time on every machine.
The reviewed question asks for a deterministic polynomial-time approximation beating makespan factor two by one universal constant.
Assigning every job to its favorite machine can create a severe load bottleneck.

cards.context:
Each job can have a completely different processing time on each machine. There need not be a single ranking from fastest to slowest machines, as in the related-machine model. The challenge is to balance total load while respecting which assignments are expensive or forbidden. Even when every job has an individually attractive machine, sending all jobs to their favorite machines can create a severe bottleneck.

Lenstra, Shmoys and Tardos obtain a polynomial-time factor-2 approximation by rounding a fractional assignment. For a candidate makespan T, assignments with pᵢⱼ>T are forbidden; the relaxation divides each job fractionally among the remaining machines while bounding each machine’s fractional load by T. Their rounding can charge the overload to at most one additional job per machine. Since every eligible job fits individually within T, the resulting schedule has load at most 2T.

The same foundational work establishes NP-hardness of approximation below 3/2. This leaves a genuine gap: the known hardness is compatible with an algorithm of ratio 1.9, 1.75 or 1.5. Moreover, Shchepin and Vakhania improve the general guarantee to 2−1/m. That is strictly less than two for each finite number of machines, but it approaches two as m grows. The ε in this question must be one fixed positive constant, so this refinement is not a resolution.

A stronger relaxation uses configurations: a variable represents an entire subset of jobs that fits on one machine within T. This remembers much more local packing structure than individual fractional assignments. Nevertheless, Verschae and Wiese construct an integrality gap approaching two even when each job is eligible on at most two machines. Thus rounding this relaxation solely against its own optimum cannot prove a universal constant improvement. This is a limitation of the relaxation, not a hardness theorem for all algorithms.

Restricted assignment is a special case in which job j has one processing time pⱼ on all eligible machines. It is substantially more structured than arbitrary unrelated processing times. Bamas and coauthors obtain a polynomial-time (1.75+δ)-approximation for the further restriction to two finite job sizes. Their general two-value unrelated-machine result instead gives 2−1/nᵟ for fixed δ>0, whose improvement still depends on instance size. Neither guarantee extends to the full target here.

The same SODA 2024 paper gives a formal connection to the Santa Claus allocation problem, where indivisible resources must be distributed to maximize the least satisfied player’s additive value. A (2−1/α)-approximation for makespan, for constant α≥2, would yield an (α+δ)-approximation for general Santa Claus for any fixed δ>0. Thus even a small fixed improvement here would also resolve a major constant-factor approximation question in fair allocation.

Baba, Bampis and Mitropoulos’ June 2026 preprint studies predictions of assignments for heavy jobs. For accurate predictions their algorithm approaches factor one, while its worst-case guarantee with arbitrary prediction error remains two. This identifies valuable information that helps scheduling, but the classical question supplies no such information. A worst-case proof cannot assume that a learned assignment resembles an optimal schedule.

The fundamental issue is whether indivisibility forces an approximation barrier at two, or whether a stronger global argument can control the interactions that fractional rounding loses. Progress would clarify both the power of optimization relaxations and the complexity of balancing heterogeneous resources.

cards.title: Breaking factor two for precedence-constrained makespan
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant ε∈(0,1) and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, for every instance of P|prec|Cmax with an input number m of identical parallel machines, produces a feasible nonpreemptive schedule of makespan at most (2−ε)OPT?
cards.definitions: An input specifies n≥1 jobs, a positive integer processing time p_j for each job, a directed acyclic graph of precedence constraints, and a positive integer machine count m. All numbers are encoded in binary and the graph is given explicitly. The machine count is not fixed in advance; one may cap it at n because additional machines cannot help. A feasible schedule chooses a machine a_j∈{1,…,m} and a nonnegative start time s_j for every job. Job j occupies that machine continuously during [s_j,s_j+p_j), without preemption or migration. Intervals assigned to the same machine must be disjoint. For every precedence edge i→j, require s_j≥s_i+p_i. Every job can run on every machine and its processing time is independent of the chosen machine. There are no release dates, deadlines, communication delays, setup costs or extra resource constraints. The makespan is Cmax=max_j(s_j+p_j); OPT is the minimum over feasible schedules using the same m unit-speed machines. With integer processing times, an optimal schedule with integer start times exists, so the algorithm can output binary-encoded integer starts. Polynomial time is measured in the full input bit length, not in Σ_j p_j. The same fixed ε must apply for all n, all m, all processing times and all precedence DAGs. The algorithm receives the whole instance before constructing the schedule.
cards.answer_criterion: Give one such fixed ε and prove a polynomial-time (2−ε) guarantee for all inputs, or rule out every fixed improvement below two with any complexity assumptions explicitly stated. A bound 2−1/m does not supply a universal ε. Guarantees for fixed m, unit jobs only, special precedence orders, quasipolynomial running time, extra machines or faster processors do not prove the requested statement. A conditional hardness result based on a stronger conjecture must remain labelled conditional.
cards.why: Determine whether arbitrary precedence constraints allow a constant improvement over the classical factor-two makespan guarantee on identical machines.

importance.reason: A central long-standing approximation question in scheduling, connecting greedy critical-path analysis, global dependency structure and conditional hardness.

references.title: Inapproximability of Unique-Machine Precedence Scheduling for Unit-Length Jobs
references.authors: Venkatesan Guruswami; Xuandi Ren; Shaoxuan Tang
references.locator: v1, 29 July 2026; each job has one fixed eligible machine; introduction explicitly contrasts this with Graham’s identical-machine guarantee

cards.status_note: No polynomial-time fixed (2−ε) improvement found through 11 September 2026. Svensson’s factor-two hardness requires the specified possibly stronger Unique Games variant. Recent fixed-machine approximation schemes and exact unit-job algorithms have narrower scope, while July 2026 UMPS hardness imposes machine eligibility restrictions absent here.

context_blocks.text: Two basic obstructions limit how quickly dependent jobs can finish. Total work W=Σ_j p_j needs at least W/m time across m machines. A precedence chain must execute sequentially, so the length L of a longest weighted path is another lower bound. A schedule must manage both parallel throughput and the timely completion of jobs that unlock later work. Even with identical machines and no communication costs, these priorities can conflict.

Graham’s list scheduling follows a fixed priority order and starts available jobs whenever machines become free. A job is available once all its predecessors have finished. Its analysis gives Cmax≤W/m+(1−1/m)L, and hence Cmax≤(2−1/m)OPT. The bound approaches two as the machine count grows. Therefore the fact that each individual instance has a guarantee strictly below two does not resolve the constant improvement in this question.

A simple example shows why choosing priorities matters. Take m(m−1) independent unit jobs and one independent job of length m. If the long job comes last in the list, the units occupy all machines for m−1 time, and the final job finishes at 2m−1. An optimal schedule starts the long job immediately and runs the unit jobs on the other m−1 machines, finishing at time m. This proves a limitation of that list order, not hardness for every algorithm: the example has no precedence edges.

Classical NP-hardness excludes approximation factors below 4/3 unless P=NP, leaving room between that barrier and two. Svensson’s STOC 2010 work, published in 2011, connects the missing hardness to a different scheduling objective: minimizing total weighted completion time on one machine with precedences. Sufficiently strong hardness near factor two for that problem transfers to makespan on identical parallel machines, even with unit processing times.

Combined with Bansal and Khot’s hypothesis, the reduction gives hardness for every fixed factor below two. The hypothesis is a particular Unique Games variant with additional structure: near-perfect satisfiability on large subsets in the yes case and an expansion requirement in the no case. Svensson explicitly describes it as possibly stronger than the usual Unique Games conjecture. Thus this is substantial conditional evidence, but it should not be presented as a theorem following solely from P≠NP.

There has been strong progress when the number of machines is a fixed constant and jobs have unit length. Levey–Rothvoss initiate a line of approximation schemes based on hierarchy relaxations, followed by faster bounds. Das and Wiese provide a simpler quasipolynomial scheme by guessing selected jobs and time intervals and filling the remaining positions greedily. Their paper was published at ESA 2022, despite being uploaded to arXiv in January 2025. Its fixed-machine and running-time restrictions are essential.

Nederlof, Swennenhuis and Węgrzycki advance exact algorithms for unit jobs. Their bound (1+n/m)^{O(√(nm))} is subexponential when m=o(n), and they also give an exponential improvement when m is proportional to n. The work appeared at SODA 2025 and was published online in ACM Transactions on Algorithms in January 2026. Exactness is stronger than approximation, but these running times are not polynomial and the processing-time promise remains narrower than this card’s model.

Guruswami, Ren and Tang’s July 2026 preprint proves that even unit-length jobs can be hard to approximate within any constant when each job has one predetermined eligible machine. That extra restriction prevents the scheduler from freely distributing ready jobs. It is a different model, called unique-machine precedence scheduling, and its hardness transfers to certain communication-delay models. It does not contradict the factor-two guarantee available when every job may use any identical machine.

A fixed improvement below two would show that global information about the precedence graph can reliably overcome the worst interactions between chain length and machine utilization. A matching hardness theorem under a standard assumption would explain why a very old greedy guarantee remains near the limit of efficient scheduling. The question isolates that issue without combining it with heterogeneous machines, strategic reports, or communication delays.

cards.title: The minimax rate of sequential binary calibration
cards.formal: Determine C(T)=inf_A sup_B E[∑_{p∈P_A}|∑_{t:p_t=p}(y_t−p)|] up to universal multiplicative constants as the integer horizon T tends to infinity, in the finite-forecast sequential game below. The requested rate includes logarithmic factors.
cards.definitions: Before play, forecaster A selects a finite set P_A⊆[0,1], which may depend on T. Both players know this set and T. At each time t, A selects p_t∈P_A and adversary B selects y_t∈{0,1} simultaneously; neither sees the other’s current selection. Each may randomize using independent coins and the full history (p_s,y_s)_{s<t}, and after the round both selections become public. The infimum is over every such finite set and randomized forecaster, and the supremum is over all randomized adaptive adversaries. There is no computational restriction. The displayed sum measures unnormalized ℓ₁ calibration error and is finite; groups are defined by exact equality of predictions. Expectation is over both players’ coins.

context_blocks.text: Calibration asks whether forecasts agree with empirical frequencies on the rounds when each probability was announced. The minimax rate measures the unavoidable error in this requirement against an adaptive sequence of binary events.

The long-standing T^{2/3} upper bound has already been improved by a constant in the exponent. A lower bound strictly above √T is also known. Thus neither the old two-thirds barrier nor a square-root target is an appropriate new open question. The remaining problem is the optimal rate itself.

cards.why: A fundamental quantitative problem in sequential prediction, with consequences for calibrated learning and decision making.
cards.answer_criterion: Determine the stated minimax quantity up to universal multiplicative constants, including all logarithmic factors, with matching upper and lower bounds. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.

cards.title: Does P≠NP imply a samplable NP problem outside AvgP?
cards.formal: Is the implication $\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\Longrightarrow(\mathrm{NP},\mathrm{PSamp})\nsubseteq\mathrm{AvgP}$ true? That is, assuming P≠NP, must there exist a language L∈NP and a polynomial-time samplable distribution ensemble D={Dₙ} such that no deterministic exact decider for L runs in average polynomial time under D, in the moment-based sense defined below?
cards.definitions: A sampler is one randomized Turing machine S which, given 1ⁿ, halts within q(n) steps on every random tape for a fixed polynomial q. Its output distribution Dₙ is over finite binary strings x; |x|≤q(n), and n is the ensemble parameter, not necessarily |x|. Sampling is exact with independent unbiased coin flips, and S has no advice or oracle. An exact decider A receives (1ⁿ,x), halts, and returns the membership bit of L correctly for every n and x. Write T_A(1ⁿ,x) for its running time. The pair (L,D) belongs to AvgP if there exist such an A, ε>0, C>0, and integer k≥1 with $\mathbb E_{x\sim D_n}[T_A(1^n,x)^\varepsilon]\le C(n+1)^k$ for every n≥1. The constants and A may depend on L and S but not on n. This moment definition is the robust Levin notion, not the requirement that the first moment itself be polynomial. The algorithm is deterministic and never gives a wrong answer; difficult inputs may take a long time. NP uses ordinary polynomially bounded certificates and deterministic polynomial-time verification. Both the hard language and its sampler must be fixed across all input lengths.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This asks whether worst-case intractability necessarily survives on inputs generated by a feasible process. It is the basic bridge between the standard theory of NP-completeness and distributional complexity, and a prerequisite issue in attempts to derive useful cryptographic hardness from P≠NP alone.

importance.reason: One of the central missing implications in complexity theory, connecting worst-case lower bounds to feasible instance generation and the limits of algorithms on typical inputs.

progress.text: Levin develops robust average-time definitions and distributional completeness; Impagliazzo and Levin extend completeness to samplable ensembles. The survey develops the moment definition and this completeness theory.

Bogdanov and Trevisan show limitations of nonadaptive worst-case-to-average-case oracle reductions for NP. Their result is a conditional obstruction to a reduction method, not a disproof of the unrestricted implication.
Wigderson’s Open Problem 4.5 and the revised Bogdanov–Trevisan survey explicitly ask whether P≠NP implies average-case NP hardness.

Liu and Pass obtain a worst-case-to-average-case reduction for an exact time-bounded Kolmogorov problem under an exponential circuit-hardness derandomization assumption. The extra hypothesis is stronger and more specific than P≠NP.

cards.status_note: The original question is explicitly open in Wigderson’s book and the revised average-case survey. Current primary literature was checked through 10 September 2026; no resolution from P≠NP alone was located. The card fixes deterministic exact AvgP and strict polynomial-time sampling, rather than conflating them with randomized heuristic hardness.

context_blocks.text: Worst-case hardness says that an algorithm has difficult inputs. It does not say that a feasible instance generator produces them with enough probability to obstruct average efficiency. The sampler is therefore part of the mathematical problem. It may depend on the language, but it cannot contain an uncomputable table selecting a hard input at every length.

A padding example shows why a fixed familiar distribution is insufficient. Encode a formula x as 0 followed by |x|²−1 further zeros, a separator 1, and x. Satisfiability of these padded strings remains NP-complete under polynomial reductions. Under the uniform distribution on strings of a fixed length, valid encodings are so rare that checking the format and brute-forcing the rare valid formulas has polynomial average cost. An easy uniform distribution does not remove worst-case hardness.

Levin’s moment condition makes average efficiency stable under polynomial slowdowns. If a machine is simulated with its running time raised to a fixed power, a correspondingly smaller positive moment still suffices. This prevents the answer from depending on an incidental choice of machine representation. Exact computation with this runtime guarantee differs from a heuristic allowed to give incorrect answers on a small fraction of inputs.

Distributional completeness is already available: Impagliazzo and Levin extend the theory to polynomial-time samplable ensembles. Completeness identifies a common average-case target; it does not prove that this target is hard from P≠NP.

There are barriers for nonadaptive oracle reductions from worst-case NP hardness to average-case NP hardness: the relevant reductions would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. Such a barrier leaves other proof mechanisms open. Recent reductions for specific time-bounded Kolmogorov problems use additional assumptions or specific forms of hardness, so they do not supply the implication on this card.

category_assignment.reason: Average-case complexity and hardness

sentences: Worst-case NP hardness means that some efficiently verifiable problem resists polynomial-time solution on all inputs.
The question asks whether P unequal to NP forces such a problem to remain hard on average under an efficiently samplable distribution.
The hard instances must occur often enough in a distribution that can itself be generated feasibly.
A positive implication would connect worst-case complexity with the distributional hardness needed in many algorithmic and cryptographic settings.
The reviewed target uses deterministic exact decisions and Levin's moment-based average-time definition, which differs from allowing errors on rare inputs or requiring only a polynomial first moment.

cards.context:
Worst-case hardness says that an algorithm has difficult inputs. It does not say that a feasible instance generator produces them with enough probability to obstruct average efficiency. The sampler is therefore part of the mathematical problem. It may depend on the language, but it cannot contain an uncomputable table selecting a hard input at every length.

A padding example shows why a fixed familiar distribution is insufficient. Encode a formula x as 0 followed by |x|²−1 further zeros, a separator 1, and x. Satisfiability of these padded strings remains NP-complete under polynomial reductions. Under the uniform distribution on strings of a fixed length, valid encodings are so rare that checking the format and brute-forcing the rare valid formulas has polynomial average cost. An easy uniform distribution does not remove worst-case hardness.

Levin’s moment condition makes average efficiency stable under polynomial slowdowns. If a machine is simulated with its running time raised to a fixed power, a correspondingly smaller positive moment still suffices. This prevents the answer from depending on an incidental choice of machine representation. Exact computation with this runtime guarantee differs from a heuristic allowed to give incorrect answers on a small fraction of inputs.

Distributional completeness is already available: Impagliazzo and Levin extend the theory to polynomial-time samplable ensembles. Completeness identifies a common average-case target; it does not prove that this target is hard from P≠NP.

There are barriers for nonadaptive oracle reductions from worst-case NP hardness to average-case NP hardness: the relevant reductions would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. Such a barrier leaves other proof mechanisms open. Recent reductions for specific time-bounded Kolmogorov problems use additional assumptions or specific forms of hardness, so they do not supply the implication on this card.

benchmark_focus.reason: One of the central missing implications in complexity theory, connecting worst-case lower bounds to feasible instance generation and the limits of algorithms on typical inputs.

cards.title: The computational threshold for dense tensor PCA
cards.formal: For every fixed integer k≥3, rational ε with 0<ε<(k−2)/4, and rational c∈(0,1), is the following impossibility statement true? No uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm, given the finite-precision observation of Y=n^{k/4−ε}v^{⊗k}+Z specified below, achieves |⟨u,v⟩|≥c with probability at least 2/3 for every sufficiently large dimension n, where v is uniform on the unit sphere in R^n and the n^k ordered entries of Z are independent N(0,1) variables.
cards.definitions: The experiment draws v, Z and the algorithm’s random bits independently. For an ordered tuple (i₁,…,i_k)∈{1,…,n}^k, the signal entry is n^{k/4−ε}v_{i₁}⋯v_{i_k}. Noise is not pre-symmetrized and each entry has variance one. To give polynomial time a precise bit-model meaning, for n≥2 set b=⌈10k log₂n⌉ and Q_b(x)=2^{−b}⌊2^b max(−2^b,min(x,2^b))⌋. The input consists of n and all entries Q_b(Y_{i₁,…,i_k}), represented as signed dyadic rationals with O(log n) bits each. This fixed rounding convention is an explicit finite-precision version of the usual Gaussian-model question. An algorithm may depend on the fixed constants k, ε and c, but is one probabilistic Turing machine for all n, with worst-case running time polynomial in n on every input and random tape. For fixed k this is polynomial in the input size. It outputs a nonzero rational vector w, interpreted as the unit vector u=w/‖w‖₂; zero or invalid outputs fail. Success is the event |⟨w,v⟩|≥c‖w‖₂. The algorithm receives no side information about v, informative initial vector, or additional independent observations. The probability averages over the spike, noise and internal randomness. Absolute correlation makes the target invariant under the unavoidable sign ambiguity when k is even.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that for every fixed (k,ε,c) in the stated ranges, each such polynomial-time algorithm has success probability below 2/3 for arbitrarily large n; or refute this by giving one fixed triple and one algorithm that succeeds with probability at least 2/3 for all sufficiently large n. Proving failure only for low-degree polynomials, a chosen iterative method, or a different spike prior does not prove the full assertion. An improvement by logarithmic factors at n^{k/4} does not supply the fixed power saving n^ε requested here.
cards.why: Determine whether the canonical statistical–computational gap for a dense Gaussian tensor persists against all polynomial-time recovery algorithms.

importance.reason: A central average-case inference problem linking tensor algorithms, statistical thresholds, low-degree methods and computational hardness.
