cards.status_note: The May 2026 low-degree paper retains the conjectured gap for unrestricted algorithms and distinguishes spherical from independent-coordinate priors. The 2024 power-iteration and October 2025 stochastic-gradient improvements concern particular methods and do not provide a fixed-power improvement below n^{k/4}. No full resolution found through 11 September 2026. The card explicitly fixes a finite-precision bit model; restricted lower bounds in the standard unrounded model are evidence, not a proof for all algorithms here.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary principal component analysis looks for a hidden direction in a noisy matrix. Tensor PCA asks the analogous question when observations have three or more indices. Here the clean signal has rank one: every entry is a product of coordinates of the same hidden unit vector. Gaussian noise obscures those products. The goal is only a constant correlation with the direction, much weaker than estimating every coordinate accurately.

For fixed tensor order, information-theoretic recovery in the standard Gaussian model becomes possible at a signal scale of order √n. Montanari and Richard established the basic statistical-versus-computational distinction while studying tensor unfolding, power iteration and message-passing methods. Their noise normalization differs from the variance-one convention used in this card; their constant statistical threshold corresponds to order √n here.

Known polynomial-time methods reach signal strength around n^{k/4}, up to factors that do not change this leading exponent. Wu and Zhou’s 2024 introduction records both this algorithmic scale and the conjectured gap from √n. The interval for ε deliberately places our target strictly between them: λ/√n=n^{(k−2)/4−ε} grows without bound. There is therefore ample statistical signal in the usual model, while efficient recovery remains unproved.

For example, at order four and ε=1/8, the observation contains n^4 noisy numbers and signal strength n^{7/8}. The statistical scale is n^{1/2}, and the conjectured efficient scale is n. A polynomial-time algorithm below that latter scale would have to exploit structure that current threshold evidence misses. Merely reading all n^4 entries is allowed: the question concerns computation polynomial in the complete input, not a sublinear-access restriction.

Low-degree polynomial estimators provide one rigorous way to test proposed computational barriers. Kunisky, Moore and Wein establish the predicted degree-versus-signal tradeoff for detection with a spherical spike and derive a matching reconstruction lower bound for odd tensor orders. Their reconstruction theorem is specifically for odd orders; they explain that even orders require a sign-invariant estimand such as vvᵀ and additional work. Detection and recovery are separate tasks, and a detection lower bound should not silently be relabelled as their reconstruction theorem.

Fu and Sohn’s May 2026 preprint advances low-degree estimation bounds for tensor PCA with independent, mean-zero, variance-one spike coordinates and bounded moments. Its general-prior theorem controls estimation of fixed products of coordinates and obtains the predicted signal-versus-degree scaling within a stated degree range. Independent-coordinate priors are different from a vector conditioned to have unit norm. The result strengthens evidence for the computational gap without establishing an unrestricted polynomial-time lower bound for this card’s spherical prior.

Some recent algorithmic improvements resolve narrower conjectures. Wu and Zhou lower the threshold for randomly initialized power iteration by a polylogarithmic factor. Ding, Gu, Liu and Fang obtain improved guarantees for an overparameterized stochastic-gradient method using multiple independent observations. For even order, their stated sample-signal condition reaches the familiar n^{k/4} scale after averaging the observations. Neither result supplies the fixed-power improvement below that scale demanded here.

The rounding convention prevents an ambiguity about algorithms operating on exact Gaussian real numbers. Each coordinate is given with logarithmically many bits. Outside the clipping event, the total rounding error in Euclidean norm across the tensor is at most n^{k/2}2^{−b}, an extremely small inverse power of n; clipping has vanishing probability. This is a specified computational model, rather than an assertion that every exact-real algorithm automatically transfers to it. Likewise, polynomial-estimator theorems for unrounded observations do not by themselves cover arbitrary algorithms that process rounded entries.

A resolution would clarify whether a simple, highly symmetric random model can hide statistically recoverable information from every efficient algorithm. A successful method would challenge a widely used picture of algorithmic thresholds. A full impossibility proof would require a complexity argument beyond the restricted algorithm families currently understood. Both outcomes would inform how computational hardness assumptions are formulated for inference problems.

cards.title: Can random 3-SAT at constant density be refuted in polynomial time?
cards.formal: Do there exist an integer C≥6 and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm A such that A never outputs UNSAT on any satisfiable 3-CNF formula, and Pr[A(F)=UNSAT]→1 as n→∞ for F drawn from R_3(n,Cn)? The probability is over both the formula and A’s independent random bits.
cards.definitions: For n≥3, R_3(n,m) is the distribution on ordered lists of m clauses obtained independently with replacement. Each clause selects a uniformly random three-element subset of {1,…,n} and independently negates each of its three variables with probability 1/2. Each clause is their disjunction; the formula is the conjunction of the list, with duplicate clauses permitted. On every input A outputs UNSAT or UNKNOWN. Soundness is exact: for every satisfiable formula and every random tape A returns UNKNOWN. Its time is bounded by a fixed polynomial in the explicit binary input length on every input and every random tape, including adversarial formulas; variable names are binary integers and n is part of the encoding. A may use only fresh independent fair random bits and has no advice or external oracle. The constant C, the machine, and the time polynomial are chosen before n. The probability limit means that for every η>0 there is n0 such that the probability is at least 1−η for all n≥n0. There is no requirement to use a specified refutation proof system: a sound decision procedure certifying unsatisfiability suffices. Restricting the existential choice to integers C≥6 loses no larger constant-density regime, since an algorithm at a smaller density can run on the corresponding prefix of the random clause list.

context_blocks.text: At a sufficiently large fixed clause density, a random 3-CNF formula is unsatisfiable with probability approaching one. That fact alone does not give a sound algorithm for a particular input: a procedure that always announces unsatisfiability would incorrectly reject satisfiable adversarial formulas. The question is whether an efficient algorithm can recognize almost all random instances while retaining exact soundness on every satisfiable instance.

The random distribution and the algorithmic quantifiers have different roles. A is constrained on all inputs, but its success guarantee applies to the stated distribution. C is an absolute constant, so success only at a density growing with n does not meet the target. Likewise, proving that short certificates exist does not automatically yield an algorithm that finds them.

Allen, O’Donnell and Witmer define refutation as a sound UNSAT-or-fail procedure and develop refutation algorithms for random constraint satisfaction problems. They distinguish this task from planted-instance detection and from strong refutation, which certifies that every assignment violates a positive fraction of constraints. These distinctions determine which hardness assumptions and consequences apply.

Feige’s random-3-SAT hypothesis is often presented in a stronger gap formulation. For example, Barak’s formulation requires soundness even on nearly satisfiable formulas. This card records the exact-satisfiability, constant-density refutation question requested in the proposal; it does not identify that formulation with every version called Feige’s hypothesis. The gap formulation is documented as related context.

Chan, d’Orsi and Xu’s 2026 work generalizes density, sum-of-squares degree and refutation-strength tradeoffs for random CSPs. Its broader predicate model is not a polynomial-time, constant-density solution of this random-3-SAT target. The question remains a distinct counterpart to the catalogue’s planted-clique detection problem.

cards.why: Separate the typical absence of satisfying assignments from the computational ability to certify that absence soundly.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with the stated model, domains, promises and quantifiers. A conditional theorem settles only its conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof matching the full target.

importance.reason: A foundational average-case refutation problem with documented connections to proof complexity, learning and approximation. It supplies a different average-case task from planted recovery or detection. The exact-satisfiability variant is recorded without importing consequences of stronger gap hypotheses.

cards.title: Does average-case NP hardness imply infinitely-often one-way functions?
cards.formal: Does $\mathrm{DistNP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{HeurBPP}$ imply the existence of a polynomial-time computable function f with the following property? For every probabilistic polynomial-time inverter I and every constant c>0, infinitely many lengths n satisfy $\Pr[|z|=n\ \land\ f(z)=f(x)]<n^{-c}$, where $x\sim U(\{0,1\}^n)$ and $z\leftarrow I(1^n,f(x))$. The probability includes inverter randomness. This card fixes the infinitely-often security convention used by the cited characterization.
cards.why: It asks whether distributional hardness alone suffices for basic cryptography: a central connection between average-case complexity and cryptographic constructions.

progress.text: The revised paper characterizes the remaining obstruction by the gap between approximation factors $\ell^{1-o(1)}$ and $O(\ell)$ for minimum-description-length agnostic learning. Here $\ell$ is advice complexity of sampling. The original April version states a different quantitative claim.

cards.review_note: The earlier shorthand omitted the infinitely-often qualifier. This version fixes it to match Theorem 1.5 of revision 1. The all-sufficiently-large-length variant must not be silently identified with this statement. Importance is editorial and proofs have not been independently audited.

context_blocks.text: Hardness of deciding typical instances and hardness of finding preimages are different requirements. The assumption P ≠ NP alone is weaker and belongs to a separate existing question.

An average-case decision problem asks an algorithm to classify instances drawn from a specified distribution. A one-way function creates a different experiment: sample an input, reveal its efficiently computed image, and ask an adversary to find any valid preimage. The sampling process and the form of the required answer both matter.

A reduction has to turn the first kind of difficulty into the second while preserving efficient generation and a meaningful success probability. It cannot simply use a hard yes/no question as a function and assume its inverse is hard. The question is whether some average-case hardness can exist without yielding the basic inversion obstacle on which one-way-function cryptography is built.

cards.definitions: DistNP consists of pairs (L,D) with L in NP and D_n a polynomial-time samplable distribution on n-bit inputs. Such a pair is in HeurBPP if a single randomized algorithm A runs in time polynomial in n and 1/delta and, for every n and $0<\delta<1$, at least a $1-\delta$ fraction of x drawn from D_n have $\Pr[A(x,\delta)=L(x)]\ge2/3$. The output is a decision bit. Infinitely-often security is weaker than requiring negligible inversion probability at all sufficiently large lengths; the latter is a distinct stronger target.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the implication under the two explicit distributional and security definitions, or prove that average-case NP hardness can hold while every polynomial-time function fails that infinitely-often inversion guarantee. A result only about an oracle world does not settle the unrelativized implication.

importance.reason: Links average-case NP hardness to the existence of a basic cryptographic primitive; resolving it would clarify the foundations of complexity-based cryptography.

cards.title: Polynomial smoothed complexity of FLIP for Max-Cut
cards.formal: Are there absolute constants C,a,b>0 such that, for every n≥1, every simple undirected graph G on n vertices, every φ≥1/2 and every collection of independent edge-weight distributions supported on [−1,1] with probability densities bounded by φ, the expected length of the longest strictly improving single-vertex-flip path is at most C(n+1)^a(1+φ)^b?
cards.why: A flagship unresolved explanation of why a canonical PLS local-search algorithm works efficiently on perturbed inputs.
cards.status_note: The ESA 2024 source explicitly retains the arbitrary-graph problem. Searches for subsequent work through 11 September 2026 found no resolution of this expected longest-path target. The general high-probability upper bound and the smoothed 3-FLIP lower bound were separated from the required guarantee. Proofs have not been independently audited.
cards.review_note: Fixed the source’s signed [-1,1] bounded-density model and one-shot independent sampling. Made expectation of the longest path, arbitrary initial cuts, strict improvement and iteration cost explicit. Preserved the expected-time target; did not replace it by a tail bound or a choice of pivot rule.

progress.text: Theorem 1.1 gives the general upper bound φn^{O(√log n)} with high probability, controlling every directed path in the improvement graph.
The sparse-graph theorem gives polynomial expected and high-probability bounds for arboricity O(log^{1−δ}n), with any fixed δ∈(0,1]. The paper retains arbitrary graphs as an open case.
The author manuscript gives a smoothed superpolynomial lower bound for 3-FLIP and unperturbed exponential single-FLIP examples; both have a different scope from this target.

cards.definitions: The graph and one Lebesgue-measurable density f_e for each edge are chosen adversarially before the random weights. Each f_e is nonnegative, integrates to 1 on [−1,1], and is at most φ almost everywhere; weights w_e are sampled independently once from these densities and then held fixed. They may be negative and need not be identically distributed. A cut is a subset S⊆V, with value W_w(S)=Σ_{uv∈E: exactly one of u,v lies in S} w_uv. A legal step replaces S by S△{v} for one vertex v, and requires a strictly larger cut value. Define L(G,w) as the largest number of steps in any such path, maximized over all starting cuts and all choices of improving vertices after w is known; set L=0 if there is no step. There are finitely many cuts and strict improvement prevents revisiting one, so L≤2^n−1 and its expectation is well-defined. The expectation is over w alone, with the maximum over paths inside it. The resource counted is improving steps, not the bit cost of exact real arithmetic or of sampling distributions. The target concerns all graphs and all allowed densities with one common polynomial. A run ends at a single-flip local maximum, which need not maximize cut value globally.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed universal polynomial bound on E_w[L(G,w)], or prove its logical negation by exhibiting admissible families that exceed every such polynomial. A bound for selected graph classes or for one favorable pivot rule does not establish the proposition. A rare long path or an unperturbed worst-case instance alone does not refute an expected bound under these density constraints.

context_blocks.title: What FLIP improves
context_blocks.text: The procedure repeatedly moves a vertex to the opposite side when this increases the weight crossing the cut. Different choices can produce different paths, so the question controls the longest one. This includes starting cuts and choices made after seeing the sampled weights, rather than relying on a particular implementation to avoid a bad path.

context_blocks.title: Local optimality has a different goal
context_blocks.text: Consider a four-cycle 1–2–3–4–1 with weights 0.9 on edges 12 and 34 and weights 1 on edges 23 and 41. The cut {1,2} has weight 2, and moving any single vertex decreases it by 0.1. Nevertheless, the alternating cut {1,3} has weight 3.8. Fast termination here would mean finding a state with no improving single move, without asserting that FLIP finds a global maximum.

context_blocks.title: What the smoothing parameter permits
context_blocks.text: The adversary chooses the graph and the distributions, while independent draws supply the randomness. Density bounded by φ prevents a distribution from putting too much probability in an arbitrarily short interval: an interval of length h has probability at most φh. Larger φ permits more concentrated weights, and the requested running-time bound may grow polynomially with φ.

context_blocks.title: Known bounds cover only part of the target
context_blocks.text: The general-graph theorem of Chen and coauthors gives φn^{O(√log n)} steps with high probability, uniformly over improving paths. Schwartzman proves polynomial expected length when arboricity is O(log^{1−δ}n) for fixed δ>0; arboricity is the minimum number of forests needed to partition the edges. This includes sparse graph classes but not arbitrary graphs. The expectation requirement matters: a high-probability statement by itself does not bound the contribution of a long tail.

context_blocks.title: A nearby negative result uses larger moves
context_blocks.text: Michel and Scott show superpolynomial smoothed behavior for 3-FLIP, where a step may move up to three vertices together. Their single-FLIP exponential examples instead concern the setting without random perturbations. Neither statement refutes polynomial expected length for the single-vertex, independently perturbed model here.

cards.title: Can all vertices of a rational polytope be enumerated in output-polynomial time?
cards.formal: Do there exist a deterministic Turing machine A and a polynomial p such that, for every rational matrix M and rational vector b with P={x∈R^d:Mx≤b} bounded, A lists each vertex of P exactly once and halts within p(L+S) bit operations, where L is the binary input length and S is the total binary length of the required vertex list? The dimension d is part of the input.
cards.definitions: The input specifies integers m,d≥1, M∈Q^(m×d), and b∈Q^m. Every rational is written as a reduced signed integer numerator and positive integer denominator in binary, with delimiters; L includes this entire explicit representation. P may be empty or lower-dimensional, and redundant inequalities and degeneracy are allowed. A vertex is an extreme point: v∈P such that v=(x+y)/2 with x,y∈P implies x=y=v. Every vertex is rational. The output is a finite list in arbitrary order of these vectors, with each coordinate in the same reduced rational encoding, followed by an end marker. S includes separators and the end marker; it is determined independently of the algorithm, so padding or duplicate outputs cannot enlarge the permitted bound. The empty polytope has an empty vertex list. The bound concerns total running time, including writing the output, without a polynomial-delay or polynomial-workspace requirement. Correctness and the bound are required on the bounded-polyhedron promise; behavior outside that promise is immaterial.

context_blocks.text: A finite system of inequalities describes a convex region implicitly, while a vertex list describes its extremal feasible points explicitly. Linear programming can optimize one linear objective without producing that list. Enumerating the list asks whether the entire conversion can be performed with only polynomial overhead relative to the information that must actually be returned.

The number of vertices can be exponential in the input length, so a running-time bound polynomial in the input alone would be inappropriate. Output-polynomial time allows that unavoidable cost. It still excludes an algorithm that examines exponentially many intermediate objects when the final list is short. Degeneracy is particularly relevant because many collections of tight inequalities can describe the same vertex.

Reimers and Stougie explicitly identify total-polynomial vertex enumeration for bounded polyhedra as a longstanding open question. They obtain such an algorithm under a bounded branch-width condition. Their paper also distinguishes the general unbounded-polyhedron problem, for which output-polynomial enumeration would imply P=NP. That hardness statement does not resolve the bounded target here.

Dong, Fan, Xiong and Zeng study vertices of hyperplane arrangements. An arrangement includes intersections that may lie outside the feasible region selected by a system of inequalities. Consequently, an output-sensitive bound for the entire arrangement is measured against a different output and does not establish the required bound in the number of vertices of this polytope.

This card adds geometric enumeration to a category that already contains counting and hypergraph-transversal questions. Its target is the exact finite output of an algorithm in variable dimension. Neither approximate vertices nor a fast method restricted to simple polytopes meets that target.

cards.definitions: H=([n],E), n≥0, is supplied as the explicit vertex list and a finite list of edges e⊆[n], each edge an increasing list of binary vertex identifiers. Repeated edges have no effect. L(H) is the bit length of this input including delimiters. A transversal is a set T⊆[n] intersecting every e∈E; it is inclusion-minimal when no proper subset has this property. Output each such T as an increasing list of its binary vertex identifiers with a delimiter, in arbitrary order; no duplicate, nonminimal or incomplete output is allowed. L_out(H) is the sum of the bit lengths of these records, counting one delimiter even for T=∅. If E is empty, the unique minimal transversal is ∅. If E contains ∅, there is no transversal and L_out=0. Time includes all computation, output and termination detection. The polynomial and algorithm are independent of n, E, edge size and output size; there is no separate delay or workspace bound, advice, oracle or randomization. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

cards.title: Hadwiger’s conjecture: high chromatic number forces a clique minor
cards.formal: For every integer t≥1 and every finite nonempty simple undirected graph G, does χ(G)≥t imply that G contains K_t as a graph minor? Equivalently, is every K_t-minor-free graph (t−1)-colorable?
cards.definitions: A simple graph has no loops or parallel edges. A proper coloring assigns colors to vertices so that adjacent vertices receive different colors; χ(G) is the minimum number of colors. K_t is the complete graph on t vertices. A K_t minor is witnessed by t pairwise disjoint nonempty vertex sets B_1,…,B_t such that each induced subgraph G[B_i] is connected and every pair B_i,B_j has at least one edge between it. These branch sets can be contracted and all unwanted vertices or edges deleted. They may have arbitrary sizes; the minor need not be induced and no parity condition is imposed. Equivalently, the Hadwiger number h(G), the largest t for which G has a K_t minor, must satisfy h(G)≥χ(G). The statement concerns existence, with no running-time requirement on finding the coloring or branch sets.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A flagship structural graph problem connecting coloring, contractions, and excluded-minor classes. A resolution would identify the exact universal coloring obstruction in every minor-closed setting; improvements also develop structural tools relevant to graph algorithms and approximation.

importance.reason: One of the central graph-theoretic conjectures, with an exact extremal target and consequences across coloring and minor structure.

progress.text: Hadwiger proposes the relation between chromatic number and complete graph minors; the current preprint restates the original assertion.
Kostochka and Thomason establish the asymptotically sharp average-degree threshold yielding O(t√log t) colors; sharpness of this density method does not give a matching chromatic lower bound.
Robertson, Seymour, and Thomas prove the K_6-minor case using the Four-Color Theorem.
Delcourt and Postle prove O(t log log t) coloring and their reduction to small graphs. The preprint began in 2021 and the journal version appeared in 2025.
Kühn, Sauermann, Steiner, and Wigderson disprove the stronger odd-minor version, leaving ordinary Hadwiger open.
Version 2 of Liu and Luo’s preprint claims an absolute-C upper bound χ(G)≤Ct log log log t for every K_t-minor-free graph and t≥16 (Theorem 1.1). This does not reach χ(G)≤t−1.

references.authors: Marcus Kühn; Lisa Sauermann; Raphael Steiner; Yuval Wigderson
references.locator: 23 December 2025 preprint; ordinary formulation in Conjecture 1.1, odd-minor definition, and Theorem 1.3

cards.status_note: Ordinary Hadwiger remains explicitly open in the 9 September 2026 preprint; checked through 10 September 2026. The new triple-logarithmic upper bound is a preprint claim. The December 2025 disproof concerns the stronger odd-minor conjecture.

context_blocks.text: A graph can have very few large complete subgraphs and still need many colors. Hadwiger asks whether contracting connected pieces always reveals a complete graph as large as the number of colors originally needed. This would make a global obstruction to coloring visible through a precise structural certificate: disjoint connected regions linked in every pair. The complete graph K_(t−1) shows that the proposed upper bound for K_t-minor-free graphs cannot be reduced.

The conjecture encompasses the Four-Color Theorem because planar graphs exclude K_5 minors. Wagner’s structure theorem makes the t=5 case equivalent to four-colorability of planar graphs. Robertson, Seymour, and Thomas extended this equivalence to t=6 by proving that a minimal counterexample in that case would be apex: deleting one vertex leaves a planar graph. Thus the known exact cases extend through K_6 minors; the first unresolved case is t=7.

The earlier general approach forced clique minors from high average degree. The resulting O(t√log t) degeneracy bound gives a coloring bound of the same order by repeatedly removing a low-degree vertex and coloring in reverse. That density threshold is sharp, so simply improving its numerical constant cannot yield Hadwiger’s linear target. The chromatic-number question requires using structure beyond this degree argument.

Delcourt and Postle obtain O(t log log t) colors through a reduction to coloring much smaller minor-free subgraphs, on roughly t times a polylogarithmic number of vertices. Their reduction also shows that proving a linear bound on these small graphs would imply a linear bound without a size restriction. It narrows where a genuinely new coloring argument is needed, without imposing the small-size hypothesis on the conjecture itself.

Liu and Luo’s September 2026 preprint builds on that reduction and claims O(t log log log t). Its proof combines contractions that reduce degeneracy with fractional colorings, which distribute weight across independent sets. Even this extra logarithm removed leaves both the O(t) weakening and the sharp coefficient in the original conjecture unresolved. The result is recorded as a new preprint claim, not as an independently verified proof.

An odd clique minor imposes additional compatibility conditions on two-colorings inside its branch trees. Kühn, Sauermann, Steiner, and Wigderson construct graphs with no odd K_t minor and chromatic number approximately 1.5t, disproving the odd Hadwiger conjecture. Their graphs are not counterexamples to the ordinary-minor assertion asked here: forbidding odd minors permits more graphs than forbidding all clique minors.

It is a central structural principle behind the relationship between graph decomposition and coloring.

cards.context:
A graph can have very few large complete subgraphs and still need many colors. Hadwiger asks whether contracting connected pieces always reveals a complete graph as large as the number of colors originally needed. This would make a global obstruction to coloring visible through a precise structural certificate: disjoint connected regions linked in every pair. The complete graph K_(t−1) shows that the proposed upper bound for K_t-minor-free graphs cannot be reduced.

The conjecture encompasses the Four-Color Theorem because planar graphs exclude K_5 minors. Wagner’s structure theorem makes the t=5 case equivalent to four-colorability of planar graphs. Robertson, Seymour, and Thomas extended this equivalence to t=6 by proving that a minimal counterexample in that case would be apex: deleting one vertex leaves a planar graph. Thus the known exact cases extend through K_6 minors; the first unresolved case is t=7.

The earlier general approach forced clique minors from high average degree. The resulting O(t√log t) degeneracy bound gives a coloring bound of the same order by repeatedly removing a low-degree vertex and coloring in reverse. That density threshold is sharp, so simply improving its numerical constant cannot yield Hadwiger’s linear target. The chromatic-number question requires using structure beyond this degree argument.

Delcourt and Postle obtain O(t log log t) colors through a reduction to coloring much smaller minor-free subgraphs, on roughly t times a polylogarithmic number of vertices. Their reduction also shows that proving a linear bound on these small graphs would imply a linear bound without a size restriction. It narrows where a genuinely new coloring argument is needed, without imposing the small-size hypothesis on the conjecture itself.

Liu and Luo’s September 2026 preprint builds on that reduction and claims O(t log log log t). Its proof combines contractions that reduce degeneracy with fractional colorings, which distribute weight across independent sets. Even this extra logarithm removed leaves both the O(t) weakening and the sharp coefficient in the original conjecture unresolved. The result is recorded as a new preprint claim, not as an independently verified proof.

An odd clique minor imposes additional compatibility conditions on two-colorings inside its branch trees. Kühn, Sauermann, Steiner, and Wigderson construct graphs with no odd K_t minor and chromatic number approximately 1.5t, disproving the odd Hadwiger conjecture. Their graphs are not counterexamples to the ordinary-minor assertion asked here: forbidding odd minors permits more graphs than forbidding all clique minors.

cards.title: The Erdős–Hajnal conjecture for every forbidden induced graph
cards.formal: For every finite undirected simple graph H with at least two vertices, does there exist a real constant c(H)>0 such that every n-vertex undirected simple graph G with n≥1 and no induced copy of H satisfies max{α(G),ω(G)}≥n^{c(H)}?
cards.definitions: An induced copy of H is an injective map f:V(H)→V(G) such that distinct u,v are adjacent in H if and only if f(u),f(v) are adjacent in G. Thus both edges and nonedges must match. α(G) is the maximum size of a set of pairwise nonadjacent vertices, and ω(G) is the maximum size of a set of pairwise adjacent vertices. The constant c(H) may depend arbitrarily on the entire fixed graph H, but not on G or n. No density, degree, dimension or algorithmic promise is imposed on G. The claim concerns existence of a clique or independent set, without requiring a polynomial-time construction. A hereditary graph class is one closed under taking induced subgraphs; the class of H-free graphs is hereditary.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A foundational prediction that forbidding any fixed induced pattern forces polynomial-size order inside a graph. Its links to hereditary classes, neighborhood complexity and sparse/dense decompositions make it a central structural question with connections to algorithmic graph theory.

importance.reason: A major unifying conjecture for hereditary graph classes, with a sharp qualitative gap between general bounds and the target and substantial recent progress on special cases.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The 2026 primary literature explicitly retains the full conjecture as open. Sági’s historical revised claim is recorded separately and is not treated as a verified solution; the withdrawal of its earlier version does not itself refute the revision. context_blocks.text: Ramsey’s theorem guarantees a clique or independent set of logarithmic size in every sufficiently large graph, and random graphs show that this order of magnitude is unavoidable without further restrictions. Erdős–Hajnal predicts a dramatic change after forbidding even one fixed induced pattern: the guaranteed set should grow as a positive power of the number of vertices. The conjecture therefore asks how much global organization a single local structural exclusion forces.

For a simple example, a graph with no induced three-vertex path is a disjoint union of cliques. If it has t components, choosing one vertex from each gives an independent set of size t, while the largest component has at least n/t vertices and is a clique. One of these sets has size at least √n. This proves the conjecture for that forbidden graph and illustrates the desired polynomial gain through a structural decomposition.

The general theorem of Erdős and Hajnal gives a lower bound exp(c_H√log n). Bucić, Nguyen, Scott and Seymour improve it to exp(c_H√(log n·log log n)) for a positive constant depending on H. Their 2024 journal paper is the first improvement of this general bound. It is still smaller than nᵟ for every fixed δ>0 as n grows, so the extra logarithmic factor does not reach the conjectured scale.

Closure under complementation and vertex substitution lets proofs for a few building blocks settle many further forbidden graphs. Substitution replaces one vertex by a graph whose vertices all have the same neighbors outside the replacement. The remaining five-vertex building blocks were the bull, the five-cycle and the five-vertex path, together with its complement. Nguyen, Scott and Seymour’s proof for the path, published in March 2026, completes all forbidden graphs on at most five vertices.

For longer fixed paths, their separate all-path theorem gives homogeneous sets of size 2^{(log n)^{1−o(1)}}. This is close to the polynomial scale in its exponent but still does not assert n^c for any fixed positive c. In particular, the five-vertex result should not be described as resolving the conjecture for paths of arbitrary length.

Huang, Ju and Zhou’s August 2026 revision proves two additional six-vertex cases using an extension of iterative sparsification. The E-graph is a five-vertex path with a new leaf attached to its middle vertex. The Bird starts from a triangle with leaves attached to two different triangle vertices, then extends one of those leaves by one more edge. Both contain an induced five-vertex path, so excluding either permits a larger class than excluding the path itself.

A 28 August 2026 preprint by Tran and Nguyen reports another six-vertex case, specified without a drawing by vertex set {a,b,c,d,e,f} and edge set {ab,bc,cd,de,af,bf,df}. It develops the comb and sparsification framework further. This is an individual new forbidden pattern, rather than a proof for every six-vertex graph.

Another strand connects the conjecture with finding large nearly empty or nearly complete induced subgraphs. Bucić, Fox and Pham prove equivalence with polynomial quantitative versions of the Rödl and Nikiforov statements. This makes the problem relevant to structural decompositions and induced-pattern density, beyond locating a single clique or independent set.

There are also stronger quantitative results under additional hypotheses. Sun, Wang and Zeng’s July 2026 preprint gives exponent at least (Cd)⁻ᵈ for graphs of neighborhood VC-dimension at most d. This dimension bounds the size of a vertex set on which neighborhoods realize every possible subset. Such a restriction controls neighborhood complexity; arbitrary H-free graphs are not assumed to satisfy a fixed VC-dimension bound.

cards.title: Reed’s χ–ω–Δ conjecture
cards.formal: Does every nonempty finite simple undirected graph G satisfy χ(G)≤⌈(Δ(G)+1+ω(G))/2⌉?
cards.definitions: A graph is simple when it has neither loops nor parallel edges. A proper k-colouring is a map from V(G) to {1,…,k} assigning different colours to endpoints of every edge; χ(G) is the minimum such k. The degree of a vertex is its number of neighbours, and Δ(G) is the maximum degree. A clique is a vertex set whose distinct vertices are all adjacent, and ω(G) is its largest possible size. The ceiling ⌈x⌉ is the least integer at least x. The statement concerns all such graphs, including disconnected graphs and graphs with isolated vertices. For an edgeless nonempty graph, χ=ω=1 and Δ=0. The empty graph can be included with χ=ω=Δ=0, without changing the question. There are no restrictions on graph size, maximum degree, forbidden subgraphs or the method used to obtain a colouring.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated inequality for every finite simple graph, or give a finite graph and a proof that its chromatic number exceeds the displayed ceiling. The target is an existence theorem, so a polynomial-time colouring algorithm is not required. An asymptotic bound with an additive error, a convex combination with clique coefficient less than 1/2, or a theorem restricted to sufficiently large maximum degree is partial progress unless the remaining cases are also covered.
cards.why: A central structural colouring problem with an exact, best-possible target. It asks how much the absence of a large clique must reduce the number of colours, and guides probabilistic, structural and algorithmic approaches to colouring.

importance.reason: A defining universal conjecture linking three basic graph parameters, with sharp examples and broad influence on colouring theory and its algorithmic methods.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The September 8 primary revision explicitly retains the exact undirected inequality as open. Small-clique estimates, sufficiently-large-degree interpolation bounds, and the recolouring and directed variants do not settle the full statement. The published 0.119 bound’s stated dependency is preserved in the context.

context_blocks.text: Two elementary bounds frame graph colouring. A clique needs a distinct colour for every vertex, so χ≥ω. On the other hand, greedily colouring vertices in any order uses at most Δ+1 colours: at most Δ colours are forbidden by already coloured neighbours. Reed asks whether an upper bound halfway between these two numbers always suffices, after rounding up. This would sharply connect a local obstruction, the size of a clique, to the global task of partitioning all vertices into independent sets.

The rounding is essential even for a five-cycle. It has maximum degree two and clique number two, but it needs three colours because an odd cycle is not bipartite. The unrounded average is 5/2. Complete graphs also meet the proposed upper bound exactly. These examples show that the question is about a precise universal inequality, rather than merely reducing the leading constant in a loose estimate.

There is also a useful family explaining the coefficient 1/2. Replace each vertex of a five-cycle by a clique of size t, joining every vertex of two replacement cliques whenever their cycle vertices were adjacent. The resulting graph has 5t vertices, maximum degree 3t−1 and clique number 2t. An independent set contains at most two vertices, so at least ⌈5t/2⌉ colours are necessary. A universal bound ⌈(1−ε)(Δ+1)+εω⌉ with ε>1/2 would give fewer colours for large t. Thus the conjectured interpolation coefficient cannot be increased.

Reed established a weaker universal interpolation with some fixed positive coefficient ε in place of 1/2. This already gives a saving proportional to the gap between maximum degree and clique number. Proving such a saving is difficult because high degree need not mean that a neighbourhood resembles a clique, and local savings must coexist across many overlapping neighbourhoods.

Hurley, de Joannis de Verclos and Kang report ε=0.119 for sufficiently large maximum degree, using a refined random colouring procedure and local sparsity estimates. Their published paper explicitly records a dependency: the 0.119 calculation uses a then-unreviewed result of Delcourt and Postle. Remark 3.1 gives ε=0.113 using an alternative published ingredient. The September 2026 digraph paper continues to cite the 0.119 bound. Both constants remain far below the conjectured 1/2.

A different advance handles graphs with much smaller cliques. Bonamy, Kelly, Nelson and Postle bound the chromatic number by O(Δ√(log ω/log Δ)), with related list and correspondence colouring results. For suitable relations between ω and Δ this is much stronger than a small fixed improvement on the greedy bound. It does not prove the desired average bound across the full range of clique sizes.

Recent related work also changes the task. The 2025 recolouring paper studies whether proper colourings can be connected by Kempe changes: swap two colours on a connected component induced by those colours. Its general conjectured interpolation coefficient is 1/3 because reconfiguration has obstructions beyond the existence of one colouring. Its positive results on odd-hole-free graphs therefore need to be read in that separate model.

Kawarabayashi and Picasarri-Arrieta extend the framework to directed graphs, where each colour class must induce an acyclic digraph. Their SODA 2025 work, revised in September 2026, proves a positive-ε interpolation and proposes the exact half-average analogue. Replacing each undirected edge by arcs in both directions recovers ordinary colouring, so the proposed directed statement would imply Reed’s conjecture. The directed partial theorem does not supply the missing coefficient.

cards.title: Is graph isomorphism solvable in polynomial time?
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic classical algorithm that, for every pair of finite simple undirected graphs G and H given by explicit adjacency matrices, decides whether G and H are isomorphic in time polynomial in the total input length?
cards.definitions: Two graphs on equally many vertices are isomorphic if a bijection of their vertex sets preserves adjacency in both directions. The input contains the complete graph descriptions; unequal vertex counts are rejected immediately. The algorithm must be uniform, deterministic and correct on every graph pair, with no promise of bounded degree, rigidity, expansion, or random input. Polynomial time is measured in the binary input length, so the Θ(n²) adjacency data may be read in full. The question concerns ordinary vertex-permutation isomorphism, not quantum isomorphism, graph canonization under a different output requirement, or isomorphism of groups or tensors. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Tests whether the central equivalence problem for finite combinatorial structures can be recognized in deterministic polynomial time after the quasipolynomial barrier was broken.

importance.reason: A canonical unresolved problem at the intersection of algorithms, permutation groups and complexity theory, with a precise best-known general upper bound.

context_blocks.text: Graph isomorphism asks whether two finite graphs differ only by a relabelling of their vertices. A proposed relabelling is easy to verify, so the problem lies in NP, but ruling out all relabellings can be difficult for highly symmetric graphs.

Many special cases have polynomial-time algorithms, including bounded-degree graphs and several classes with strong structural restrictions. These results do not automatically combine into an algorithm for arbitrary graphs, whose automorphism groups can have a much richer structure.

Babai’s breakthrough gives a deterministic quasipolynomial-time algorithm, with running time exp((log n)^{O(1)}), improving the earlier subexponential bound. Quasipolynomial time is still asymptotically larger than every fixed polynomial, so the final gap to P remains exactly the question on this card.

Graph canonization is closely related: producing a canonical labelled representative is at least as demanding as deciding isomorphism in many standard reductions, but a theorem about one output formulation must preserve the required runtime and uniformity before it answers the decision problem. Quantum graph-isomorphism relations and BQP algorithms likewise concern different computational problems.

No general polynomial-time algorithm or unconditional lower bound excluding one was found in the checked literature through 11 September 2026. The problem remains a clean benchmark for the boundary between efficiently verifiable symmetry and efficient recognition of symmetry.

Graph isomorphism asks whether two finite graphs differ only by a relabelling of their vertices. A proposed relabelling is easy to verify, so the problem lies in NP, but ruling out all relabellings can be difficult for highly symmetric graphs.

Many special cases have polynomial-time algorithms, including bounded-degree graphs and several classes with strong structural restrictions. These results do not automatically combine into an algorithm for arbitrary graphs, whose automorphism groups can have a much richer structure.

Babai’s breakthrough gives a deterministic quasipolynomial-time algorithm, with running time exp((log n)^{O(1)}), improving the earlier subexponential bound. Quasipolynomial time is still asymptotically larger than every fixed polynomial, so the final gap to P remains exactly the question on this card.

Graph canonization is closely related: producing a canonical labelled representative is at least as demanding as deciding isomorphism in many standard reductions, but a theorem about one output formulation must preserve the required runtime and uniformity before it answers the decision problem. Quantum graph-isomorphism relations and BQP algorithms likewise concern different computational problems.

No general polynomial-time algorithm or unconditional lower bound excluding one was found in the checked literature through 11 September 2026. The problem remains a clean benchmark for the boundary between efficiently verifiable symmetry and efficient recognition of symmetry.

cards.title: The Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture
cards.formal: For every finite nonempty tree T and every integer r≥1, does there exist a finite integer B(T,r) such that every finite simple undirected graph G with clique number at most r and no induced subgraph isomorphic to T has chromatic number at most B(T,r)?
cards.definitions: A tree is a connected graph with no cycle. All graphs here are finite, simple and undirected. The clique number ω(G) is the largest number of pairwise adjacent vertices, and the chromatic number χ(G) is the least number of colours in a proper vertex colouring, in which adjacent vertices receive distinct colours. Both parameters are zero for the empty graph. For S⊆V(G), the induced graph G[S] retains all edges of G with both endpoints in S. Saying that G contains an induced T means there is an injective map φ:V(T)→V(G) such that xy is an edge of T if and only if φ(x)φ(y) is an edge of G. Extra edges between image vertices are forbidden. The quantifier order is ∀T ∀r ∃B ∀G: the integer B may depend arbitrarily on T and r, but not on |V(G)|, maximum degree or any additional parameter of G. Equivalently, for each T there is a function f_T:N→N with χ(G)≤f_T(ω(G)) for every induced-T-free graph G. No prescribed polynomial growth, computability requirement for f_T, or efficient colouring algorithm is part of the target. The statement concerns ordinary chromatic number, not fractional, list, oriented or domatic colouring parameters.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated bound for all finite trees and all fixed clique bounds, or exhibit one fixed tree T and one fixed integer r together with induced-T-free graphs G_k satisfying ω(G_k)≤r and χ(G_k)→∞. A single finite graph can disprove a proposed numerical bound but cannot refute the existence of some larger bound. A bound that still grows with |V(G)|, or a theorem with a different excluded object or extra host-graph promise, is not a full resolution.
cards.why: Determine whether every fixed induced tree is an unavoidable pattern in graphs whose chromatic number grows while their clique number stays bounded.

importance.reason: A central organizing conjecture for hereditary graph colouring and forbidden induced subgraphs, defining the proposed forest boundary for χ-boundedness.

context_blocks.text: A clique explains one elementary reason for needing many colours: its vertices must all receive different colours. But graphs can require arbitrarily many colours even when every clique has size at most two. The conjecture proposes that forbidding any one fixed induced tree eliminates this unbounded gap. Once the tree and clique bound are fixed, the same finite palette should suffice no matter how many vertices the graph has.

The induced condition is essential. A copy of a tree as an ordinary subgraph can ignore unwanted edges between its vertices. An induced copy must reproduce both adjacency and nonadjacency. Complete graphs contain every sufficiently small tree as an ordinary subgraph, while most of those trees do not occur as induced subgraphs. The difficult step in building the desired tree is therefore arranging its branches without creating extra edges among them.

Trees are the natural boundary for this kind of one-forbidden-pattern statement. High-girth graphs can have arbitrarily large chromatic number while containing no short cycles. If a fixed forbidden graph contains a cycle, choosing larger girth avoids that graph while retaining an unbounded chromatic number and a bounded clique number. The corresponding obstruction is absent for forests. This is why the conjecture is a proposed classification, rather than an arbitrary choice of forbidden shape.

There are substantial positive cases. Kierstead and Penrice proved the conjecture for every tree of radius at most two: some central vertex is within distance two of every other vertex. Paths and further tree families are also known. Scott and Seymour subsequently strengthen the radius-two result under exclusion of a fixed complete multipartite subgraph, with polynomial bounds in its part size. Such results exploit restrictions on how branches can interact.

Nguyen, Scott and Seymour’s 2023 preprint, published in 2024, obtains a copy of any fixed rooted tree under the conjecture’s high-chromatic-number hypotheses, with every path from the root induced. This controls unwanted edges along ancestor–descendant paths. It still permits edges between different branches, and those edges may prevent the whole vertex set from inducing a tree. The distinction isolates one of the remaining obstacles.

Their later work on near-linear stable sets applies to every fixed excluded forest and fixed clique bound. It proves an independent set of size n^{1−o(1)}, and consequently a chromatic bound n^{o(1)}, where n is the number of vertices. Thus every fixed positive power n^ε eventually exceeds the available upper bound. Nevertheless, a function such as log n is also n^{o(1)} and is unbounded, so subpolynomial growth does not establish the constant B(T,r) sought here.

That work also proves a bounded fractional chromatic number for multibrooms, formed by identifying the roots of several paths that have additional leaves at their far ends. Fractional colouring covers vertices by weighted independent sets and minimizes the total weight. Ordinary colouring requires an actual partition into colour classes. The paper retains the full conjecture for general multibrooms despite its stronger fractional conclusion.

Davies and Yuditsky establish the conjecture, with a polynomial bound in the clique number, for intersection graphs of axis-aligned boxes in every fixed dimension d. Their result first appeared in 2024 and was published in April 2026. Both the excluded forest and dimension are fixed parameters. Allowing the dimension to grow with the input would let the bound vary with an extra parameter, so the theorem does not cover arbitrary graphs with the uniform bound required here.

For algorithms, this conjecture identifies a structural source of bounded colouring complexity and large independent sets. It does not itself promise that a suitable colouring can be found efficiently. A proof with an effective construction would offer additional algorithmic information; a counterexample would reveal a family of sparse-clique graphs whose chromatic obstruction survives exclusion of one fixed induced tree. The size-independent existence statement is already fundamental.

cards.title: The optimal quantitative Excluded Grid Theorem
cards.formal: For each integer r≥2, let f(r) be the least nonnegative integer t such that every finite simple undirected graph of treewidth at least t contains the r×r square grid as a minor. Determine the asymptotic order of f(r) up to universal constant factors, including the correct logarithmic dependence.
cards.definitions: The r×r grid has vertex set {1,…,r}², with an edge between (i,j) and (i′,j′) exactly when |i−i′|+|j−j′|=1. It has r² vertices; r denotes side length. A graph H is a minor of G if H can be obtained by deleting vertices, deleting edges and contracting edges, after removing loops and merging parallel edges. Equivalently, a model of H consists of one nonempty connected vertex set in G for each vertex of H, all pairwise disjoint, with an edge of G joining the corresponding sets for every edge of H. Additional edges are permitted. A tree decomposition of G is a tree T with bags B_t⊆V(G), such that every vertex belongs to some bag, the endpoints of every edge belong together to some bag, and the bags containing any given vertex form a connected subtree of T. Its width is max_t |B_t|−1; treewidth tw(G) is the minimum such width. Robertson–Seymour’s Grid-Minor Theorem guarantees that f(r) is finite. The quantifier over G includes graphs of arbitrary size, degree and genus. This is an extremal existence threshold; no efficiency requirement for finding the grid model is imposed. Polylogarithmic factors mean (log r)^c for a fixed constant c, and matching bounds here must resolve such factors rather than suppress them.
cards.answer_criterion: Identify an explicit asymptotic function h(r) and universal constants a,b>0 such that a h(r)≤f(r)≤b h(r) for all sufficiently large r. The upper bound must force a grid minor in every graph above the stated threshold; the lower bound must give graphs of comparable treewidth that exclude it. In particular, this determines whether f(r)=O(r²(log r)^c) for some fixed c. Merely improving a nonmatching polynomial exponent, solving the planar-host case, or replacing minors by a different containment relation is progress rather than a complete answer.
cards.why: Determine the exact asymptotic loss when converting large treewidth into a square-grid minor, a foundational link between graph structure and algorithms.

importance.reason: A central quantitative problem in graph minor theory with direct implications for structural decompositions, routing, packing and parameterized algorithms.

cards.status_note: The checked general bounds remain Ω(r² log r) and O(r⁹ polylog r). The November 2025 product-structure result and SODA 2026 fixed-minor result refine different aspects and do not determine the all-graphs threshold. No matching asymptotic bounds found through 11 September 2026. The problem does not assume that either the near-quadratic or cubic conjecture is correct.

context_blocks.text: Treewidth measures how large the interacting pieces of a graph must be when organized along a tree. Many algorithms work by dynamic programming across the bags of a tree decomposition, with a strong dependence on bag size. A grid provides a canonical obstruction to small treewidth: its rows and columns create many overlapping connections that cannot be separated into very small bags. The Excluded Grid Theorem states that every graph of sufficiently large treewidth contains such an obstruction as a minor.

The unknown quantity is how much treewidth must be spent to force a grid of a given side length. The qualitative theorem only says that some finite threshold exists. A sharp quantitative bound would explain how efficiently general tangled connectivity can be organized into a planar grid. This is not a statement that the graph itself is planar, or that a grid must appear as an induced subgraph.

A vertex-count example already rules out a linear threshold. The complete graph on r²−1 vertices has treewidth r²−2, but cannot contain an r×r grid minor because taking a minor cannot increase the number of vertices. Thus f(r)≥r²−1. Its many edges cannot replace the need for r² disjoint nonempty branch sets in a minor model. This is why the fact that the r×r grid itself has treewidth r does not imply a linear bound for arbitrary host graphs.

The known lower bound is stronger: f(r)=Ω(r² log r). Robertson, Seymour and Thomas obtain it using bounded-degree expanders of logarithmic girth. Such graphs have treewidth proportional to their number of vertices, while every cycle is long. A large grid contains quadratically many vertex-disjoint small cycles; lifting those cycles through a minor model requires quadratically many disjoint long cycles in the host. This consumes a logarithmic factor of additional vertices.

Chekuri and Chuzhoy obtain the first polynomial upper bound, replacing an enormous quantitative gap by a polynomial relationship between treewidth and grid size. Their proof is constructive: a randomized polynomial-time algorithm finds a grid model at the scale established by their theorem. This makes the result useful both as a structural guarantee and as a subroutine, although this card asks only for the optimal existence threshold.

Chuzhoy and Tan improve the general upper bound to O(r⁹(log r)^c) for an absolute constant c. Their SODA 2019 paper, published in journal form in 2021, builds on well-linked sets and paths of connected clusters. Well-linkedness supplies many disjoint connections; the challenge is arranging them into the grid’s particular pattern without losing too much width at successive stages. The lower and upper bounds still differ by a large power of r.

The same paper records competing predictions: Robertson–Seymour–Thomas conjectured that the r² log r lower bound is tight, while Demaine and coauthors proposed a cubic threshold. Consequently, the catalogue target is the actual asymptotic order. A near-quadratic upper bound would be a major result, but should not be described as the only conjectured answer. Even r² times an unspecified power of log r would leave part of the present target unresolved.

The 2025 paper The Grid-Minor Theorem Revisited strengthens the structural description of graphs excluding a fixed planar minor. It represents them inside clique blow-ups of graphs whose treewidth is controlled by the excluded graph’s treedepth. The blow-up size is an unspecified function of the excluded graph. This gives useful product structure and colouring applications, while leaving the optimal numerical threshold f(r) undetermined.

Catching Rats in H-minor-free Graphs, presented at SODA 2026, makes another substantial refinement under an extra host-graph restriction. For a fixed excluded graph H with t vertices and Euler genus g, a graph excluding both H and the r×r grid has treewidth O(gr+t^{2304}), hence O(t²r+t^{2304}). This is linear in r when H is fixed. General graphs in our question need not exclude any fixed H, so that additional parameter cannot be treated as a universal constant.

The threshold influences the quantitative strength of grid-based routing arguments, packing-versus-covering theorems and parameterized algorithms. Better bounds can improve how a large-treewidth case yields useful structure, or how a no-grid case bounds the state space for dynamic programming. A matching lower bound would be equally informative: it would identify an unavoidable loss in converting unrestricted graph connectivity into a planar obstruction.

cards.title: Almost-linear triangle detection
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every finite simple undirected graph with n vertices and m edges given by adjacency lists, decides whether a triangle exists with success probability at least 2/3 and worst-case running time (n+m+2)^{1+o(1)}?
cards.definitions: A triangle is a set of three distinct vertices u,v,w for which all three unordered edges {u,v},{v,w},{w,u} are present. The input gives labelled vertices 1,…,n and explicit adjacency lists; it is promised to describe a simple undirected graph, and can be disconnected or contain isolated vertices. The RAM has words of w=⌈4 log₂(n+2)⌉ bits, random-access memory, and unit-cost word reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo 2ʷ, and integer division by a nonzero word. Independent random words may be generated at unit cost. Input reading and all preprocessing count toward time. The running-time bound holds for every graph and every random tape, while correctness probability is over the algorithm’s internal randomness. The o(1) is a function tending to zero as n+m tends to infinity, for this one fixed algorithm; equivalently, for every ε>0 the same algorithm eventually uses at most (n+m+2)^{1+ε} operations. There is no promise on density, degree, arboricity or triangle count. Matrix multiplication and other algebraic techniques are allowed if their implementation fits this machine model. Only one yes/no answer is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct and analyze an algorithm meeting the stated all-input time and probability guarantees, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A deterministic O(n+m) algorithm would be an even stronger positive answer. A fixed exponent above one, an O(n²) bound that is only input-linear on dense graphs, output-sensitive listing, or an algorithm restricted to bounded-arboricity graphs does not settle the question. The target fixes the original draft’s “linear or at least almost-linear” alternative at the precise almost-linear threshold.
cards.why: Determine whether detecting the simplest cyclic graph pattern requires a superlinear amount of computation beyond reading the input.

importance.reason: A fundamental graph primitive and fine-grained hardness assumption with consequences for dynamic data structures, joins and string matching.

progress.text: Chiba–Nishizeki give O(m·a(G)) triangle listing, yielding linear time for bounded-arboricity families.

Dumitrescu withdraws the claimed faster combinatorial algorithm because its case analysis is invalid.
Kumabe–Uezato use triangle hardness to exclude almost-linear matching for a restricted two-use backreference class, conditionally.
A separate Aegypti revision claims O(n²), which is not an almost-linear guarantee for all graph densities; correctness not adjudicated here.

context_blocks.text: Triangle detection is among the smallest nontrivial pattern-finding tasks in a graph. The pattern has only three vertices, but a graph may contain an enormous number of possible triples. The question asks whether all the relevant combinations can be handled in essentially the time required to read the graph. It must also handle triangle-free instances, where an algorithm cannot stop upon finding a convenient local witness.

Detection is different from listing. A complete graph has Θ(n²) input edges and Θ(n³) triangles, so explicitly listing every triangle cannot take linear time in the input size. A yes/no answer has constant output size and faces no such output-size obstruction. Likewise, approximate counting or finding triangles in a distribution of random inputs does not supply an exact decision guarantee on every adversarial graph.

Chiba and Nishizeki give triangle listing in O(m·a(G)) time, apart from reading isolated vertices, where arboricity a(G) is the minimum number of forests needed to cover the graph’s edges. This gives linear time on any family of bounded arboricity, including planar graphs. General graphs can have arboricity of order √m, so this approach has a superlinear worst-case cost. A sparse graph can still contain a dense, difficult region.

Alon, Yuster and Zwick improve the general sparse-graph bound using a degree threshold. Handle triangles touching a low-degree vertex by local enumeration, and use matrix multiplication on the smaller set of high-degree vertices. For an available square matrix-multiplication exponent τ, the resulting standard bound is O(n+m^{2τ/(τ+1)}), roughly O(n+m^{1.407}) at familiar current exponents. The optimization balances the cost of the two parts.

Even setting the matrix-multiplication exponent to two in this particular reduction leaves exponent 4/3 in m. Thus faster dense multiplication alone, inserted into the same degree-splitting argument, would not make the sparse algorithm almost linear. This is an observation about the upper-bound method, not a proof that a different graph algorithm cannot do better.

Abboud and Vassilevska Williams formulate a no-almost-linear triangle hypothesis and use it to derive conditional lower bounds for dynamic problems. The conjecture concerns general algorithms on logarithmic-word RAMs. Their separate combinatorial Boolean-matrix-multiplication conjecture restricts the kinds of techniques used; it should not be substituted for the unrestricted question here. Reductions transfer assumed hardness, rather than establish an unconditional superlinear lower bound.

The distinction remains useful in current work. Kumabe and Uezato’s ICALP 2026 paper reduces triangle detection to matching certain fixed regular expressions with two backreference uses. Consequently, an almost-linear algorithm for that matching task would also give an almost-linear triangle algorithm. This illustrates why a small graph pattern can govern complexity in a seemingly unrelated setting.

Search results require source checks. Dumitrescu’s March 2024 claim of faster combinatorial triangle algorithms was withdrawn three days after posting; the author states that the algorithm may fail and identifies an invalid case analysis. It is not an established improvement.

I also checked the parent-edge rule in Vega’s August 2025 linear-time proposal. Consider the path 0–1–2–3–4–5–6 plus edges 0–3, 3–6 and 0–6. A legal DFS follows the whole path. Its unique triangle is {0,3,6}, consisting entirely of back edges. No test restricted to a DFS parent, its child and a common neighbour can find it. A local simulation and exhaustive triple check confirm this counterexample to the stated rule; this is not a test of later replacement implementations.

A separate September 2026 Aegypti revision claims O(n²) time via bucket reduction. That claimed bound is not almost linear for every sparse input, even if its correctness were established. I have not adjudicated its different proof. An all-density statement must keep both n and m visible: a dense-case breakthrough and an input-linear sparse algorithm are distinct achievements.

A resolution would identify whether a basic three-way adjacency condition inherently requires substantial work beyond scanning an explicit graph. A positive algorithm would affect graph-pattern routines and invalidate hardness assumptions used by many reductions. A negative result would provide a major unconditional lower bound for a simple polynomial-time graph problem on a strong, standard machine model.

cards.title: Exact directed maximum flow in O((m+n) polylog n) time
cards.formal: For every fixed integer a≥1, do there exist a constant k≥0 and a uniform classical randomized algorithm A_a that, on every directed graph with n≥2 vertices, m arcs, distinguished distinct vertices s,t and integer capacities in {0,…,n^a}, outputs an exact maximum s–t flow with probability at least 2/3 in worst-case time O((m+n)(log(n+2))^k)?
cards.definitions: The graph is explicitly given by its labelled vertex set {1,…,n} and an arc list, with no loops and at most one arc per ordered vertex pair; opposite arcs are allowed. A flow assigns an integer f_e to each arc, with 0≤f_e≤u_e and equal incoming and outgoing sums at every vertex other than s,t. Its value is the outgoing sum at s minus the incoming sum at s; maximum refers to the largest such value. Output the m flow values, not only an approximate value. Use a word RAM with word length B_a⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ for a fixed integer B_a large enough to store capacities, total flow and memory addresses. Unit-cost operations are random-access word reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction, multiplication modulo 2^w and integer division of nonzero divisors. Multiword computations are charged for their component operations. Independent fair random bits are allowed, with each generated word charged. All preprocessing and output are included, and the time bound holds on every random execution. There are no oracles or input-dependent advice. A_a, k, B_a and the hidden constant may depend on a, but not on the graph. The m+n convention includes explicitly listed isolated vertices.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.

context_blocks.text: Maximum flow is a basic model for routing through capacity constraints. A feasible solution must obey conservation at intermediate vertices, and optimality measures the largest transferable amount between two terminals. Even a graph with small integer capacities can require globally coordinated changes to a feasible routing. The question asks whether finding the exact optimum can cost only a polylogarithmic factor more than reading the graph.

Almost-linear algorithms already represent a major qualitative advance. Chen and coauthors obtained exact maximum flow and minimum-cost flow in m^(1+o(1)) time for polynomially bounded integral data. Li and Wice’s August 2026 preprint obtains an almost-linear maximum-flow bound through a different framework. Neither stated asymptotic guarantee is O(m polylog n).

The distinction concerns the remaining overhead. For example, exp(√log n) is subpolynomial in n but exceeds every fixed power of log n. A running time containing that factor can be almost linear without satisfying this card. Removing the residual gap would identify a sharper computational cost for a central graph optimization primitive.

Exactness is also a substantive part of the target. A flow whose value is within a fixed relative error of optimum does not determine the optimum integer value when that value is large. Conversely, restricting capacities to polynomial magnitude means their binary encodings occupy logarithmically many bits each. The question is therefore not asking an algorithm to read arbitrarily long capacities in a graph-size-only time bound.

The primary topic is a static graph algorithm, so the current catalogue places the question in Structural graph theory and graph algorithms. Dynamic maintenance, parallel computation and strong polynomiality for unbounded-bit linear programming impose different requirements. No existing maximum-matching or dynamic-connectivity card represents this flow target.

cards.title: Barnette’s Hamiltonicity conjecture
cards.formal: Is every finite simple undirected graph that is 3-connected, cubic, bipartite and planar Hamiltonian?
cards.definitions: A simple graph has neither loops nor parallel edges. It is 3-connected if it has at least four vertices and deleting any set of at most two vertices leaves a connected graph. Cubic means every vertex has degree exactly three. Bipartite means its vertices admit a partition into two sets with no edge having both endpoints in the same set. Planar means it has a drawing in the plane whose edge interiors do not intersect and contain no vertices; different edges may meet only at shared endpoints. A Hamiltonian cycle is a cyclic ordering v_1,...,v_n of all vertices, each appearing exactly once, such that {v_i,v_(i+1)} is an edge for every i, with v_(n+1)=v_1. The cycle must use only edges already present in the graph. No algorithmic running-time guarantee is requested.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.

cards.title: Is Exact Matching on general graphs in deterministic polynomial time?
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm, polynomial in the input bit length, that decides the following problem? Given a simple undirected graph G on an even number n of vertices, each edge colored red or blue, and an integer $0\le k\le n/2$, determine whether G has a perfect matching containing exactly k red edges. The algorithm must be correct on every input. No bipartition is promised, and no randomness or computational hardness assumption is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that this decision problem belongs to P, or prove that it does not. A randomized polynomial-time algorithm, an approximation to the red count, or an algorithm restricted to bipartite graphs does not establish the positive answer.
cards.why: I include this because it is a concrete combinatorial derandomization target with a short, checkable definition. It asks whether randomness is necessary for an exact constraint on top of an otherwise tractable optimization problem, connecting matching algorithms to algebraic identity testing.
cards.definitions: P denotes languages decidable by a uniform deterministic Turing machine in time polynomial in the ordinary adjacency-list encoding and the binary encoding of k. A perfect matching is a set of disjoint edges covering every vertex. If a polynomial-time decision algorithm exists, a matching can also be recovered by polynomially many decisions on residual instances. This target concerns sequential polynomial time, not deterministic NC.

progress.text: Mulmuley, U. Vazirani, and V. Vazirani provide the randomized algebraic matching framework underlying polynomial-time Exact Matching algorithms.
El Maalouly surveys algorithms and related problems while retaining general deterministic polynomial-time Exact Matching as open.
Du claims a deterministic bipartite algorithm. Version 3 states eight explicit hypotheses in its Lean formalization. That paper does not claim a general-graph solution.

Sato and Yamaguchi’s revised preprint tests all possible red counts simultaneously with high probability using O(n^ω) finite-field operations, where ω denotes the matrix-multiplication exponent used by their algebraic routines. The algorithm remains randomized; the introduction explicitly retains deterministic polynomial-time Exact Matching as open.

context_blocks.text: Perfect matching already has efficient deterministic algorithms on general graphs. Requiring a prescribed number of red edges adds an exact constraint that the ordinary matching objective does not express. A minimum-red matching and a maximum-red matching only identify two ends of the attainable range; intermediate counts can be missing.

For example, color a six-cycle alternately red and blue. Its two perfect matchings have respectively three and zero red edges. Neither one nor two is attainable. This obstruction appears even in a bipartite graph; allowing odd cycles adds further structure that a general algorithm must handle.

A yes answer is easy to verify once a matching is supplied: check that every vertex is covered once and count the red edges. The difficulty is finding a deterministic procedure that also certifies no instances in polynomial time. The existing algebraic route uses random choices to prevent the cancellation that can hide a feasible matching.

The graph class is essential. A 2026 preprint claims a deterministic solution for bipartite Exact Matching, and the separate catalogue entry records that claim and its formalization limits. This card concerns all graphs. Even a validated bipartite theorem would need another argument before it could settle the proposition here.
