cards.title: Linear-time directed shortest paths with positive integer weights
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic word-RAM algorithm which computes all single-source distances in every directed graph with positive integer edge weights in O(m+n) worst-case time?
cards.definitions: Use a uniform word-RAM with word length w, addressed word memory, addition and subtraction modulo 2^w, multiplication modulo 2^w, Boolean bit operations, shifts by less than w, comparisons and conditional branches, each costing one step. No nonuniform tables are supplied; initialization and preprocessing are charged. The graph has vertex set [n], m explicitly listed directed edges, a designated source s, and weights in {1,…,2^w−1}, with w≥⌈log₂(n+m+2)⌉. Parallel edges and loops are allowed. A distance is the minimum sum of weights on a directed s-to-v path, or infinity if no such path exists. Finite distances can be represented in at most two words; output costs count. The algorithm must work for every w with a universal constant in O(m+n).

context_blocks.text: Positive weights make directed shortest paths a fundamental optimization primitive, yet direction obstructs the classical linear-time result for undirected integer-weighted graphs. The target removes all superlinear overhead in the integer RAM model.

Recent algorithms break the sorting barrier for directed real-weighted shortest paths. Their sublogarithmic overhead and the later almost-linear results are substantial advances, but neither “almost linear” nor “nearly linear” means O(m+n). This card fixes the weight representation and charges preprocessing.

cards.title: Bipartite Exact Matching: deterministic polynomial time
cards.formal: Given a bipartite graph $G=(L\cup R,E)$ with $|L|=|R|=n$, a red/blue coloring of its edges, and $k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$, decide whether $G$ has a perfect matching containing exactly $k$ red edges. The historical question asks for a deterministic algorithm polynomial in the ordinary bit encoding of $(G,k)$. An April 2026 preprint claims such an algorithm. This entry records that claimed resolution and its verification limits; it is no longer labeled as a confirmed open problem.
cards.why: I retain and expand this entry because exact cardinality constraints can remain difficult even when unconstrained optimization is easy. It is also a useful status correction: a research catalogue should preserve the problem and the claimed advance, while distinguishing an attributed preprint theorem from a proof that has been independently checked.
cards.definitions: A perfect matching consists of pairwise vertex-disjoint edges covering every vertex. Exactly k is an equality constraint, not an upper bound or an approximation target. This card concerns sequential deterministic polynomial time. Ordinary bipartite perfect matching in NC and Exact Matching on general graphs are separate questions.

progress.text: El Maalouly’s survey develops algorithms and reductions around Exact Matching while describing deterministic polynomial time as unresolved.
Du’s first preprint version claims a deterministic $O(n^6)$ algorithm for all bipartite graphs and describes its proof as formally verified.

Version 3 states $O(n^6)$ arithmetic complexity and qualifies the Lean result: the main theorem is reduced to eight explicit hypotheses. The claimed mathematical resolution and the formalization scope must be assessed separately.

cards.status_note: Claimed resolution, verification pending. Reviewed 10 September 2026 using version 3. The preprint and its eight formalization hypotheses have not been independently proved or audited here.

context_blocks.text: An ordinary perfect matching assigns every left vertex to a different right vertex. Here an additional equality constraint counts how many selected edges are red. Minimizing or maximizing the red-edge count does not decide whether a particular intermediate count is attainable.

Consider two left vertices and two right vertices, with every possible edge present. Color the two diagonal edges red and the two off-diagonal edges blue. The only perfect matchings have either two red edges or none. There is no perfect matching with exactly one red edge, although one lies between the minimum and maximum attainable counts. Even this small example defeats an interval-based feasibility test.

The randomized algebraic approach encodes matchings in a polynomial and tests whether a relevant coefficient vanishes. Finding a deterministic replacement has made the problem a particularly concrete meeting point of graph algorithms and polynomial identity testing. Approximation results relax the equality constraint and therefore answer a different question.

Du’s April 2026 preprint claims a deterministic solution for every bipartite graph. Version 3 describes its Lean formalization as reducing the main theorem to eight explicit hypotheses, rather than independently checking all ingredients. The paper states that these hypotheses correspond to mathematical results proved there or in prior work. That qualification matters when assessing the original version’s stronger formal-verification wording.

cards.title: An explicit static problem requiring superlogarithmically many cell probes
cards.formal: Does there exist a fixed integer k≥2 and a uniformly polynomial-time computable family of Boolean functions F_n on an n-word database and a k⌈log₂ n⌉-bit query such that its optimal deterministic static cell-probe query complexity t*F(n), with word size ⌈4log₂ n⌉ bits and n⌈log₂ n⌉² memory cells, satisfies t*F(n)/log₂ n→∞ as n→∞?
cards.definitions: For each integer n≥2 put w=⌈4log₂ n⌉ and s=n⌈log₂ n⌉². A database is D∈({0,1}^w)^n, a query is q∈{0,1}^{k⌈log₂ n⌉}, and F_n(D,q)∈{0,1}. Explicit means that a single deterministic Turing machine computes F_n(D,q), given (1^n,D,q), in time polynomial in n; no advice is allowed in this definition. A data structure may preprocess D by any map E_n into s cells of w bits each. Preprocessing time is unrestricted, and this encoding may be nonlinear and nonuniform. For each query, a deterministic adaptive decision tree reads cells, choosing the next address from the query and previously read contents, and must output F_n(D,q) exactly for every database. Computation between probes is free. The trees may depend on n, F and the query, but their only access to D is through E_n(D). Each query starts without free database-dependent private information; memory is static and read-only. Define t*F(n) as the minimum, over all such encodings and trees, of the maximum number of probes over all D and q. All memory cells count toward s. This card fixes a near-linear-space, short-query, one-bit-answer specialization of the broader static lower-bound challenge; it does not assert equivalence to every space or word-size variant.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that some fixed k and admissible uniform family F satisfy: for every real B>0 there is N such that t*F(n)>B log₂ n for every n≥N. Alternatively, prove the exact negation: for every fixed k and every admissible family F, there is a finite B>0 such that t*F(n)≤B log₂ n for arbitrarily large n. In particular, the negative answer need not establish an O(log n) bound for all sufficiently large n.
cards.why: A central unconditional lower-bound bottleneck for data structures: establish that a short, explicitly defined static query fundamentally needs more than logarithmically many memory accesses despite unrestricted preprocessing.

importance.reason: A model-wide challenge connecting algorithms, communication complexity, pseudorandomness and circuit lower bounds, with implications beyond any single geometric or graph problem.

cards.status_note: Primary sources and later-result searches checked on 11 September 2026 did not supply a resolution of the stated static specialization. The STOC 2026 paper retains the broader static barrier as Open Problem 1.1. The fixed near-linear space, short-query Boolean output and uniform polynomial-time family are an expressly recorded specialization; conditional proof barriers and bounds for dynamic memory or superpolynomial query sets do not resolve it.

context_blocks.text: A static data structure pays an initial cost to organize a database and then answers queries against that fixed information. In the cell-probe model, only the number of memory cells read during a query matters. The query algorithm has unlimited computational power between reads. Consequently, a lower bound must identify information that cannot be made locally accessible even by an ingenious encoding; showing that a particular search procedure or arithmetic computation is slow is insufficient.

The space allowance is central. With enough space, preprocessing could store every answer in a table, giving constant-probe queries. Here there are at least n² possible queries, while the stored representation has only O(n log³ n) bits. Conversely, the database itself fits in n cells, so reading all n cells always suffices. The target therefore lies strictly between two elementary strategies: an unrestricted table with one entry for every possible query exceeds the budget, but the problem is always solvable without a computational-time obstruction.

The one-bit answer avoids obtaining a large probe bound merely because the output contains many independent bits. The query length is O(log n), with a fixed constant k. Increasing the query length to n bits can create communication lower bounds of an entirely different magnitude. Likewise, allowing only linear combinations in preprocessing or forbidding adaptive reads changes the collection of encodings and algorithms that a lower bound must defeat.

Koucký, Loff, Molli and Saks formulate the broad static challenge explicitly as Open Problem 1.1. Away from storage that is extremely close to the information-theoretic minimum, familiar general lower-bound approaches have not exceeded the logarithm of the number of queries. The present card turns this challenge into one yes/no proposition by fixing the word size, storage overhead, output alphabet and uniform meaning of an explicit problem. Its stricter conventions should be kept in mind when transferring results from a survey.

Korten, Pitassi and Impagliazzo obtain stronger tradeoffs through local pseudorandom generators. Their improvements are especially informative when the number of probes is small and the cells contain few bits. Their general bound includes an explicit dependence on word size. A gain proved for one-bit cells therefore cannot simply be carried over unchanged to Θ(log n)-bit words. These results advance the tradeoff frontier without proving the superlogarithmic lower bound at the parameters fixed here.

Ko’s 2025 result illustrates another important parameter distinction. For random linear operators with m possible row queries, the lower bound is Ω(min{log(m/s), n/log s}) in a bit-cell formulation. It can exceed log n when the number m of queries grows sufficiently rapidly. With only polynomially many queries, the first term is at most O(log n). The random choice of an operator also does not by itself supply the uniformly polynomial-time explicit family required in this card.

The STOC 2026 natural-proofs paper supplies conditional obstacles to a broad class of proof methods. Such a proof recognizes a sufficiently large, efficiently testable property of function tables that implies data-structure hardness; conjectured local pseudorandom functions would obstruct that recognition. Those update constraints are absent here: the whole database may be preprocessed without a time bound before any query arrives. Neither dynamic result automatically gives the requested static lower bound.

A positive solution would identify a uniformly computable query whose information cannot be recovered with only logarithmically many reads, even after unrestricted preprocessing. This separates a memory-access bottleneck from the running time of known implementations. The limit in the statement is stronger than an arbitrarily large ratio on an infinite subsequence: the ratio must eventually exceed each fixed constant and remain above it. That distinction also affects the exact negative answer.

cards.context:
A static data structure pays an initial cost to organize a database and then answers queries against that fixed information. In the cell-probe model, only the number of memory cells read during a query matters. The query algorithm has unlimited computational power between reads. Consequently, a lower bound must identify information that cannot be made locally accessible even by an ingenious encoding; showing that a particular search procedure or arithmetic computation is slow is insufficient.

The space allowance is central. With enough space, preprocessing could store every answer in a table, giving constant-probe queries. Here there are at least n² possible queries, while the stored representation has only O(n log³ n) bits. Conversely, the database itself fits in n cells, so reading all n cells always suffices. The target therefore lies strictly between two elementary strategies: an unrestricted table with one entry for every possible query exceeds the budget, but the problem is always solvable without a computational-time obstruction.

The one-bit answer avoids obtaining a large probe bound merely because the output contains many independent bits. The query length is O(log n), with a fixed constant k. Increasing the query length to n bits can create communication lower bounds of an entirely different magnitude. Likewise, allowing only linear combinations in preprocessing or forbidding adaptive reads changes the collection of encodings and algorithms that a lower bound must defeat.

Koucký, Loff, Molli and Saks formulate the broad static challenge explicitly as Open Problem 1.1. cards.title: Fully dynamic near-optimal matching with polylogarithmic updates
cards.formal: For every fixed rational ε∈(0,1), is there a randomized fully dynamic algorithm that maintains an explicit matching M with |M|≥ν(G)/(1+ε) in every current general graph G using polylogarithmic expected amortized update time against an oblivious adversary?
cards.definitions: The graph is simple, undirected and unweighted, on the fixed vertex set [n], n≥2; ν(G) is its maximum matching cardinality. It starts empty. An update inserts one absent edge or deletes one present edge. Updates arrive online, but the entire valid sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm’s random bits and is not revealed in advance. More precisely, for every fixed ε and constant a≥1, require constants K,d,B and a uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm A_{ε,a} such that every sequence of T≤n^a updates has expected total initialization-plus-update cost at most K[n+T(log₂(n+2))^d]. Words have B⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ bits; standard word operations, memory access and retained random bits are charged. With probability at least 1−n^{−3}, after every update in the sequence an explicit mate array represents a valid matching satisfying the approximation bound. Reading a vertex’s mate or the matching cardinality takes O(1) time; enumerating all matching edges costs O(n) and need not occur after every update. Changes to the mate array count toward update cost. Constants may depend on ε and a, but not on n, T or the sequence. No polynomial dependence on 1/ε, adaptive-adversary guarantee or worst-case per-update bound is required. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo 2^w, integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length w=Θ(log n) (or Θ(log N) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No polylogarithmic-update algorithm meeting the fixed-accuracy, explicit-matching target was found. Matching-size estimators, ordered-RS-dependent bounds and the 2026 maximal-matching improvement do not resolve it.

context_blocks.text: A maximum matching allocates the largest possible number of disjoint pairs. When an edge changes, recomputing it from scratch ignores the substantial information retained from the preceding graph. The dynamic problem asks how much of that information can be reused while keeping a solution within an arbitrarily small fixed relative loss of optimum. Both insertions and deletions are allowed, so previously useful structure can disappear.

The graph’s optimum changes by at most one after a single edge update, but a particular solution may require coordinated replacements. On a long alternating path, gaining one additional matched edge can involve changing many pairs. Approximation creates room to postpone or distribute some repairs. The difficulty is to do so without accumulating a large loss or spending too much time discovering the repairs that are needed.

An explicit solution is part of the target. A number close to ν(G) need not identify even one edge that can safely be used with the others. A mate array makes this distinction observable: a query at a vertex must return its current partner or report that it is unmatched. Requiring the whole array to be printed after every update would impose an artificial linear output cost, so the formulation instead charges only actual changes and queries.

Maximality is also weaker than near-optimality. In a four-vertex path, selecting only the middle edge gives a maximal matching of size one, while the two outside edges give a maximum matching of size two. Randomized maximal-matching algorithms already achieve very small update times against oblivious sequences. Chuzhoy–Khanna–Song’s STOC 2026 result improves deterministic maximal matching to n^{1/2+o(1)} amortized time; its guarantee still concerns maximality.

A separate sequence of breakthroughs beats the factor-two barrier for estimating matching size in polylogarithmic update time. Azarmehr–Behnezhad–Roghani’s SODA 2024 result obtains an estimate corresponding to a 2−√2−η fraction of optimum in general graphs, for fixed η>0. The paper explicitly studies size estimation. Its title alone can therefore suggest a stronger maintenance result than the theorem actually supplies.

For maintaining actual near-optimal matchings, Assadi–Khanna–Kiss’s SODA 2025 work develops a connection to ordered Ruzsa–Szemerédi graphs. Such a graph has its edges partitioned into matchings, with each matching induced in the union of itself and later matchings. Dense examples quantify how often certain expensive matching searches can recur. Their update bound is expressed through this extremal quantity and works even against adaptive adversaries.

The dependence is roughly n^{o(1)} times the ordered-RS count for matchings of linear size, with accuracy-dependent parameters. A strong enough combinatorial upper bound would yield subpolynomial update time. This does not currently establish polylogarithmic time: n^{o(1)} can grow faster than every fixed power of log n, and the required extremal bounds are themselves unresolved. This connection is not an unconditional lower bound.

Pratt’s SOSA 2026 note relates the ordered and ordinary RS notions at the level of polynomial exponents. Dense ordered examples would imply nearly comparably dense ordinary examples. It resolves a structural question about the reduction’s graph families, but does not determine the density needed for a polylogarithmic dynamic algorithm.

Liu’s 2024 work gives a different advance for bipartite graphs: amortized update time n/2^{Ω(√log n)} times a polynomial in 1/ε. It also relates stronger update bounds to online matrix-vector problems. The dependence on accuracy is essential in those statements. In particular, the ordinary-OMv equivalence stated for approximate vertex cover should not be silently transferred to matching, and a barrier using inverse-polynomial accuracy does not settle this card’s fixed-ε question.

The adversary convention leaves useful flexibility. An oblivious sequence may be carefully chosen to be difficult, but it cannot react to random decisions or the current matching. The algorithm nevertheless receives updates one at a time; knowing that the sequence was fixed does not give access to future deletions. Similarly, amortization permits occasional expensive repairs as long as their expected total cost satisfies the bound.

The inherited Max Planck report explicitly identifies near-optimal fully dynamic matching with polylogarithmic updates as a long-term target. Its page 123 also distinguishes maintaining matching edges from estimating their number, and describes faster progress in the insertion-only setting. Allowing deletion of a vertex, which removes all its incident edges together, does not automatically supply an algorithm for arbitrary individual edge deletions.

The fundamental issue is whether a changing combinatorial optimum can be tracked almost as cheaply as the graph itself is updated. A positive result would close a major gap between coarse approximation and near-optimal explicit solutions. It would also clarify how much global matching structure must be recomputed when each input change is local.

cards.title: Can exact fully dynamic APSP have edge-linear amortized updates and polylogarithmic queries?
cards.formal: For every fixed positive integer c, do there exist a deterministic data structure and constants a,d >= 1 such that the following holds for all n >= 2 and $n\le m\le n^2$? Maintain a directed simple graph on a fixed set of n vertices, with at most m edges at every time and integer edge weights in {1,...,n^c}, under single-edge insertions, deletions, and weight changes. Return the exact current distance from any queried vertex s to any queried vertex t in $O(\log^a n)$ worst-case time. After $O(n^d)$ preprocessing, require $O(m\log^a n)$ amortized time per update and polynomial space. Constants may depend on c, but not on n, m, the initial graph, or the operation sequence.
cards.definitions: The capacity m is supplied in advance and bounds the maximum number of live edges throughout the sequence; it is not a count of all updates. Each ordered vertex pair has at most one edge and there are no self-loops. An insertion adds an absent edge, a deletion removes a present edge, and a weight change replaces the weight of one present edge by another permitted weight. A distance query returns the minimum sum of edge weights on a directed s-to-t path, zero for s=t, and a distinguished infinity value if no path exists. Only the distance is requested, not every path or the whole distance matrix. All answers must be exact for any interleaving of updates and queries. Use a word RAM with Theta(log n)-bit words, with a sufficiently large constant for the fixed weight exponent and polynomially bounded addresses; comparisons, arithmetic, Boolean operations, shifts, and random access cost one step. Amortization means that after preprocessing any U updates and Q queries together cost $O(U m\log^a n+Q\log^a n)$; the query bound must also hold for each query individually.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a data structure with these guarantees for every fixed polynomial weight bound, or prove that the quantified proposition is false. A conditional lower bound must state its assumption. A near-quadratic-in-n update bound only meets the target for dense graphs; a subpolynomial approximation ratio or a guarantee only for insertions does not meet the exact fully dynamic specification.
cards.why: This asks whether exact shortest-path information can be maintained at a cost reflecting the number of input edges, rather than all possible vertex pairs. It is a central dynamic-graph trade-off between update work, sparse structure, and immediate exact access to global information.

importance.reason: A broad exact dynamic-graph frontier with a major sparse-versus-dense gap. It tests whether global metric information can be maintained at input-scale update cost while preserving fast queries.

progress.text: Demetrescu and Italiano give deterministic O(n^2 log^3 n) amortized updates and constant worst-case distance queries for general directed nonnegative-weight graphs.

Henzinger asks for fully dynamic APSP with edge-linear update cost and constant query cost, both allowing polylogarithmic factors. The fixed weight, edge-update, and amortization conventions here make that direction precise.
Mao’s revised paper gives a Monte Carlo algorithm with tilde-O(n^(5/2)) worst-case vertex-update time and near-quadratic space. This addresses a different update guarantee.

context_blocks.text: Recomputing distances from every source after each change is expensive, while postponing the work until a query can make a single query expensive. A dynamic distance oracle tries to divide this work so that both kinds of operation remain useful. The requested update budget is roughly the size of the current graph representation, even when that graph is sparse.

A single changed edge can alter distances for quadratically many vertex pairs. That observation does not by itself rule out a fast oracle: the representation may store those changes implicitly, and the interface only asks for one pair at a time. Proving a lower bound therefore requires more than counting changed entries in a materialized distance matrix.

The classical Demetrescu–Italiano algorithm achieves O(n^2 log^3 n) amortized update time and constant distance-query time for nonnegative weights. This is already close to the proposed bound when m is quadratic in n. The substantial gap is the sparse regime, where the desired amortized update cost can be nearly a factor n smaller.

Several nearby frontiers have different guarantees. Mao’s revised 2024 result targets worst-case vertex-update time and gives a randomized bound at the n^(5/2) scale. ESA 2025 sparsification gives extremely fast dynamic approximate distances, with a growing approximation factor. Neither result establishes the exact, edge-sensitive, amortized target on this card. Fixing those distinctions is necessary when assessing progress.

For an empty collection, OPT is zero. The output is an explicit string over the input alphabet, and containment means ordinary forward contiguous occurrence without reversal, reverse complementation or cyclic wraparound. cards.title: Can LZ77 random access use linear compressed space and logarithmic query time?
cards.formal: Given the greedy LZ77 parse with z phrases of a string $S[1..N]$ over an integer alphabet of size at most N, is there a deterministic word-RAM data structure using O(z) words in total that returns S[i] for any $1\le i\le N$ in worst-case O(log N) time? Words have $\Theta(\log N)$ bits. A phrase is a new literal or a longest prefix of the unparsed suffix having an occurrence starting earlier in S; overlapping copies are allowed. Space includes the stored parse and all query-support information. The uncompressed string is unavailable at query time.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a uniform data structure meeting both bounds for every greedy LZ77 parse, or prove that no such structure exists in the stated model. Linear space measured by a larger grammar or an LZ-End parse does not meet the O(z) requirement.
cards.why: I include this because compression is most useful when a small representation remains usable for selective queries. This question asks whether an extra logarithmic storage cost is an inherent price of navigating repeated data or a consequence of converting to a more convenient representation.
cards.definitions: All asymptotic constants are universal. The model permits standard arithmetic, multiplication, shifts, bitwise operations, comparisons, and indirect addressing on a constant number of words. A copied phrase beginning at b and referring to a<b is decoded sequentially, so self-overlap is well-defined. Preprocessing may take polynomial time in N; the target concerns final storage and query time, not construction in compressed time. Use 1+log N at the smallest lengths.

progress.text: Ganardi, Jeż, and Lohrey show that a straight-line grammar can be balanced to logarithmic derivation depth with only constant-factor size growth. This settles the corresponding logarithmic-access target in terms of grammar size.
Gawrychowski explicitly asks for linear space in the Lempel–Ziv representation and logarithmic-time character access.

Boneh and Gawrychowski obtain deterministic O(z_end)-space random access in $O(1+\log^2(N/z_{\rm end}))$ time for LZ-End. Their introduction retains classical LZ77 random access as open and records $O(z\log(N/z))$-space solutions for it.

This can encode a long text with few phrases, but a position inside one copied phrase may lead to another copy, and then another. Random access asks for just one character without expanding the whole text.

The challenge is not that every deeply referenced string is hard. A long run of one repeated character can be accessed immediately once its simple structure is recognized. The target must work for arbitrary mixtures of copied material, where both the reference chains and the phrase lengths vary. Any shortcuts used to navigate those chains must fit in the compressed-space budget.

Converting the parse to a balanced grammar supplies a route to fast navigation, but the grammar can be larger than the original parse by a logarithmic factor. A space bound proportional to that grammar therefore need not be linear in z. Balancing a grammar already supplied as input is a different, solved representation problem.

The July 2026 LZ-End result is close in spirit: it obtains linear space and improved polylogarithmic access for a variant that restricts copy endpoints. Its parameter counts LZ-End phrases. Since the parsing rule and the number of phrases differ, those guarantees cannot be substituted directly for the classical LZ77 target.

cards.title: Can grammar random access use O(g log g) bits with logarithmic query time?
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic data structure that, for every binary straight-line program G with g rules generating a binary string T of length N, stores a representation in $O(g\log(g+2))$ bits and returns T[i] for any $1\le i\le N$ in $O(\log(N+2))$ worst-case time? Preprocessing must take time polynomial in g and is given G, not an expanded copy of T. The space bound includes every persistent index and any retained grammar. Use the word-RAM model below. The representation may replace G; it need only answer queries to T correctly.
cards.definitions: A binary straight-line program has ordered variables X_1,...,X_g, one rule per variable, and start variable X_g. A rule is X_j -> 0, X_j -> 1, or X_j -> X_a X_b with a,b < j. All variables must be reachable from the start variable. Expansion is unique and finite; g counts rules, not expanded occurrences. The input specifies rule types and indices in O(g log(g+2)) bits. Machine words have $\Theta(\log(N+g+2))$ bits; random access, comparisons, word addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division, Boolean operations, and shifts cost one step. Arithmetic results are restricted to a word. Stored bits may be packed; charge the final partially filled word as well. Queries may use O(log(N+2)) temporary words, initially empty and discarded afterward; this workspace contains no persistent advice. Every input-dependent table retained between queries counts toward the representation budget.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a uniform representation, preprocessing algorithm, and query algorithm satisfying all bounds for every valid G, or prove that no such data structure exists. Space linear in g machine words is insufficient when log N is asymptotically larger than log g. A scheme whose preprocessing first expands an exponentially longer T does not meet the polynomial-in-g preprocessing requirement.
cards.why: Random access is the simplest useful operation on a compressed string. Resolving this target would determine whether the extra address-length information is an inherent price of efficient access or an artifact of current representations, and would make the distinction between compressed bits and machine words precise.

importance.reason: A basic compressed-space versus access-time frontier at the bit level, relevant to many grammar-based operations. The fixed logarithmic target gives a sharper scope than the broader random-access trade-off landscape.

progress.text: Navarro asks whether efficient grammar random access can avoid the extra space used to store all expansion lengths.
Takasaka and I obtain space-efficient SLP encodings supporting logarithmic access; their leading expansion-length term remains g log N in this card’s notation.

Duyster and Kociumaka sharpen and largely match grammar random-access trade-offs in their stated parameter regimes. Theorem 1.1 assumes a space budget above g log N bits; it does not supply the representation asked for here.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026 against the April encoding paper and ICALP 2026 trade-offs. This fixes a particular target within the source’s space-reduction question; results using O(g) words must not be read as O(g log g) bits.

context_blocks.text: A grammar rule stores references to smaller pieces, so its two references need only logarithmically many bits in the number of rules. A position in the expanded string can require many more bits. For example, a short chain of doubling rules can describe an exponentially long string. This difference is why a space bound stated in machine words can hide a substantial overhead relative to the grammar encoding.

To locate a position inside a concatenation, the usual navigation step compares that position with the length of the left expansion. Storing an exact expanded length with every variable is straightforward, but can consume g log N bits. The target asks whether this information can be organized or recovered using a representation comparable in bits to the original grammar, while keeping logarithmic access time.

The April 2026 encoding result improves the grammar representation and keeps logarithmic query time, but retains a g log N expansion-length term. The authors explicitly distinguish their encoding savings from removing that term. Their observation supports treating the latter as a separate question.

ICALP 2026 gives much sharper time-space trade-offs in a broad range of parameters. Its main upper-bound theorem uses a space budget above the g log N scale. Consequently, the optimality statements in that range do not automatically settle the smaller bit budget here. This card fixes logarithmic query time, a binary alphabet, polynomial preprocessing, and explicit workspace rules as a concrete specialization of the seminar’s fewer-auxiliary-bits direction.

cards.definitions: There are n agents and m indivisible goods, with [0]=∅. Agent i values a bundle S by v_i(S)=Σ_{g∈S}v_ig; values are finite, nonnegative real numbers. A partition consists of pairwise disjoint bundles whose union is all goods; empty bundles are allowed. Every good must be allocated exactly once. There are no payments, chores, probabilistic allocations or discarded goods. The displayed condition is envy-freeness up to any positively valued good (EFX): the removed good is tested using the values of agent i, not those of agent j. If v_i is zero on all of A_j, there is no inequality to check for that pair. This fixes the EFX convention of Definition 5 and Open Problem 2 of the cited survey. No algorithm, runtime, or restriction to rational or strictly positive values is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every valuation matrix in the statement admits such a complete partition, or give an instance with n≥4 and finite m for which no complete partition satisfies all the EFX inequalities. The target concerns existence with nonnegative additive values; neither efficient computation nor any stronger fairness or efficiency property is required.

context_blocks.text: Indivisibility prevents ordinary envy-freeness even in the smallest examples. If four people all value a single good at one, whoever receives it is envied by the others. The allocation nevertheless satisfies EFX: removing that good leaves an empty bundle. EFX permits this unavoidable envy while limiting envy that survives the removal of any positively valued item. The removal is a hypothetical comparison; the actual allocation still assigns every good.

The word “any” makes the guarantee demanding. Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 4 and another bundle’s two goods at 6 and 1. Removing the 6-valued good eliminates her envy, so this pair satisfies the weaker EF1 test. Removing the 1-valued good leaves value 6, so this pair violates EFX. All comparisons use the potentially envious agent’s values, which can differ from the recipient’s.

Zero values require a convention. If an agent has value zero for her own bundle and values the goods in another bundle at 1 and 0, removing the positively valued good passes this card’s test. Requiring removal of the zero-valued good to pass as well would fail. That stronger condition on an individual allocation is often called EFX₀. The problem statement retains the survey’s positive-good EFX convention.

For three additive agents, Chaudhury, Garg and Mehlhorn prove complete EFX existence for any number of goods. Thus the universal question starts at four agents; it is the unrestricted number of goods at that first unresolved agent count that already presents a difficulty.

The four-agent theorem of Berger, Cohen, Feldman and Fiat leaves at most one good unassigned. Completeness matters: adding that final good can create new envy, so an almost complete allocation does not itself answer the stated question.

In August 2026, Alkassar, Fouz and Mehlhorn reported complete EFX₀ existence for four agents and at most nine goods, allowing arbitrary nonnegative real values. Their theorem uses reductions and a computational certificate corpus. EFX₀ implies the EFX condition here, but the bounded number of goods leaves the unrestricted target open. The theorem’s stated scope was checked; its computations were not rerun.

Recent nonexistence results concern broader valuation classes. Mackenzie and Suzuki give counterexamples with submodular and subadditive valuations, where the value of a bundle need not equal the sum of its individual goods’ values. Such examples do not meet the additive hypothesis on this card. Likewise, a chores result concerns unwanted items and a different fairness comparison.

The issue is existence for every input valuation matrix, without an efficiency requirement. An affirmative theorem would guarantee a complete allocation with this strong relaxation of envy-freeness. A negative answer needs one additive instance in the stated domain for which every complete partition fails; finding a poor allocation or a failing allocation algorithm is insufficient.

cards.title: A constant-factor approximation for general Santa Claus allocation
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: Is there a universal constant C≥1 and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that allocates indivisible items with arbitrary nonnegative additive agent-specific values so that, with probability at least 2/3, every agent receives total value at least OPT/C, where OPT is the largest achievable minimum agent value?
cards.definitions: An input consists of n≥1 agents, m≥1 items and an explicit n×m matrix (v_ij) of nonnegative rational values, encoded by binary numerators and positive binary denominators. Agent i values a bundle S⊆[m] at v_i(S)=Σ_{j∈S}v_ij. An allocation is a tuple of pairwise disjoint bundles (S_1,…,S_n); unallocated items are permitted. Its value is F(S_1,…,S_n)=min_{i∈[n]}v_i(S_i), and OPT is the maximum of F over all allocations. Let L be the total input bit length. There must be one algorithm, one C independent of n,m and all numerical values, and one polynomial P such that the algorithm always outputs a feasible allocation within P(L) bit operations, for every random tape, and Pr[F≥OPT/C]≥2/3 on every input. The probability refers only to the algorithm’s independent internal random bits and requires the guarantee for all agents simultaneously. A deterministic algorithm is allowed as a special case. Zero values and OPT=0 are allowed, and no positive lower bound on OPT is supplied. The input values are used as given: one may not rescale each agent separately without changing the optimization problem. No identical-valuation, restricted-assignment, bounded-number-of-agents, bounded-number-of-values or bounded-item-degree assumption is imposed. All values are available to a centralized algorithm; incentives, payments and valuation oracles are not part of this problem.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a polynomial-time algorithm achieving the stated guarantee for some fixed C, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Hardness results conditional on a complexity assumption must identify that assumption, including the distinction between deterministic and randomized algorithms. A factor depending on the number of items or agents, a quasi-polynomial-time constant approximation, an estimate without an allocation, or an expected-value guarantee separately for each agent does not meet the target.

cards.status_note: The SODA 2024 reduction paper and SODA 2025 submodular paper explicitly retain the general additive constant-approximation question. Later checked constant guarantees concern restricted assignment or identical valuations, not arbitrary additive matrices. No general resolution found through 11 September 2026. Randomization and simultaneous success for all agents are explicit in this formulation.

context_blocks.text: The objective protects the least satisfied participant. Suppose two agents value each of two items at one. Allocating one item to each gives minimum value one, whereas giving both items to either agent gives minimum value zero. A lottery that gives both items to a uniformly chosen agent gives each agent expected value one, but its minimum value is always zero. This illustrates why the guarantee must concern the quality of one simultaneous allocation.

Even additive values allow substantial heterogeneity: an item can be extremely valuable to one agent, moderately valuable to another, and worthless to a third. Maximizing total welfare would assign each item to an agent valuing it most, independently of the other items. Maximizing minimum welfare couples those decisions because every agent needs adequate value from resources that cannot be reused. The valuations are inputs to the optimization problem, without strategic reporting constraints.

The name Santa Claus is used differently across papers. Some reserve it for restricted assignment, where each item j has a single intrinsic value w_j and v_ij is either w_j or zero. This card uses the broader max-min allocation problem with arbitrary entries. The difference is decisive: constant-factor algorithms are known for restricted assignment, while the general constant-factor question remains open.

Chakrabarty, Chuzhoy and Khanna give an approximation within m^ε for every fixed ε>0, where m is the number of items in this card’s notation. Their approximation–time tradeoff also yields a polylogarithmic factor in quasi-polynomial time. Choosing a smaller fixed ε improves the approximation exponent but increases the polynomial running-time exponent. Letting ε depend on m to try to force a constant factor does not preserve the known polynomial-time guarantee.

Their work also highlights a limitation of a standard configuration relaxation. For a target T, a configuration for agent i is a bundle worth at least T; fractional variables select configurations while respecting item capacities in aggregate. Integral feasible configurations would give every agent enough value. In the general setting, however, the relaxation can overestimate the integral optimum by a factor of order √n. The algorithm uses the relaxation recursively on transformed instances, instead of relying on a constant-loss rounding of its original optimum.

Restricted assignment has stronger structure. Haxell and Szabó’s 2025 work improves its configuration-LP integrality-gap bound from 3.808 to 3.534 using topological criteria for independent transversals. This is a bound on the distance between fractional and integral optima in the restricted model. It does not assert a 3.534 algorithm for the arbitrary-value matrix, and an existence argument for a good integral solution must be distinguished from an efficient way to construct it.

There is a striking link with minimizing makespan on unrelated machines. Bamas, Lindermayr, Megow, Rohwedder and Schlöter show that a (2−1/α)-approximation for unrelated makespan, for fixed α≥2, would yield an (α+δ)-approximation for general Santa Claus for every fixed δ>0. Thus any fixed improvement below two in that scheduling problem would answer this question positively. Their general implication goes in this direction; equivalence is established for a specified two-value case.

Bamas, Morell and Rohwedder’s SODA 2025 result extends the m^ε and quasi-polynomial polylogarithmic guarantees to arbitrary monotone submodular valuations. It uses a recursively structured LP with exponentially many variables and constraints. This broadens the class of preferences that can be handled, while retaining a growing approximation factor even on the additive instances considered here.

More recent constant guarantees also require attention to their input promise. Boehmer’s April 2026 paper obtains value at least 0.4OPT for identical monotone submodular valuations. Identical preferences are a substantial restriction, even though submodularity is more general than additivity. The outstanding question concerns unrestricted disagreement about item values. Settling it would clarify whether balancing heterogeneous indivisible resources admits a constant loss at polynomial computational cost.

cards.definitions: There are exactly three agents, indexed 1,2,3, and m≥0 goods indexed by [m]={1,…,m}. The input gives m and each value v_i,g=p_i,g/q_i,g with integers p_i,g≥0 and q_i,g>0 encoded in binary. N is the total bit length of this explicit table and its delimiters. For any bundle S⊆[m], v_i(S)=∑_{g∈S}v_i,g. A complete allocation is an ordered partition (A₁,A₂,A₃) of [m]; bundles may be empty. The output assigns each good one owner in {1,2,3}. It is EFX if v_i(A_i)≥v_i(A_j∖{g}) for every i,j∈{1,2,3} and every g∈A_j, including goods with v_i,g=0. The removed good is evaluated by agent i. An empty A_j gives no inequality; a singleton leaves the empty bundle of value zero. Removal is hypothetical and does not discard a good from the output. Values may have arbitrary magnitudes and denominators. The algorithm is uniform, deterministic and always correct, with ordinary bit-operation cost and no oracle, payments or divisible goods. Its running time must be polynomial in N, not in the numeric values.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer gives an algorithm and proves completeness, every EFX inequality, and a worst-case polynomial bit bound on all inputs. A negative answer proves that no such polynomial-time algorithm exists. Existence alone is already established for this three-agent additive model; a particular unfair allocation, pseudopolynomial runtime or a relaxed fairness guarantee does not answer the computational question.

context_blocks.title: Every possible removed good matters
context_blocks.text: Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 4 and the goods in another bundle at 5 and 1. Removing the good worth 5 would remove her envy, but removing the one worth 1 would leave value 5, still above 4. This pair passes the weaker “some good” test of EF1 and fails EFX. The test always uses the envious agent’s values, since the agents may disagree about an item’s worth.

context_blocks.title: Existence has already been proved
context_blocks.text: Chaudhury, Garg and Mehlhorn establish complete EFX allocations for three additive agents. Their definition tests all goods, and their perturbation lemma handles zero values and ties. Thus this card asks how efficiently such an allocation can be found. The general existence card TCS-0011 concerns more agents and uses its explicitly stated positive-good convention.

context_blocks.title: Why pseudopolynomial time is insufficient
context_blocks.text: A value as large as 2^L needs only L+1 binary digits. An algorithm whose time grows polynomially in that value may therefore take exponentially many steps in its encoding length. The inherited question requires a bound polynomial in the complete valuation table’s bit length, including denominators. It does not require the stronger guarantee that the number of arithmetic operations be independent of value bit lengths.

context_blocks.title: Nearby guarantees do not give exact EFX
context_blocks.text: Ashuri, Gkatzelis and Sgouritsa’s 2025 result computes EF2X for three agents in polynomial time: envy disappears after removing any two goods, a weaker requirement. Their paper explicitly leaves exact EFX at the pseudopolynomial frontier. The May 2026 preprint reports improved multiplicative approximations, including 2/3-EFX for up to eight agents; this also permits remaining envy and does not settle exact EFX for three.

cards.definitions: An instance has n≥1 agents, m≥0 goods and an explicit table of values v_i,g=p_i,g/q_i,g, with integers p_i,g≥0 and q_i,g>0 in binary. Its bit length N includes n, m and the table. For S⊆[m], v_i(S)=∑_{g∈S}v_i,g. An allocation (A₁,…,A_n) partitions [m] into labeled bundles, possibly empty; its output lists one owner for each good. It is α-EFX if v_i(A_i)≥α·v_i(A_j∖{g}) for every pair i,j and every g∈A_j, including goods worth zero to i. All comparisons use i’s values. Empty A_j imposes no inequality; a singleton leaves value zero. Each fixed α in the set must have one finite, always-correct deterministic Turing machine and constants C,k with runtime at most C(N+1)^k on every instance. The machine, C and k may depend on α, but not on n, m or the valuations. α is a fixed guarantee, not an input; no polynomial dependence on an accuracy parameter is required. The supremum is the least upper bound of these achievable factors; attainment at the endpoint is not assumed. The set is nonempty since α=0 is trivial, and is bounded by 1 by definition.
cards.answer_criterion: Identify a real a∈[0,1] and prove that a=α_alg: achievable polynomial-time factors approach a arbitrarily closely from below, and no such algorithm guarantees any factor greater than a within [0,1]. An algorithm attaining a suffices for the first part but is not required. A conditional hardness result establishes only the corresponding conditional bound; a guarantee for one fixed number of agents does not establish the universal value.

context_blocks.title: How to read the approximation factor
context_blocks.text: Higher α means a stronger guarantee, with α=1 giving exact EFX. Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 4 and the goods of another bundle at 5 and 1. For this pair, the restrictive removal leaves value 5, so the inequality holds exactly when α≤4/5. This illustrates one pair’s test, not a lower bound for every allocation of an instance.

context_blocks.title: The known general guarantee
context_blocks.text: Amanatidis, Markakis and Ntokos give a polynomial-time algorithm with factor (√5−1)/2≈0.618. Their definition covers every good, even zero-valued ones. Thus the checked bounds are (√5−1)/2≤α_alg≤1; the upper endpoint here comes from the definition, not from an impossibility theorem.

context_blocks.title: Why the number of agents matters
context_blocks.text: The May 2026 preprint reports a 2/3-EFX algorithm for up to eight agents. This improves the guarantee on that restricted domain, while the present question requires a single algorithm for arbitrarily many agents. Its stronger-looking factors for EF2X and other k-good relaxations allow more removals and therefore do not give the same EFX guarantee.

context_blocks.title: Existence, computation and a supremum
context_blocks.text: TCS-1116 asks about universal existence without an efficiency requirement; this card additionally requires polynomial bit complexity. The 2023 survey treats the existence frontier and explains the known algorithmic guarantees. Even α_alg=1 would not by itself provide an exact EFX algorithm: different algorithms might approach 1 without any attaining it. The word supremum deliberately preserves this distinction.

Amanatidis, Markakis and Ntokos give a polynomial-time algorithm with factor (√5−1)/2≈0.618. Their definition covers every good, even zero-valued ones. Thus the checked bounds are (√5−1)/2≤α_alg≤1; the upper endpoint here comes from the definition, not from an impossibility theorem.

The May 2026 preprint reports a 2/3-EFX algorithm for up to eight agents. This improves the guarantee on that restricted domain, while the present question requires a single algorithm for arbitrarily many agents. Its stronger-looking factors for EF2X and other k-good relaxations allow more removals and therefore do not give the same EFX guarantee.

TCS-1116 asks about universal existence without an efficiency requirement; this card additionally requires polynomial bit complexity. The 2023 survey treats the existence frontier and explains the known algorithmic guarantees. Even α_alg=1 would not by itself provide an exact EFX algorithm: different algorithms might approach 1 without any attaining it. The word supremum deliberately preserves this distinction.

cards.definitions: An instance has n≥1 agents, m≥0 indivisible chores, and finite real costs c_i,g≥0. Agent i assigns a bundle S⊆[m] the additive cost c_i(S)=∑_{g∈S}c_i,g; lower cost is better. Let Π_n([m]) be the finite set of ordered partitions of [m] into n disjoint bundles, allowing empty bundles. Define μ_i=min_{(P₁,…,P_n)∈Π_n([m])} max_{1≤j≤n} c_i(P_j). All bundles in this minimum are evaluated using the same agent i’s costs. A complete allocation belongs to Π_n([m]): each chore has exactly one owner, with no splitting, disposal or payments. The allocation must satisfy all agents’ inequalities simultaneously, although their benchmark partitions can differ. The inequalities also apply when μ_i=0, without dividing by zero; in that case every chore has zero cost to i. There is no computation-time requirement or fixed bound on n or m. The smallest universal factor exists: for each finite instance its feasible factors form a closed upper interval, and the known universal upper bound makes the intersection of these intervals nonempty.
cards.answer_criterion: Identify a real a≥1 and prove both that every instance admits an allocation with c_i(A_i)≤aμ_i for all i, and that for every β with 1≤β<a there is an instance with no such β-allocation. The lower-bound instances may depend on β; one instance need not attain the worst universal ratio. A guarantee restricted to a fixed number of agents or a special class of costs does not determine α*.

context_blocks.title: The burden an agent can guarantee herself
context_blocks.text: Imagine partitioning all chores into n bundles before receiving the most costly bundle. The minimax share is the smallest worst burden that the agent can arrange. With two bundles and chore costs 4, 3 and 3, this benchmark is 6, achieved by {4} and {3,3}; the proportional cost is only 5. Indivisibility is why the two benchmarks differ.

context_blocks.title: Exact fairness can fail
context_blocks.text: Different agents can disagree about which chores are difficult, so their individually optimal partitions need not fit together. Feige, Sapir and Tauber give a three-agent, nine-chore example in which every agent’s minimax share is 43 but every complete allocation gives someone cost at least 44. Thus α*≥44/43>1.

context_blocks.title: The universal gap
context_blocks.text: Huang and Segal-Halevi prove that factor 13/11 always suffices. Together with the negative example, the checked bounds are 44/43≤α*≤13/11, approximately 1.0233 to 1.1818. The upper bound is an existence statement at the exact factor; finding such an allocation within a specified running time is an additional question.

context_blocks.title: What newer guarantees cover
context_blocks.text: The 2025 bin-packing paper gives a 15/13 multiplicative guarantee for personalized bivalued costs and improves a different, ordinal MMS benchmark in general. These do not replace the general multiplicative bound here. The September 2026 comparison-query preprint still uses 13/11 as the general frontier and studies how little preference information an algorithm needs.

context_blocks.title: Why this optimum matters
context_blocks.text: The factor measures the unavoidable loss caused by allocating whole burdens while respecting everyone’s own costs. A factor closer to 1 means that every agent can be kept closer to her personal benchmark. The easy/difficult-chores source gives exact fairness in special cost models, illustrating why those models must be distinguished from unrestricted additive costs.

cards.definitions: The goods are M=[m]. For i∈{1,2}, finite real numbers v_i,g>0 define v_i(S)=∑_{g∈S}v_i,g for every S⊆M. Different bundles may have equal value. Budgets b₁,b₂ are arbitrary positive real numbers. A price vector assigns each good a real price p_g≥0, with p(S)=∑_{g∈S}p_g. A competitive equilibrium consists of p and a partition (A₁,A₂) of M, allowing an empty bundle, such that p(A_i)≤b_i and v_i(A_i)≥v_i(S) for every S⊆M with p(S)≤b_i, for both agents simultaneously. All goods must be allocated once. Agents value only their goods: unspent budget has no utility and need not be exhausted. Ties among best affordable bundles are permitted. For each fixed valuation pair, its exceptional set lies in (0,∞)² and must have Lebesgue measure zero, meaning it can be covered by countably many rectangles whose total area is smaller than any prescribed ε>0. The exceptional set may depend on the valuations. The allocation and prices may depend on the valuations and budgets. This is an exact existence statement with no running-time or finite-encoding requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that the exceptional budget set has measure zero for every finite positive additive two-agent instance, or give one such instance and prove that its nonexistence set has positive two-dimensional Lebesgue measure. Failure at a single budget pair, including equal budgets, is insufficient for a negative answer; approximate clearing or a result confined to near-equal budgets is insufficient for a positive answer.

context_blocks.title: Why equal budgets can fail
context_blocks.text: Suppose both agents value one good positively and each has budget 1. At any price at most 1 both can afford and prefer the good, but only one can receive it; at a price above 1 neither can buy it. If the budgets become 1 and 1.01, a price of 1.005 gives a competitive equilibrium: only the richer agent can afford the good. This simple example explains why an exceptional line of budget pairs may be allowed.

context_blocks.title: What almost all means
context_blocks.text: The question covers budgets with arbitrarily unequal purchasing power as well as nearly equal ones. It permits a set of failures with zero area, rather than requiring existence at every pair or merely at many sampled pairs. A positive answer would mean that a budget pair drawn from any continuous density avoids the exceptional set with probability one.

context_blocks.title: The gap beyond known cases
context_blocks.text: Babaioff, Nisan and Talgam-Cohen establish existence for two additive agents with sufficiently close unequal budgets, and generic existence for identical preferences under their stated preference conventions. Segal-Halevi’s account gives almost-all existence with at most four goods and leaves the arbitrary additive case with five or more goods open. Failure examples for more general monotone preferences do not automatically give additive counterexamples.

context_blocks.title: Prices as allocation rules
context_blocks.text: Budgets represent purchasing entitlements and prices coordinate which bundles are simultaneously affordable. The target retains exact allocation of every good and exact optimality for each agent. Adding utility for cash, allowing unsold goods or replacing each whole good by fractions produces a different market.

cards.title: FIXP-hardness of exact Hylland–Zeckhauser equilibrium
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: Is computing an exact Hylland–Zeckhauser equilibrium for a one-sided matching market FIXP-hard under the standard FIXP reductions?
cards.definitions: There are equally many agents and unit-supply goods with explicitly given nonnegative rational utilities. Each agent has budget one and consumes a lottery totaling one unit. At equilibrium the lotteries clear the market and maximize each agent’s expected utility subject to budget and unit-demand constraints. Exact equilibrium coordinates may be irrational. FIXP is the class of fixed-point search problems defined by algebraic circuits with rational constants and the standard arithmetic/max/min operations.

context_blocks.text: The Hylland–Zeckhauser market turns random assignment into a pricing equilibrium with fairness and efficiency properties. Exact equilibrium is known to belong to FIXP, while approximation is PPAD-complete.

The source explicitly leaves exact FIXP-hardness open. This is not the already established hardness of approximate equilibrium, nor a claim that every exact output can be written as a short rational vector. An exact classification would identify the real-algebraic difficulty of this central assignment mechanism.

cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.

cards.definitions: An input consists of a list of n≥1 agents, a list G of m≥0 goods, and an explicit n-by-m table of nonnegative integers vᵢg written in binary. Input length N counts these lists and all value bits. Agent i assigns a bundle S⊆G the additive value vᵢ(S)=∑g∈S vᵢg, with vᵢ(∅)=0. Let Πₙ(G) be the finite set of labeled partitions (P₁,…,Pₙ) of all goods into n disjoint bundles; empty bundles are allowed. Define μᵢ=maxP∈Πₙ(G) min1≤j≤n vᵢ(Pⱼ). Each agent uses her own valuation for every bundle in this benchmark partition. A complete allocation is A∈Πₙ(G), and the input is a yes-instance exactly when some A satisfies vᵢ(Aᵢ)≥μᵢ for every i. A zero benchmark imposes the inequality vᵢ(Aᵢ)≥0 and involves no division. Benchmark values are not supplied as part of the input. There are no connectivity constraints, arrivals, transfers, discarded goods or fractional allocations. Computation uses the usual deterministic bit-cost model unless a complexity class explicitly permits nondeterminism or an oracle. The nonnegative rational binary-value version has the same polynomial-time classification: each agent’s row can be scaled by a positive common denominator of polynomial bit length without changing the fairness inequalities.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a proved classification or matching bounds for this exact existence decision predicate, under an explicitly fixed precision and reduction convention. The source import does not yet fix that requested precision, so the card remains an incomplete computational benchmark. Hardness of computing μᵢ, finding an optimal allocation, or solving a constrained variant does not by itself classify this yes/no predicate.

context_blocks.title: Choose a partition, receive its least valuable bundle
context_blocks.text: An agent’s maximin share is what she can guarantee by dividing the goods into n bundles and then taking the bundle she values least. Each agent may prefer a different partition. The question is whether a single allocation can simultaneously meet all these personal guarantees.

context_blocks.title: An example and an important distinction
context_blocks.text: For two agents who both value three goods at 4, 3 and 3, each maximin share is 4. Giving one agent the first good and the other the last two meets both benchmarks, although the first agent receives less than her proportional share of 5. Identical valuations always admit an MMS allocation by the definition of an optimal common partition. Consequently, difficulty in computing that partition need not make its existence difficult to decide.

context_blocks.title: What is known about the decision problem
context_blocks.text: The 2023 survey states that NP-hardness is unknown for general nonnegative additive goods valuations. The existence problem has a Δ₂ᴾ upper bound, also recorded in the 2020 work on the broader graph-constrained model. Here Δ₂ᴾ=Pᴺᴾ means deterministic polynomial time with an oracle answering NP decision questions. This upper bound does not give an ordinary polynomial-time algorithm.

context_blocks.title: Nearby hardness results concern different tasks
context_blocks.text: Maximin share and minimax share reverse the order of the minimum and maximum and need not agree. Likewise, computing a fair allocation under an existence promise is a search problem. The August 2026 temporal preprint studies fairness after every round of irreversible arrivals. Hardness in any of these settings cannot be transferred to the static unconstrained existence question without an appropriate reduction.

context_blocks.title: Why a classification matters
context_blocks.text: An exact allocation need not exist when agents value goods differently. Understanding how hard it is to detect existence would separate the cost of evaluating a fairness benchmark from the cost of deciding whether the benchmarks can coexist. It would also clarify when a failure to find an exact allocation reflects computational difficulty rather than an impossible demand.

cards.definitions: An instance consists of a finite set G of m≥0 indivisible goods and n agents. Each number vᵢg is a nonnegative real, and vᵢ(S)=∑g∈S vᵢg for S⊆G. Let Πd(G) denote all labeled partitions (P₁,…,Pd) of G into d pairwise disjoint bundles, allowing empty bundles. The 1-out-of-d maximin share of agent i is μᵢ(d)=maxP∈Πd(G) min1≤j≤d vᵢ(Pⱼ). The maximum is attained because the set of partitions is finite. A complete allocation A belongs to Πₙ(G): every good goes to exactly one agent, with no copies, payments, disposal or fractional goods. Define Dₙ as the set of positive integers d such that for every m and every valuation table there exists such an A with all n inequalities. Then d*(n)=min Dₙ. Increasing d weakens each benchmark. Known universal upper bounds make Dₙ nonempty, so this minimum is attained. The quantifiers are ∀n, choose d*(n), then ∀instances, ∃allocation; d may not depend on the number or values of the goods. This is an existence extremum, with no computation-time or preference-query restriction.
cards.answer_criterion: Give the exact function d*(n) for all positive integers n, with a universal existence proof at the proposed value and a matching impossibility proof for every smaller positive denominator. By monotonicity, when d*(n)>1 a counterexample at d*(n)−1 suffices for the latter part. An improved upper bound, an asymptotic leading constant, or a result permitting additional copies does not determine the requested exact function.

context_blocks.title: Relax the number of benchmark bundles
context_blocks.text: An agent imagines dividing all goods and then receiving her least valuable bundle. Ordinary MMS uses n bundles, one per real agent. Using a larger imaginary number d lowers the required share, while the actual allocation still has n recipients. The question is how little this benchmark must be weakened to make it universally achievable.

context_blocks.title: A small example
context_blocks.text: If an agent values each of six goods at 1, her 1-out-of-2 share is 3 and her 1-out-of-3 share is 2. Those numbers describe her personal benchmarks, not how many agents must actually receive goods. Different agents can value the same goods differently, so their best benchmark partitions need not coincide.

context_blocks.title: What ordinal means here
context_blocks.text: The fairness comparison is determined by each agent’s ranking of complete bundles. It is preserved if that ranking stays the same. Knowing only an ordering of individual goods does not generally determine the ordering of their sums. Thus this question does not assume an algorithm receives only individual-item rankings.

context_blocks.title: The known denominator bounds
context_blocks.text: For n≥2 the checked results give d*(n)≤min{2n−2, ⌊3n/2⌋, 4⌈n/3⌉}; retaining the minimum handles rounding for small n. The last bound comes from the 2024 result. Trivially d*(1)=1 and d*(n)≥n: with only d<n goods valued at 1 by everyone, a 1-out-of-d guarantee would require a good for every agent. The exact universal denominator remains undetermined.

context_blocks.title: Why the exact threshold matters
context_blocks.text: An exact answer would identify how much competition an indivisible-resource fairness benchmark must tolerate before everyone can be protected. Recent work combines ordinal shares with envy guarantees in restricted preference classes. Those additional guarantees are useful, but they do not settle the unrestricted denominator function asked for here.

cards.definitions: For agent i, each good g has a nonnegative real value vᵢg and every bundle B⊆G has value vᵢ(B)=∑g∈B vᵢg; the empty bundle has value zero. A complete allocation partitions all goods into n labeled, disjoint bundles, possibly empty. Each good goes to exactly one agent. The displayed condition is envy-freeness up to any k goods, abbreviated EFkX: each comparison uses the potentially envious agent i’s values on both sides. The removed set S is hypothetical and is chosen universally, not chosen by the allocation algorithm to make the inequality easier. Actual goods are not removed or discarded. If |Aⱼ|≤k, the comparison is automatically satisfied because its right side is zero; this agrees with treating the source’s k-item condition as vacuous for shorter bundles. Zero-valued goods count as goods and may belong to S. The constant k is chosen before the instance and is independent of n, the number of goods and all values. This is exact existence; it imposes no efficiency requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that at least one universal constant k satisfies the stated existence claim, or prove its negation: for every integer k≥1 there is a finite additive goods instance such that every complete allocation violates at least one of its required inequalities. A counterexample for one k, or an allocation with a multiplicative factor below 1, does not resolve this quantifier structure.

context_blocks.title: How much envy can indivisibility explain?
context_blocks.text: One indivisible valuable item can prevent exact envy-freeness. EFkX allows a bounded number of items in the envied bundle to account for that discrepancy. It requires envy to disappear even after deleting the least helpful k items from the envious agent’s perspective. The question is whether some fixed allowance works for arbitrarily many agents.

context_blocks.title: Any removal versus a favorable removal
context_blocks.text: Suppose an agent values her own bundle at 5 and another bundle’s three goods at 6, 1 and 1. Removing its 6-valued good eliminates her envy, but removing either 1-valued good leaves value 7, so the pair fails EF1X. It also fails EF2X: removing the two 1-valued goods leaves value 6. This illustrates why an existential choice of removed goods is a different, weaker condition.

context_blocks.title: The connection to EFX
context_blocks.text: For k=1 this is the usual any-item EFX condition, including zero-valued items. A universal EFX existence theorem would answer this question positively. This card permits any fixed k, so it asks for a weaker universal guarantee. Choosing k separately for each instance, for example as its total number of goods, would make the property vacuous and is excluded.

context_blocks.title: Exact results for a fixed number of agents
context_blocks.text: The AAAI 2025 result establishes EF2X for four agents, in a valuation class that includes additive goods. That is a concrete exact existence theorem. It fixes the number of agents and therefore does not supply the universal constant-k guarantee for unrestricted n.

context_blocks.title: The 2026 approximation result
context_blocks.text: The May 2026 preprint gives (k+1)/(k+2)-EFkX allocations for every fixed k≥2 and any number of agents. This relaxes the inequality to vᵢ(Aᵢ)≥αvᵢ(Aⱼ∖S), where α<1. Although α approaches 1 as k grows, no finite k in that theorem attains exact fairness. Its negative graph-orientation results additionally restrict who may receive a good.

sentences: EFkX compares each agent’s bundle with another bundle after any k of that other bundle’s goods are hypothetically removed.
The same agent’s valuation is used on both sides, and all actual goods must still be allocated.
The question asks whether one constant k works for every number of agents and every nonnegative additive goods instance.

cards.definitions: The n agents are indexed by {1,…,n}. Each utility is an arbitrary real-valued function on all subsets of the finite set M, normalized only at the empty set; no additivity, monotonicity, submodularity, common ranking or identical-utilities assumption is imposed. A complete allocation is an ordered partition of M into n pairwise disjoint bundles, with empty bundles allowed. An agent i envies j when uᵢ(Aᵢ)<uᵢ(Aⱼ). The displayed condition is envy-freeness up to one item (EF1) for mixed items. If there is no envy, X=∅ works. Otherwise one may hypothetically remove one item from i’s bundle or one item from j’s bundle, and compare both remaining bundles using i’s utility. Removing one item from both bundles simultaneously is not permitted. The choice of X may depend on i,j and the whole allocation. These removals only define the fairness comparison; no item is discarded or transferred from the complete allocation. Items have no required permanent designation as goods or chores, since an item’s marginal utility may depend on the surrounding bundle. The question concerns existence and imposes no input encoding, value-query bound or running-time requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove EF1 existence for every n≥3 and every normalized arbitrary utility profile on a finite item set, or give a finite profile and prove that every complete allocation violates the displayed inequality for some ordered pair, for every allowed one-item removal. An impossibility result for a stronger fairness notion does not refute EF1, and an existence theorem permitting two removed items does not establish it.

context_blocks.title: Why either bundle can supply the removed item
context_blocks.text: With desirable goods, envy can disappear after ignoring a valuable item held by someone else. With burdens, it can disappear after ignoring a costly item in the envious agent’s own bundle. For example, if i values her bundle at −4 and j’s at 2, and deleting one item from her own bundle raises its value to 2, that comparison satisfies EF1.

context_blocks.title: One item can change character
context_blocks.text: An arbitrary utility can satisfy u({a})=u({b})=1 but u({a,b})=−3. Each item is beneficial when received alone and harmful when added to the other. This is allowed by the question, so a fixed classification of every item as a good or chore would restrict the model.

context_blocks.title: What was known in the survey
context_blocks.text: The survey records EF1 existence for two agents with arbitrary utilities and for any number of agents under additive or doubly-monotonic utilities. Doubly-monotonic means that, for each agent, every item has a fixed nonnegative or nonpositive marginal effect in every bundle. Open Question 1 removes that restriction for three or more agents.

context_blocks.title: One removal versus two
context_blocks.text: The AAAI 2026 paper proves related existence statements for a relaxation allowing one removal from each compared bundle, for nonnegative or nonpositive valuations. That may remove two items in a comparison. The present target allows at most one item in total and permits arbitrary real utility values.
