context_blocks.text: Computing gˣ mod p is efficient by repeated squaring, even when x is given in binary and is as large as p−2. The inverse problem asks which exponent produced a residue. A polynomial-time solution would remove the computational asymmetry used in finite-field discrete-logarithm cryptography. It would also solve the corresponding computational Diffie–Hellman problem by recovering an exponent, although hardness of discrete logarithms alone does not establish every stronger security assumption.

A proposed answer is easy to verify: check the exponent range and compute gˣ mod p. Consequently a bounded-error polynomial algorithm could be repeated until a verified answer is obtained, giving expected polynomial time with no incorrect output. Conversely, a verified expected-polynomial-time solver can be truncated and repeated to obtain constant success within a polynomial budget. This makes the fixed runtime convention compatible with the usual Las Vegas formulation.

The number field sieve exploits arithmetic structure that generic group algorithms cannot see. It gathers multiplicative relations among suitably smooth objects, solves a large linear system, and reduces an individual target to the resulting logarithms. Its usual large-characteristic complexity estimates have the heuristic subexponential form exp(O((ln p)^{1/3}(ln ln p)^{2/3})). This grows faster than every polynomial in the bit length.

Generic lower bounds do not settle the concrete prime-field problem. Shoup proves a square-root barrier in the size of the largest prime factor of a group’s order when elements are accessed through an abstract random encoding. The present algorithm receives actual residues and can use their number-theoretic structure, as the sieve already does. A proof against the oracle model cannot simply be transferred to this richer interface.

The field regime is crucial. Kleinjung and Wesolowski give a rigorous expected-time bound (p·d)^{2log₂d+O(1)} for discrete logarithms in F_{p^d}. For fixed p and growing extension degree d this is quasipolynomial in the input size. For prime fields d=1 and growing p, that expression is merely polynomial in p, which is exponential in its binary length. Their breakthrough therefore leaves this question open.

Later sieve work also studies how preprocessing can be shared across targets and across fields. The Discrete Logarithm Factory paper develops such improvements, especially for non-prime fields, and distinguishes the cost of a target logarithm from the cost of building reusable data. Here all preprocessing is charged to the algorithm on a single input, so a cheap online lookup after a very expensive table construction is insufficient.

cards.title: Exact Euclidean SVP in single-exponential time and polynomial space
cards.formal: Do absolute constants C,d>0 and a randomized classical algorithm exist that, given any rational rank-n lattice basis B of bit length L, find a shortest nonzero Euclidean lattice vector with probability at least 2/3 using at most 2^{Cn}L^d bit operations and L^d bits of working space?
cards.definitions: The input is B∈Q^{m×n}, with m≥n≥1 and linearly independent columns; each rational entry is encoded by a signed binary numerator and a positive binary denominator. L includes the matrix dimensions and all entry encodings. The lattice is Λ(B)={Bz:z∈Zⁿ}, and λ₁(Λ)=min_{z∈Zⁿ\{0}}‖Bz‖₂, with the ordinary Euclidean norm in R^m. Output a nonzero integer coordinate vector z satisfying ‖Bz‖₂=λ₁(Λ); any minimizer is acceptable. The algorithm is a uniform probabilistic Turing machine with read-only input, write-only output and a stream of independent random bits. Every stored bit, including retained randomness and intermediate lattice vectors, counts toward space; external writable storage and preprocessing oracles are unavailable. The time and space limits must hold on every execution, and the success probability must hold separately for every valid input. The exponent n is lattice rank, not ambient dimension or coefficient precision. All preprocessing and precision management count. There is no promise of a unique shortest vector, a random lattice, a reduced input basis or approximation slack.
cards.answer_criterion: An affirmative answer gives an algorithm satisfying both bounds simultaneously with a proof of exact success on every lattice. A negative answer proves that every randomized polynomial-space algorithm fails some single-exponential-time requirement, or establishes an appropriate time-space lower bound excluding the stated constants. An example defeating one enumeration or sieving method is not enough. Exponential-space algorithms and polynomial-space algorithms taking 2^{Θ(n log n)} time leave the question open.
cards.why: A canonical time-space tradeoff question in exact algorithms: can the single-exponential speed of lattice sieving and Voronoi methods be achieved with only polynomial memory?

importance.reason: A longstanding resource boundary for exact lattice algorithms, central to enumeration versus sieving and increasingly relevant to lattice time-space hardness assumptions.

Koyuncu–Linker–Ozel discuss a coarse-grained polynomial-memory sieving regime; a general exact-success and single-exponential-time guarantee for that regime is not established in the inspected analysis.

context_blocks.text: The familiar exact algorithms offer two different resource profiles. Enumeration explores candidate lattice vectors while retaining a relatively small search state, but its proved worst-case time is n^{O(n)}. Sieving and Voronoi methods achieve 2^{O(n)} time by retaining exponentially many vectors or geometric constraints. The question asks whether one can obtain the faster asymptotic time without the exponential memory.

These time scales differ by more than a constant in the exponent: n^{cn}=2^{cn log₂n}. For any fixed C, the factor log₂n eventually makes n^{cn} exceed 2^{Cn}. Conversely, this card permits a large constant C. A polynomial-memory algorithm with time 2^{100n} would resolve the existence question affirmatively even if it were unusable in practice and slower than current exponential-memory algorithms at moderate ranks.

The output is exact, and the zero vector is excluded. Returning a vector whose length is within a fixed or polynomial factor of optimum solves a different task. Ties create no ambiguity: if several shortest vectors exist, any one is valid. Rational input also allows exact comparison of squared lengths, so the definition does not rely on floating-point tolerance or an unspecified geometric oracle.

The standard basis illustrates why practical performance alone says little about the general bound. For B=I, a shortest vector is immediately visible. A basis with long, strongly correlated columns may describe a lattice with much shorter integer combinations. Preprocessing can improve the basis substantially, but its own running time and memory must be charged. Supplying an already ideal basis would remove part of the problem.

Kannan’s enumeration method uses recursive preprocessing to control the search region. Hanrot–Stehlé’s analysis gives the more precise n^{n/(2e)+o(n)} time benchmark, up to polynomial input-size factors, and later work reduces preprocessing overhead. This refines the constant multiplying n log n; it does not change that scale to O(n). The bound is about the method, not an unconditional lower bound on every polynomial-space algorithm.

The inherited Micciancio–Voulgaris paper proves a different landmark: deterministic single-exponential algorithms using Voronoi-cell computations. Its March 2012 revision improves the bound to roughly 2^{2n} time and 2^n space, suppressing polynomial factors. The paper explicitly leaves single-exponential time with polynomial space as an open direction. Reading only the phrase deterministic single exponential in its title would miss the resource that remains unresolved.

Exponential memory can encode reusable relationships among many short vectors. Recomputing a discarded value may save space, but repeated recomputation can increase the running time beyond the allowed bound. A valid positive solution must control this global cost as well as the size of each local calculation. Streaming a large list through a small buffer is not sufficient if later steps require repeatedly reconstructing most of the list.

Theoretical and heuristic guarantees also need separation. Pruning an enumeration tree or keeping a smaller sieve pool may work well on tested lattices. A proof for the present question must additionally show that the retained search process reaches an exact minimizer with probability at least 2/3 on every input within the stated time. Successful benchmark instances cannot supply that universal guarantee.

A January 2026 paper by Koyuncu–Linker–Ozel proposes a sheaf-based sieving framework and discusses polynomial memory under coarse graining. Its §4 initially gives storage O((M+K)n) for M initial vectors and K iterations, then suggests reducing memory when most new vectors replace old ones. It does not provide a uniform proof that this replacement regime retains the exact-success guarantee and a 2^{O(n)} iteration bound on every lattice. It is therefore recorded as a related proposal rather than a resolution of this precise question.

The resource gap is also used in current cryptographic research. Albrecht–Lai–Postlethwaite’s CRYPTO 2026 work derives consequences from hypothetical algorithms for hinted inhomogeneous short-integer solutions, connecting them to single-exponential algorithms with polynomial memory for broader worst-case lattice tasks. Its hardness conclusions rely on a time-space assumption; they do not prove that such algorithms are impossible.

The importance of the problem is that it isolates memory as a potential source of exponential speedups in exact geometry. A solution could change the theoretical basis for choosing between enumeration and large-pool methods. Its cryptographic consequences would still have to be assessed through the relevant reductions and concrete parameters; the existence of some 2^{Cn}-time exact solver is not itself a polynomial-time attack.

Its §4 initially gives storage O((M+K)n) for M initial vectors and K iterations, then suggests reducing memory when most new vectors replace old ones. It does not provide a uniform proof that this replacement regime retains the exact-success guarantee and a 2^{O(n)} iteration bound on every lattice. It is therefore recorded as a related proposal rather than a resolution of this precise question.

The resource gap is also used in current cryptographic research. Albrecht–Lai–Postlethwaite’s CRYPTO 2026 work derives consequences from hypothetical algorithms for hinted inhomogeneous short-integer solutions, connecting them to single-exponential algorithms with polynomial memory for broader worst-case lattice tasks. Its hardness conclusions rely on a time-space assumption; they do not prove that such algorithms are impossible.

The importance of the problem is that it isolates memory as a potential source of exponential speedups in exact geometry. A solution could change the theoretical basis for choosing between enumeration and large-pool methods. Its cryptographic consequences would still have to be assessed through the relevant reductions and concrete parameters; the existence of some 2^{Cn}-time exact solver is not itself a polynomial-time attack.

cards.definitions: The lattice generated by B is Λ(B)={Bz:z∈ℤ^d}; d is its rank and m its ambient dimension. Its first minimum λ₁(Λ) is the minimum Euclidean length of a nonzero lattice vector. Full column rank makes this minimum positive and attained. The output is the signed binary coefficient vector z, so lattice membership and the corresponding integer vector Bz can be recovered without a real-number encoding. Any shortest vector is acceptable, with no uniqueness promise; the zero vector is excluded. Exactness means squared length equals λ₁², rather than being within a multiplicative factor greater than one. Use the standard uniform quantum circuit model: a classical polynomial-time machine generates, from 1^L, a circuit on an L-bit input register, zero-initialized ancillary qubits and output qubits, using the fixed universal gates H, T and CNOT, followed by computational-basis measurement and polynomial-time classical decoding. H is the Hadamard gate, T=diag(1,exp(iπ/4)), and CNOT maps |a,b⟩ to |a,a⊕b⟩. Circuit size, qubit count, input processing and output writing are polynomial in L. No advice, oracle, pre-supplied quantum state or unit-cost access to an exponentially large memory is provided. Failure is allowed on at most one third of runs for each valid input; it is not an average over randomly chosen lattices. Malformed encodings and rank-deficient matrices can be rejected classically. Integer bases are the imported target; clearing rational denominators preserves shortest vectors up to a common scale and increases encoding length only polynomially.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove existence of the algorithm with the stated worst-case polynomial cost and exact-search success on every valid basis, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Classical NP-hardness alone does not establish the negative answer for quantum computation. A polynomial-factor approximation, an algorithm for a promised special family, or an exponential-time speedup does not establish the positive answer.

context_blocks.title: The basis can hide a short vector
context_blocks.text: The vectors (100,1) and (101,1) are both long, but their difference is (1,0). Since every nonzero integer vector has length at least one, this difference is shortest in their lattice. SVP searches all integer combinations of the supplied basis, rather than choosing its shortest column.

context_blocks.title: Exactness is a separate demand from probability
context_blocks.text: A successful run must output a genuinely shortest vector. Bounded error permits some runs to fail; it does not permit every run to return a slightly longer vector. Similarly, a quantum state encoding many candidate vectors is not the requested classical answer until a shortest coefficient vector can be extracted with the required probability.

context_blocks.title: Why classical hardness does not settle the quantum question
context_blocks.text: Micciancio proves randomized NP-hardness even for some constant-factor Euclidean approximations, hence also for exact search. A polynomial-time quantum exact solver would therefore put all NP decision problems in BQP, the class with bounded-error polynomial-time quantum algorithms. This is a complexity consequence of the reduction, not a proved impossibility: NP⊆BQP is not known to be false.

context_blocks.title: Faster exponential algorithms still leave the target open
context_blocks.text: The 2025 paper gives exact quantum algorithms with exponential dependence on rank and explicitly separates QRAM access. Hhan’s August 2026 preprint states expected classical time about 2^{0.6039d} and quantum time about 2^{0.5411d}, up to lower-order exponential and polynomial factors; the quantum bound uses exponentially large QRAM. Kim’s concurrent sampling preprint also gives an exponential exact-SVP consequence. These recent claims were checked for scope, not independently proved. None gives polynomial time in L.

context_blocks.title: The recent coset claim has a different lattice consequence
context_blocks.text: Simon’s August 2026 DCP preprint claims polynomial-factor approximate SVP, which would not provide exact shortest vectors even if the algorithm were correct. Gupte, Ragavan and Zhandry’s response, revised on 1 September, claims a direct impossibility result for that proposed algorithm. The claim and response therefore do not supply a resolution of the exact-search problem on this card.

cards.definitions: An instance is an invertible rational matrix B∈ℚ^(n×n) and a positive rational threshold r, all represented explicitly in binary with numerator, denominator, sign and delimiters included in N. The lattice is L(B)={Bz:z∈ℤⁿ}. Its shortest nonzero Euclidean length is λ₁(L)=min{(∑i vᵢ²)^(1/2):v∈L, v≠0}; the minimum exists because B is invertible and the lattice is discrete. The promise problem n^(1+ε)-GapSVP asks for YES when λ₁(L)≤r and NO when λ₁(L)>n^(1+ε)r, promised that one holds. There is no correctness requirement in the gap between those cases. The same ε is used at every dimension. A bounded-error algorithm must give the correct answer with probability at least 2/3 on every promised instance. Use a uniform quantum computation with a fixed finite universal gate set, such as Hadamard, T and controlled-NOT, computational-basis measurements and classical control; qubits begin in the input state and zero auxiliary states, without advice, oracles or special quantum input access. Gate operations, classical control and input handling all count toward total worst-case running time, with the bound applying to every measurement branch. A single machine must work for all dimensions and bit lengths. cards.title: The optimal asymptotic binary rate–distance tradeoff
cards.formal: Determine R₂(δ)=limsupₙ→∞ (1/n)log₂ A₂(n,⌈δn⌉) for every fixed real δ∈(0,1/2), where A₂(n,d) is the largest size of a binary length-n code with minimum Hamming distance at least d.
cards.definitions: A code C is any nonempty subset of {0,1}ⁿ; it need not be linear or efficiently encodable or decodable. The Hamming distance d_H(x,y) is the number of coordinates on which x and y differ. Require d_H(x,y)≥d for every pair of distinct codewords x,y∈C; a singleton satisfies this condition vacuously. A₂(n,d) is the maximum of |C| over all such subsets. A code has rate (log₂|C|)/n, measured in information bits per transmitted bit, and relative distance d/n. The ceiling fixes integer rounding. The limsup permits code families on a subsequence of blocklengths; existence of a full limit is not assumed. δ is fixed before n grows. All logarithms in this card are base two unless stated otherwise. The binary entropy function is h₂(t)=−t log₂t−(1−t)log₂(1−t), with 0 log₂0=0. The endpoint regimes are known: R₂(0)=1 and R₂(δ)=0 for 1/2≤δ≤1.
cards.answer_criterion: Formulation unfinished. The target R₂(δ) and equality conditions are defined, but an admissible answer representation is not. An arbitrary formula can just restate the defining optimization and limsup. A fixed representation or a separately approved proposition is still needed; replacing the question by tightness of a particular coding bound would change it.
cards.why: The basic unresolved packing limit for reliable binary information. An exact answer would identify how much redundancy is intrinsically necessary for a prescribed worst-case separation, independently of algorithmic or algebraic restrictions on the code.

context_blocks.text: A binary code represents messages by selected bit strings. Keeping codewords far apart lets a receiver distinguish them after errors, while selecting many codewords increases the amount of information carried by each transmitted block. The rate–distance function asks for the best possible compromise, allowing every conceivable code. It is therefore an information-theoretic limit that must be understood before asking how efficiently an optimal code can be built or decoded.

For a small example, the repetition code {000,111} has rate 1/3 and distance three, so it corrects one arbitrary flipped bit. The full set of eight three-bit strings has rate one and distance one, so it cannot correct even one arbitrary flip. Generally, disjoint Hamming balls of radius t around codewords are necessary and sufficient for unique correction of every pattern of at most t errors; this requires minimum distance at least 2t+1.

The Gilbert–Varshamov bound guarantees R₂(δ)≥1−h₂(δ). A maximal distance-d code covers the cube by balls of radius d−1, because otherwise another codeword could be inserted. Comparing the cube’s size with the volume of these balls gives the lower bound. In contrast, disjoint balls of radius roughly d/2 give the elementary Hamming upper bound 1−h₂(δ/2). The different radii create a genuine asymptotic gap.

McEliece, Rodemich, Rumsey and Welch’s 1977 linear-programming bounds greatly sharpen the converse. The first gives R₂(δ)≤h₂(1/2−√(δ(1−δ))); the second also uses constant-weight restrictions and is never weaker. The argument constrains a code’s distribution of pairwise distances through positivity relations, extracting information that a volume count loses. These were the long-standing general benchmarks, but they are no longer the strongest reported bounds after August 2026.

Alrabiah and Guruswami’s August 2026 preprint uses classical-input, quantum-output channels to prove stronger bounds for classical binary codes, including nonlinear codes. Mixed-qubit channels strictly improve the first MRRW bound, and a masked version strictly improves the second throughout 0<δ<1/2. Quantum states enter the converse proof as an analytical tool; the codes whose sizes are bounded still consist of ordinary bit strings. The result narrows the gap without matching the Gilbert–Varshamov lower curve.

Barg’s September 2026 note explains the relationship between this channel argument and a concurrent Delsarte-certificate proof. For the improvement of the first bound, he shows that the two variational expressions coincide. The geometric change is to associate a moving subspace, rather than a single vector, with each codeword, allowing a stronger packing argument. This provides a further derivation and interpretation of the new bound; it does not establish the exact rate function.

Lower-bound improvements require equally careful interpretation. Jiang and Vardy improve the finite-length Gilbert bound by a factor proportional to n in the fixed-distance regime they cover. Yuan and Zhu’s January 2026 preprint gives a concise probabilistic proof of a square-root-n improvement for linear codes and extends the method to quantum codes; the classical square-root factor had predecessors. After taking log₂ and dividing by n, any polynomial multiplicative factor contributes only O(log n/n). Such refinements do not increase the leading rate exponent.

Changing the error model also changes the answer. Capacity for independent random bit flips and capacity for list decoding are not the same quantity as the largest rate at a prescribed minimum distance. This card asks about worst-case pairwise separation with unrestricted binary codes. It also does not transfer improvements for sufficiently large alphabets directly to binary codes: changing alphabet and concatenating codes changes their rate and distance parameters.

cards.title: The Li–Li undirected multiple-unicast conjecture
cards.formal: For every finite undirected network with positive rational edge capacities and independent unicast sessions, is the zero-error causal network-coding rate region, under the entropy-capacity convention below, equal to its fractional multicommodity-routing region?
cards.definitions: Let G=(V,E) be a finite connected undirected graph, with capacities c_e>0, and let (s_i,t_i), i=1,…,k, be ordered pairs of distinct vertices. Different pairs may share endpoints. Source s_i initially knows its own message M_i, uniformly distributed over a finite alphabet; the messages are mutually independent. A finite deterministic code specifies in advance a finite sequence of directed edge uses. Each transmitted symbol is a function of messages initially at its sender and symbols previously received there. Every t_i must recover M_i for every message tuple. Local computation and storage are unrestricted; nonlinear functions are permitted. Let X_{u→v} be the whole tuple sent from u to v on edge {u,v}, and measure Shannon entropy H in bits. For a scale b>0, the code supports r∈R_{≥0}^k when H(M_i)≥b r_i for all i and H(X_{u→v})+H(X_{v→u})≤b c_{uv} for every edge. Define C(G) as the closure in R^k of all such supported rate vectors, over all finite alphabets, codes and scales. This explicitly fixes the entropy formulation used in the cited network-coding literature, with exact decoding and capacity shared between directions; it is not a definition using two independent full-capacity arcs. Define R(G) by nonnegative real path flows f_{i,P}, for simple s_i-to-t_i paths P, satisfying Σ_P f_{i,P}≥r_i and Σ_{i,P:e∈P} f_{i,P}≤c_e. The target is C(G)=R(G) for every G and session list. No multicast destinations, correlated sources, initial side information about other messages, or computation of functions in place of message recovery is supplied.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove C(G)⊆R(G) for every specified network and session list; the reverse inclusion follows by routing and closure. Alternatively, exhibit a finite undirected instance with a coding-supported rate vector outside the closed routing polytope, together with a valid causal code and a proof of fractional-routing infeasibility. The latter can use a linear-programming dual certificate. Beating integral edge-disjoint paths, a particular routing algorithm, or a cut bound that is already larger than the routing optimum is insufficient. A multicast or directed-network advantage does not refute this unicast conjecture. A theorem about vanishing-error codes must be related explicitly to this zero-error entropy formulation.
cards.why: Asks whether computation inside an undirected network can increase the throughput of independent unicast messages, with direct connections to multicommodity flow and major computational lower bounds.

importance.reason: A central capacity conjecture whose resolution would clarify the power of network coding and influence circuit and data-structure lower bounds.

cards.status_note: The August 2026 primary papers explicitly leave the general conjecture unresolved. This card fixes causal zero-error coding with entropy capacities and closure of rates, as in the cited formal model. Restricted topology results, multicast gains and alternative error conventions are distinguished. Review cutoff: 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: Routing treats each message as a separate commodity that consumes capacity along paths. Network coding lets an intermediate node combine messages before forwarding them. If a node knows bits x and y, it may send x⊕y; a receiver that already knows y can recover x. Whether the necessary side information can be supplied cheaply enough to improve total throughput depends on the entire network. The conjecture says that undirected edges always let fractional routing match the best coding rate for independent one-destination messages.

Fractional routing is essential to the comparison. A message may be split among many paths, and different commodities may share an edge up to its total capacity. This is more flexible than requiring one path per message or requiring edge-disjoint paths. The rate region is described by a linear program, so an apparent coding improvement over a greedy routing choice does not establish a gap. One must beat the optimum over all fractional routings.

The capacity convention also matters. An undirected edge of capacity one has one combined budget for both directions, rather than a separate budget of one in each direction. The formal statement follows the cited entropy-based definition: the entropy of each complete directional transcript is counted, and decoding is exact. Taking the closure permits limiting rates. This states precisely which capacity notion is being compared instead of assuming that all zero-error, fixed-length and vanishing-error conventions are interchangeable.

Cut constraints provide a necessary upper bound: information needed across a partition must cross its boundary. For multiple commodities, satisfying every cut constraint need not make the demands fractionally routable. Jain, Vazirani, Yeung and Yuval study the small K_{3,2} example with four same-side sessions. Its sparsity bound is one, while its maximum concurrent routing rate is 3/4; their entropy inequalities show that coding also cannot exceed 3/4. The gap between cuts and flows therefore does not by itself give a coding advantage.

Braverman, Garg and Schvartzman show that a counterexample would have consequences well beyond one small network. Any fixed coding advantage greater than one can be amplified into a family with a gap growing as a positive power of log |V|. A general logarithmic upper bound comes from multicommodity-flow and cut relationships. Thus even a modest strict separation would open the door to much larger asymptotic gains.

The conjecture is also connected to computation rather than communication alone. Afshani, Freksen, Kamma and Larsen show that it implies an Ω(n log n) lower bound for constant-degree Boolean circuits multiplying two n-bit integers. Their reduction turns a sufficiently small circuit into a forbidden network-coding advantage. This is a conditional circuit lower bound, not an already proved consequence of ordinary cut arguments.

Recent positive results remain sensitive to the session arrangement. Vamsi and Thakor’s ISIT 2025 work handles specified asymmetric demands in layered networks, including partition-symmetric demands in their Type-I bipartite family. It also studies gaps between routing constructions and information-theoretic bounds for three-layer cases. Such a gap is a reason to examine an instance more closely; it is not itself a demonstrated coding scheme outside the routing region.

An August 2026 preprint by Liu, Que, Li and Li reports new cases via graph metrics, including networks with at most five terminal locations and certain planar instances supported on at most three designated face boundaries. In the planar case, each session has both endpoints on one of those faces. Five terminal locations is not the same restriction as five sessions or five total graph vertices. The general conjecture remains explicitly open in that paper.

The strongest recent undirected separation located in this review changes the demand model. Braverman and He obtain a superconstant multicast coding advantage using locally decodable codes. Each source message there must reach a set of receivers, and the routing comparison is a Steiner-tree packing problem. Replacing those copies by independent unicast messages removes exactly the shared-message structure used by the construction, so the result does not disprove Li–Li.

cards.title: Do binary codes beat the Gilbert–Varshamov rate asymptotically?
cards.formal: Do constants δ∈(0,1/2) and η>0 and binary codes C_n⊆{0,1}^n for arbitrarily large n exist with minimum Hamming distance at least δn and log₂|C_n|/n≥1−H₂(δ)+η?
cards.definitions: A code is any nonempty subset of the binary strings of length n; linearity, explicit construction and efficient decoding are not required. Hamming distance is the number of unequal coordinates, and minimum distance is the minimum over distinct codewords. H₂(t)=−t log₂t−(1−t)log₂(1−t). The constants δ and η must be chosen before n and remain fixed along an unbounded sequence of block lengths. Finite-length improvements vanishing in normalized rate do not meet the target.

context_blocks.text: The Gilbert–Varshamov bound describes a rate-distance tradeoff achievable by random binary codes. Whether an asymptotically better tradeoff exists is a fundamental question about the information lost to adversarial errors.

This is a nonconstructive existence question, independent of whether codes meeting the bound can be efficiently written down. A polynomial improvement in the number of codewords at fixed length need not yield a positive constant improvement in rate. The coding-course materials distinguish these two open challenges.

cards.why: Determine whether the basic random-coding benchmark is an intrinsic binary information limit.

cards.title: Decidability of unconditional Shannon information inequalities
cards.formal: Does a Turing algorithm exist that, given n≥1 and rational coefficients (a_S) for nonempty subsets S⊆{1,…,n}, always halts and decides whether Σ_{∅≠S⊆[n]}a_S H(X_S)≥0 holds for every joint distribution of n finite-valued discrete random variables?
cards.definitions: The finite input lists n and all nonzero coefficients, each as a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator, with its subset S encoded explicitly; omitted coefficients are zero. X_S is the tuple (X_i)_{i∈S}. Its Shannon entropy in bits is H(X_S)=−Σ_x p_S(x)log₂ p_S(x), with 0log₂0=0. Each variable has a finite alphabet, but alphabet sizes are unrestricted and are not supplied as bounds in the input. Joint probabilities may be arbitrary real numbers in [0,1] summing to one. No independence, conditional-independence, functional-dependence, fixed-marginal or support-size promise is imposed. The inequality is a single homogeneous linear inequality, with non-strict ≥0 and no affine constant, premise, disjunction or nonlinear entropy term. Runtime may be any computable function of the input length; polynomial time is not required. The number n varies with the input.
cards.answer_criterion: An affirmative answer supplies a total effective procedure for exact validity of every such rational inequality. A negative answer proves that this language of valid inequalities is undecidable. Finding a false input inequality or proving an individual new valid inequality answers an instance, not the meta-question. A procedure that may run forever on valid inputs, or requires a promised numerical gap, does not resolve exact decidability.
cards.why: A basic computability question about the laws of Shannon information, with consequences for automated proofs, network and coding bounds, and database query reasoning.

importance.reason: A foundational decision problem at the intersection of information theory, computability and database theory; it asks whether exact universal entropy reasoning can be fully automated.

Invalidity is semidecidable. Conditional undecidability, restricted set-function domains and inequality-generation algorithms do not establish undecidability or decidability of this exact problem.

context_blocks.text: For a given distribution, each subset of variables has an entropy. Collecting these numbers produces one point in a space with 2^n−1 coordinates. The question asks whether an input linear halfspace contains every such point, across all finite alphabets and distributions. It is therefore a question about all possible information structures, rather than about estimating entropies from a dataset.

Familiar examples are easy to express in this format. Subadditivity is H(X₁)+H(X₂)−H(X₁,X₂)≥0. Conditional mutual information is H(X₁,X₃)+H(X₂,X₃)−H(X₃)−H(X₁,X₂,X₃)≥0. Both hold without a premise. A negative coefficient is perfectly legitimate; it is the full linear combination, rather than each individual summand, whose sign is being decided.

The standard Shannon inequalities give a finite linear-programming proof method for each n. They express nonnegative conditional entropies and conditional mutual informations, or equivalently normalized monotone submodular set functions. If a candidate follows from them, it is universally valid. But the first non-Shannon inequality of Zhang–Yeung showed in 1998 that this proof method is incomplete. Rejecting an attempted Shannon derivation therefore cannot be used as a negative answer about entropy validity.

The unrestricted alphabet quantifier is a major part of the difficulty. A computation on binary variables explores only a small portion of the permitted distributions. Increasing a guessed alphabet bound may discover new counterexamples, but an unsuccessful search at every bound examined so far provides no effective stopping criterion. A solution cannot quietly replace all finite alphabets by one fixed support limit depending on a heuristic.

There is a rigorous semidecision procedure for invalidity. If an inequality is false, it is strictly negative at some distribution with finite alphabets. Entropy is continuous on that finite probability simplex, so a sufficiently close rational distribution still violates it. Enumerate alphabet sizes and rational distributions, and compute certified entropy approximations of increasing precision. Eventually the negative value is certified. The arithmetical-hierarchy study of Abo Khamis–Kolaitis–Ngo–Suciu places validity in co-r.e.

This explains precisely what a positive solution would add: a way to halt on every valid inequality as well. A complete effective enumeration of proofs of all valid inequalities, coupled with the counterexample search, would suffice. Existing automated methods can produce many correct certificates, but no completeness theorem for all rational unconditional inequalities is supplied by the inspected sources.

Taking the topological closure of the entropic region does not change this particular validity problem. A continuous linear form nonnegative on every entropic point is nonnegative on every limit point, and the reverse implication is immediate. Thus the same unconditional linear inequalities hold for entropic and almost-entropic vectors. This observation depends on the exact logical form; it does not authorize replacing the domain inside arbitrary conditional statements.

Cheuk Ting Li’s 2023 theorem establishes undecidability for conditional information inequalities and conditional-independence implication. Those inputs include premises that must hold exactly. Merely deleting a premise changes the statement. The theorem therefore does not by itself establish undecidability of a single unconditional inequality.

Adding a fixed penalty for violating a premise need not capture its limiting behavior. Kaced–Romashchenko explicitly show essentially conditional inequalities that do not extend to unconditional linear inequalities in the proposed manner. Their results explain why this seemingly direct route from conditional to unconditional validity needs additional justification.

Hannula’s 2024 work studies useful decidable simplifications: different classes of set functions and syntactic forms connected to database bounds. Its coNP-completeness result is for normal polymatroids, a restricted semantic domain, while another polynomial-time result uses monotone functions. These are precise complexity results for different domains, not a classification of validity over all entropy vectors.

The connection to databases gives the question an algorithmic role beyond coding theory. Entropy inequalities constrain how large a relational join can be under information about its inputs and degrees. Related logical forms occur in query containment and dependency implication. Understanding which constraints admit complete reasoning procedures helps explain why some query bounds can be computed effectively while broader formulations encounter undecidability.

The 2025 exploration by László Csirmaz compares the Copy Lemma, maximum-entropy constructions and the Ahlswede–Körner method, and leaves their completeness unresolved. Előd P. Csirmaz and László Csirmaz’s 2026 paper derives two infinite collections of five-variable inequalities and computes consequences through nine generations of its construction. Its enumeration concerns that method’s extremal inequalities; even the proposed characterization of the method is not a characterization of the entire entropy region.

cards.title: Constant-rate binary locally decodable codes with logarithmic query complexity
cards.formal: Do there exist constants r∈(0,1], δ∈(0,1/2) and A>0 such that, for arbitrarily large message lengths k, there are an integer n with k≤n≤k/r, an encoding C:{0,1}^k→{0,1}^n, and randomized local decoders Dec_i for i∈{1,…,k}, satisfying the following? For every message x, every received word z∈{0,1}^n differing from C(x) in fewer than δn positions, and every requested index i, Dec_i with oracle access to z outputs x_i with probability at least 2/3 while making at most ⌈A log₂(n+1)⌉ bit queries on every execution.
cards.why: A central locality-versus-redundancy barrier with consequences for private information retrieval and matrix rigidity.
cards.status_note: The 2 April 2026 source explicitly identifies this binary problem as open. The January 2026 HDX result has different decoding guarantees. cards.definitions: Here k counts message bits and n counts stored codeword bits; rate is k/n and Hamming distance counts unequal coordinates. “Arbitrarily large” means that every threshold K is exceeded by an admissible k; the constants r, δ and A must be fixed before K. The encoding is deterministic and injective. A decoder knows C, k, n and the requested index, but learns the received word only by querying named coordinates, each returning one bit. Queries may be adaptive. A randomized decoder can be represented as a probability distribution over finite binary decision trees with the stated depth bound, whose leaves output 0 or 1. Computation, description length and encoding time are unrestricted: this is the source’s existence question, without an additional requirement of efficient uniform construction. The success guarantee is separate for each triple (x,z,i); it does not require one random seed to recover all bits simultaneously. The adversary may choose corruptions knowing x and C, but z is fixed before the decoder’s private randomness. There is no secret key, channel-computation bound or input-dependent auxiliary information. The decoder must return the requested bit, rather than an erasure or a list of candidates.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove existence of a family with all the stated fixed constants and guarantees, or prove its logical negation. A negative result must exclude every choice of positive constant rate, positive constant error tolerance and logarithmic-query constant for unbounded message lengths. A construction over a growing alphabet or a decoder that may fail on some requested positions under the allowed corruption guarantee does not establish the proposition.

context_blocks.title: Recover one item without reading everything
context_blocks.text: A file can be protected by adding redundant bits, yet reading the whole encoded file to retrieve one bit defeats the purpose of local access. Constant rate limits the storage overhead to one fixed factor. Constant error tolerance requires recovery even when a fixed positive fraction of the stored bits have been changed adversarially.

context_blocks.title: Why simple repetition does not suffice
context_blocks.text: Repeating every message bit three times gives constant rate and a three-query majority decoder. However, an adversary can spend just three corruptions on the requested bit’s copies. For large files this fits within any fixed positive global error budget and makes those copies look like a different message. Local redundancy alone therefore does not supply the guarantee for every requested position.

context_blocks.title: The remaining query gap
context_blocks.text: The April 2026 source records a logarithmic lower bound at constant rate, while the known binary high-rate construction uses 2^{O(√(log n·log log n))} queries. A bound of this latter form is subpolynomial but still larger than logarithmic. Its large-alphabet construction reaches polylogarithmic symbol queries; one such symbol can contain many bits, so it does not give the binary result here.

context_blocks.title: Related decoding guarantees
context_blocks.text: The January 2026 HDX paper gives approximate local list decoding and low-depth list decoding. A list may contain several plausible messages, and circuit depth measures parallel stages rather than bits inspected. Those results do not supply the single requested message bit with this card’s worst-case query and success guarantees.

cards.definitions: Fix nonempty finite sets X₁,X₂,Ŷ₁,Ŷ₂, a probability mass function p on X₁×X₂, functions d_i:X_i×Ŷ_i→[0,∞) with finite values, and thresholds D_i≥0. The pairs (X₁,t,X₂,t), t=1,…,n, are independent with common law p. A length-n code consists of positive integers M₁,M₂, functions f_i:X_i^n→{1,…,M_i}, and a joint decoder g:{1,…,M₁}×{1,…,M₂}→Ŷ₁^n×Ŷ₂^n. Write (Ŷ₁^n,Ŷ₂^n)=g(f₁(X₁^n),f₂(X₂^n)). Encoder i sees only its own source block; descriptions reach the decoder without transmission errors. Codes are deterministic, agreed in advance, and there is no interaction or decoder side information. For ε>0 a code meets rates R_i and distortions D_i within ε when (log₂ M_i)/n≤R_i+ε and E[(1/n)∑ₜ d_i(X_i,t,Ŷ_i,t)]≤D_i+ε for both i. R_p(D₁,D₂) consists of nonnegative pairs (R₁,R₂) for which such codes exist for every ε>0 at all sufficiently large n. This includes limiting boundary rates. Expectation is over the source pairs. Computation and codebook size are unrestricted; rates count bits per source symbol.
cards.answer_criterion: A characterization must prove both achievability of every stated rate pair and impossibility outside its region for every model instance. Before this becomes a complete benchmark, the source must also specify the required mathematical representation or effective approximation guarantee. Repeating the operational definition does not settle that missing requirement.

context_blocks.title: Correlated observations, separate descriptions
context_blocks.text: Two sensors can observe related data without seeing each other’s recordings. Their common decoder can exploit correlation, while each sensor must choose its description from its own recording. For identical fair binary sources and zero Hamming distortion, sending the first recording at one bit per sample and sending nothing from the second sensor suffices. For independent fair bits, those same rates cannot reconstruct the second recording. Hamming distortion counts the fraction of incorrectly reconstructed symbols.

context_blocks.title: What the tradeoff measures
context_blocks.text: Higher distortion permits less accurate reconstructions and potentially lower rates. The target is the entire set of feasible pairs of description rates for fixed tolerances. It neither requires exact recovery of every block nor merely asks for the smallest sum of the two rates. A useful exact theorem must match an achievable region with a converse excluding every other pair.

context_blocks.title: Known results have specific scope
context_blocks.text: Slepian–Wolf resolves lossless reconstruction. Courtade and Weissman give an exact region for logarithmic loss, where a reconstruction is a probability distribution and the penalty is minus the logarithm of the probability assigned to the actual symbol. That setting does not settle arbitrary distortion tables on the finite reconstruction alphabets specified here. The general Berger–Tung achievable bound is not by itself a general converse.

Its May 2026 revision studies distributed computation of matrix and dot products, a different reconstruction task. The inherited question also leaves an editorial gap: “characterize” does not say which finite expression or effective guarantee a new answer must supply. The present card defines the coding model while retaining that gap.

cards.title: Effective classification of polynomially testable hereditary graph properties
cards.formal: Is there a total algorithm which, given a finite family F of finite simple graphs, decides whether induced-F-freeness admits a one-sided dense-model tester sampling at most C·ε^{−c} vertices, for some constants C,c depending only on F?
cards.definitions: The input to the classification algorithm is a finite list of adjacency matrices; the empty list is allowed. Let P_F contain exactly the finite simple graphs with no induced subgraph isomorphic to any member of F. For an n-vertex graph G, define dist(G,P_F) as the minimum number of edge additions or deletions needed to obtain a graph in P_F on the same vertex set, divided by n²; define the distance as +∞ when no such graph exists. For an integer s, the canonical tester chooses a uniformly random subset S of min{n,s} distinct vertices, queries all adjacencies in S, and rejects exactly when G[S] contains an induced member of F. Say that F is polynomially testable if there are integers C,c≥1 such that for every rational ε∈(0,1), every n≥1 and every G with dist(G,P_F)>ε, this tester with s=⌈Cε^{−c}⌉ rejects with probability at least 2/3. It automatically accepts every graph in P_F. The requested deterministic classification algorithm must halt on every finite F and answer YES exactly for these families. No runtime bound on that classification algorithm is imposed, and it need not output the constants C,c. Graph order n and accuracy ε are universally quantified in the property being classified; they are not additional inputs to the classification algorithm.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Asks whether the efficient sampling regime of hereditary graph testing can be recognized from a finite description, turning a broad classification programme into a precise decidability target.

importance.reason: An effective formulation of the major finite-family classification problem; it separates polynomial sampling from mere testability and abstract quantitative equivalences.

This card explicitly asks its effective decidability version. The August 2026 container theorem does not provide the required terminating classifier.

context_blocks.text: The source survey asks for a characterization of finite forbidden-induced-subgraph families whose canonical sample complexity is polynomial in inverse accuracy. To make the requested output unambiguous, this card fixes an effective classification question: can that class of finite inputs be decided at all? This additional effectiveness requirement is an editorial specification, rather than wording attributed to the survey. It distinguishes the target from an equivalent reformulation involving another unresolved infinite condition.

There are two separate computational tasks. Given a fixed family F and a particular finite graph, exact membership in P_F can be checked by searching for its finitely many forbidden patterns. The question here concerns a statement about every possible host graph and arbitrarily small ε. Finite decidability of each individual membership test does not by itself provide a decision procedure for the existence of uniform polynomial sampling bounds.

The dense-model normalization matters. Being ε-far means that a positive ε fraction of all possible vertex pairs must be changed, up to the fixed normalization factor. It does not mean that an ε fraction of the edges currently present must be removed. A sparse graph can therefore be close to a property even when many of its own edges would need modification. No bounded-degree or sparse-input model is implicit.

One-sided error gives rejection a concrete witness: the sampled vertices contain a forbidden induced graph. For an induced copy, both edges and nonedges must agree with the pattern. Thus a four-clique contains an ordinary four-cycle as a subgraph, but no induced four-cycle. Replacing induced copies with arbitrary copies changes the classification problem substantially.

The general hereditary testing theorem guarantees some sample bound depending only on ε, but that bound can be much larger than every polynomial. For finite F, inspecting all pairs in a sample squares its size, which preserves the distinction between polynomial and nonpolynomial dependence. Since F is fixed during testing, exhaustive checking inside the sample also has a fixed polynomial exponent, although that exponent need not be uniform across families.

Gishboliner–Shapira prove a useful sufficient condition: a finite family containing a bipartite graph, a co-bipartite graph and a split graph is polynomially testable. Here co-bipartite means a union of two cliques, and split means a partition into a clique and an independent set; the three roles may be played by the same graph. Their necessary condition requires a bipartite and a co-bipartite member, but this is not sufficient.

The gap between these conditions is real. There are finite families containing a bipartite and a co-bipartite graph that are not polynomially testable. Conversely, split graphs themselves form a polynomially testable class, described by forbidding C₄, its complement and C₅, although none of those forbidden graphs is split. Thus simply promoting either known condition to an equivalence would give wrong answers on known examples.
Even a singleton family remains instructive. Alon–Fox prove polynomial testability for cographs, which are precisely graphs with no induced four-vertex path.
Induced C₄-freeness and its complement remain the exceptional cases identified in the 2025 survey.
Gishboliner–Shapira obtain a single-exponential sample bound for induced C₄-freeness; that improves substantially on regularity-based bounds but is not polynomial in 1/ε.

An August 2026 preprint by Carenini–Seth–Yoshida gives a new quantitative characterization using ordered containers. Roughly, property-satisfying induced subgraphs inside a graph far from the property must fit into smaller vertex sets determined by short fingerprints. Theorem 1.4 translates between tester bounds and these container parameters by explicit polynomial transformations. This is relevant new progress beyond the survey.

Its effectiveness has a specific meaning: given suitable quantitative bounds on one side, the theorem supplies bounds on the other. The container premise still ranges over all sufficiently large host graphs and all accuracy parameters. The inspected theorem does not give a terminating procedure that takes only F and decides whether polynomial container parameters exist. It therefore does not establish the effective finite-family classification asked here.

The distinction is useful independently of how the eventual classification looks. An affirmative answer would provide a finite method for recognizing when global violations must have abundant small witnesses. An undecidability theorem would show that no universal terminating rule can perform this recognition from arbitrary finite forbidden lists, even though each list defines a straightforward graph-membership problem. Either outcome would identify a fundamental limit of turning qualitative testing theorems into systematic algorithm design.

No bounded-degree or sparse-input model is implicit.

One-sided error gives rejection a concrete witness: the sampled vertices contain a forbidden induced graph. For an induced copy, both edges and nonedges must agree with the pattern. Thus a four-clique contains an ordinary four-cycle as a subgraph, but no induced four-cycle. Replacing induced copies with arbitrary copies changes the classification problem substantially.

The general hereditary testing theorem guarantees some sample bound depending only on ε, but that bound can be much larger than every polynomial. For finite F, inspecting all pairs in a sample squares its size, which preserves the distinction between polynomial and nonpolynomial dependence. Since F is fixed during testing, exhaustive checking inside the sample also has a fixed polynomial exponent, although that exponent need not be uniform across families.

Gishboliner–Shapira prove a useful sufficient condition: a finite family containing a bipartite graph, a co-bipartite graph and a split graph is polynomially testable. Here co-bipartite means a union of two cliques, and split means a partition into a clique and an independent set; the three roles may be played by the same graph. Their necessary condition requires a bipartite and a co-bipartite member, but this is not sufficient.

The gap between these conditions is real. There are finite families containing a bipartite and a co-bipartite graph that are not polynomially testable. Conversely, split graphs themselves form a polynomially testable class, described by forbidding C₄, its complement and C₅, although none of those forbidden graphs is split. Thus simply promoting either known condition to an equivalence would give wrong answers on known examples.

Even a singleton family remains instructive. Alon–Fox prove polynomial testability for cographs, which are precisely graphs with no induced four-vertex path.

Induced C₄-freeness and its complement remain the exceptional cases identified in the 2025 survey.

Gishboliner–Shapira obtain a single-exponential sample bound for induced C₄-freeness; that improves substantially on regularity-based bounds but is not polynomial in 1/ε.

An August 2026 preprint by Carenini–Seth–Yoshida gives a new quantitative characterization using ordered containers. Roughly, property-satisfying induced subgraphs inside a graph far from the property must fit into smaller vertex sets determined by short fingerprints. Theorem 1.4 translates between tester bounds and these container parameters by explicit polynomial transformations. This is relevant new progress beyond the survey.

Its effectiveness has a specific meaning: given suitable quantitative bounds on one side, the theorem supplies bounds on the other. The container premise still ranges over all sufficiently large host graphs and all accuracy parameters. The inspected theorem does not give a terminating procedure that takes only F and decides whether polynomial container parameters exist. It therefore does not establish the effective finite-family classification asked here.

The distinction is useful independently of how the eventual classification looks. An affirmative answer would provide a finite method for recognizing when global violations must have abundant small witnesses. An undecidability theorem would show that no universal terminating rule can perform this recognition from arbitrary finite forbidden lists, even though each list defines a straightforward graph-membership problem. Either outcome would identify a fundamental limit of turning qualitative testing theorems into systematic algorithm design.

benchmark_focus.reason: An effective formulation of the major finite-family classification problem; it separates polynomial sampling from mere testability and abstract quantitative equivalences.

cards.title: Does polynomial testability imply polynomial distance estimation for dense graph properties?
cards.formal: For every isomorphism-invariant property P of finite simple graphs with P_n nonempty for every n≥1, does existence of a uniform randomized tester using polynomially many queries in 1/ε, independently of n, imply existence of such an additive-ε distance estimator, in the dense model defined below?
cards.definitions: P_n is a nonempty subset of graphs on [n], invariant under vertex permutations. For n≥2, dist(G,P)=min_{H∈P_n}|E(G)△E(H)|/binom(n,2); for n=1 it is zero. An algorithm receives n and an integer t≥2, with ε=1/t, and accesses G only by adaptive queries asking whether a specified unordered pair is an edge. A tester returns a bit, accepts each G∈P_n with probability ≥2/3 and rejects each G with dist(G,P)≥ε with probability ≥2/3; no condition is imposed between those cases. Polynomial testability means there exist one probabilistic Turing oracle machine and constants C,a≥1 with at most Ct^a adjacency queries on every input and every execution. An estimator is another such uniform machine and constants C′,b≥1, using at most C′t^b queries and returning a binary-encoded rational q with Pr[|q−dist(G,P)|≤1/t]≥2/3 for every G. Computation between queries and total output length have no prescribed bound, but every execution terminates. Coins are independent fair bits; programs and constants may depend on P and cannot depend on n,t or G. Neither algorithm receives a description of P or graph-dependent advice. This asks only the polynomial-testability implication named in the title. The stronger quantitative q_P(poly(ε)) conversion in source Problem 5.4 is not asserted equivalent to it.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Separates recognizing a robust violation from measuring its magnitude and asks whether polynomially efficient dense-graph testing automatically provides polynomial distance estimation.

importance.reason: A direct quantitative frontier between two central tasks in property testing, with a universal implication that would organize many existing polynomial-testing results.

context_blocks.text: Testing asks only for a robust decision: accept graphs in the property and reject graphs that are ε-far from it. Estimation asks for the actual distance to the property, so it must distinguish every pair of nearby distance scales rather than only the two extremes used by a tester.

In the dense graph model the input has Θ(n²) possible adjacency queries, yet many properties can be tested with a number of samples depending only on ε. The central quantitative issue is whether this efficiency survives when the algorithm must estimate distance rather than detect a large violation.

Known reductions convert a tester into an estimator with very large overhead. The 2025 survey of polynomial property testing records an explicit open problem asking whether q_P(ε) can be replaced by q_P(poly(ε)); for polynomial testers this would yield a polynomial estimator. Existing results establish the implication only with exponential or otherwise much larger transformations in general.

Some important classes already have polynomial estimators, including selected hereditary partition properties and several induced-subgraph examples. Such positive cases show that the gap is not caused by a universal information-theoretic obstruction, but they do not give the transformation for every graph property.

The question is about query complexity in the dense model. A result in the bounded-degree model, a computational-time bound after reading the full graph, or a tester that estimates only whether the distance is above one fixed threshold addresses a different problem.

cards.title: Polynomial-time density estimation for arbitrary Gaussian mixtures
cards.formal: Can every mixture of k Gaussians in ℝ^d be learned to total-variation error ε from independent samples in time and sample size polynomial in d,k,1/ε, without separation, weight or covariance-conditioning promises?
cards.definitions: The target distribution is Σ_{i=1}^k w_i N(μ_i,Σ_i), with w_i≥0, Σ_i w_i=1 and positive-definite covariance matrices. Total-variation distance between densities f and g is one half the integral of |f−g|. The learner may output a distribution outside the mixture class. The degree of the running-time polynomial must be independent of k, and parameter recovery is not required.

context_blocks.text: Gaussian mixtures model data with several latent populations. Density estimation asks for an accurate distributional description even when individual components cannot be identified reliably.

Moitra and Valiant establish polynomial learnability for a fixed number of components, with dependence on k that does not meet the joint polynomial target. Existing atlas cards concern compression-style unsupervised learning, robustness for fixed k, or separated parameter estimation. Those are different statistical goals.

cards.definitions: The graph is a finite loopless directed graph with vertex set {1,…,n}; opposite arcs are allowed, but parallel copies of an arc are not. An oracle query specifies a vertex v, a direction IN or OUT, and an index i∈{1,…,d}; it returns the ith neighbor in that direction or a null symbol if the slot is empty. Lists are consistent with one fixed graph and have arbitrary fixed order, so correctness must hold for every permitted ordering. Vertex labels, n,d and ε are given to the tester; it may choose any vertex label, use independent fair random bits, and adapt future queries to previous answers. Internal computation is not charged to query complexity. A directed cycle is a sequence of distinct vertices v₁,…,v_k, k≥2, with arcs v_i→v_(i+1) and v_k→v₁; acyclic means no such cycle exists. Let τ(G) be the minimum number of arcs whose deletion makes G acyclic. An input is ε-far if τ(G)>εdn. Additions cannot remove cycles, so this agrees with the minimum-edge-edit convention for this property. The tester must accept each acyclic graph with probability at least 2/3 and reject each ε-far graph with probability at least 2/3. There is no guarantee for graphs between these cases. Q is the least integer query bound attainable on all n-vertex inputs and all random branches by a randomized query procedure with these guarantees. An upper-bound family must be generated by a uniform algorithm from n,d and the binary encoding of rational ε; there is no running-time requirement beyond termination. The requested Θ bounds concern growth in n, with constants allowed to depend on the fixed d and ε. One-sided error, which must always accept acyclic inputs, is a separate restriction.
cards.answer_criterion: Give an explicit asymptotic bound F(n,d,ε), a uniform tester using O(F) queries, and a matching Ω(F) lower bound for the same adaptive two-sided, bidirectional model, for each fixed d,ε in the stated range. Hidden constants may depend on d,ε, but no factor growing with n may be left unmatched. The source’s broad best-algorithm question is made precise here as optimal query complexity; total runtime is not the cost being classified.

cards.title: Is private PAC sample complexity polynomial in VC dimension and log-star Littlestone dimension?
cards.formal: Is there a universal polynomial p such that every nonempty finite Boolean concept class C on a finite nonempty domain X admits a realizable, possibly improper PAC learner using some number $m\le p(1+\mathrm{VC}(C),1+\log^*\mathrm{LD}(C))$ of independent labeled examples, with error at most 1/10 and confidence at least 9/10, while satisfying $(1,1/(100m^2))$-differential privacy? The learning guarantee must hold for every distribution on the domain and every target concept in C. Computation time is unrestricted. Take both dimensions to be at least one; constant classes can be handled separately.
cards.why: The problem seeks a privacy analogue of a foundational characterization theorem in learning theory.

progress.text: The survey gives lower bound $\Omega(\mathrm{VC}+\log^*\mathrm{LD})$ and upper bound $\min\{O(\log|C|),\widetilde O(\mathrm{LD}^5)\}$. The $\mathrm{VC}=1$ case is nearly understood; the general gap remains.

references.title: Invited Open Problem: Does Differential Privacy Make PAC Learning Much Harder?
references.authors: Kobbi Nissim; Uri Stemmer; Eliad Tsfadia
references.locator: Open Questions 1–2; Theorems 2–3

cards.status_note: Literature checked on 10 September 2026; dates and review scope are recorded below.
cards.review_note: Concrete specialization of the quantitative target following Open Question 1: accuracy, confidence, epsilon, delta, and the meaning of polynomial overhead are fixed explicitly. The survey itself suppresses these parameters. Importance is editorial; cited proofs have not been independently audited.

context_blocks.text: VC dimension characterizes nonprivate learning. Finite Littlestone dimension $\mathrm{LD}$ characterizes the existence of private learning but does not determine its optimal quantitative cost.

A sample-complexity characterization should tell us how many labelled examples are necessary from the structure of the hypothesis class, rather than from a particular learning algorithm. Two classes can have the same ordinary capacity measure while differing in how difficult it is to hide the influence of an individual training example.

The quantitative issue matters even after learnability is settled. Knowing that some finite sample size works does not distinguish a useful bound from an enormous one. The proposed relation asks whether the extra price of privacy can be controlled by ordinary statistical complexity together with a very slowly growing function of online-learning complexity.

cards.definitions: A concept class is a finite set of functions from a domain X to {0,1}. VC(C) is the largest size of a subset of X on which all binary labelings occur. LD(C) is the greatest depth of a complete binary tree labeled by domain points such that every root-to-leaf edge-label sequence is realized by a concept. The function log-star counts base-two logarithms needed to reach at most one. A learner may output a hypothesis outside C. Privacy requires $\Pr[A(S)\in E]\le e\Pr[A(S\prime)\in E]+1/(100m^2)$ whenever the two m-record samples differ by replacement of one record. Here X is finite, distributions on X are arbitrary probability vectors, and a learner is a probability kernel from length-m labeled samples to the finite set {0,1}^X of hypotheses. The sample size m is a positive integer chosen for C before the target and distribution. For every target h∈C and distribution D on X, with probability at least 9/10 over m independent draws x_i from D and learner randomness, the returned hypothesis has D-probability of disagreement with h at most 1/10. Privacy holds for all labeled samples, including unrealizable ones, and all subsets E of the hypothesis set. The same kernel and m work for all D,h. This finite-domain convention retains the finite-class target: points in an arbitrary domain with the same label vector (h(x))_{h∈C} can be identified, giving at most 2^|C| cells and preserving both dimensions. A learner on those cells lifts to the original domain. No running-time or computable-representation requirement is imposed.

cards.title: Can all marginals be privately released in polynomial time from a polynomial-size database?
cards.formal: Do there exist an integer C≥1, a function α:N_{≥2}→[0,1] with lim_{d→∞}α(d)=0, a uniform randomized mechanism M and a uniform deterministic evaluator E, such that for every d≥2 and every database D∈({0,1}^d)^n with n=d^C, M runs in time polynomial in n,d, satisfies (1,1/(100n²))-differential privacy under replacement of one row, and outputs a finite synopsis S for which, with probability at least 2/3, E(S,q) approximates q(D) within α(d) simultaneously for every marginal query q?
cards.definitions: A marginal query is a pair (J,a), where J⊆{1,…,d} and a∈{0,1}^J, and q_{J,a}(D)=|{i∈{1,…,n}:D_{ij}=a_j for all j∈J}|/n. The empty J query has value one. Queries of every order up to d are included. The database is an explicitly stored ordered n-by-d bit matrix; neighbouring databases have the same dimensions and differ in exactly one row. Differential privacy means that for every ordered pair of neighbours D,D′ and every set O of output strings, Pr[M(D)∈O]≤e·Pr[M(D′)∈O]+1/(100n²). M uses independent fair random bits and has one worst-case polynomial bound p(n+d) on bit operations, output length and random bits. Its output is a finite binary string S. E receives d,S,J,a, has a worst-case bound given by one polynomial in d+|S| and outputs a binary-encoded rational number. E has no access to D, private state of M or an additional oracle. Both algorithms are ordinary classical Turing machines, with no nonuniform advice. The accuracy event is simultaneous over all queries and its probability is over M’s randomness alone, separately for every D. S need not encode a synthetic database or a consistent probability distribution. C,α,p,M,E and the evaluator’s polynomial are fixed before d,D are chosen. No algorithm to compute α and no prescribed rate of its convergence are required.

context_blocks.text: A marginal measures the fraction of records matching a pattern on selected coordinates. Low-order marginals describe small groups of attributes, while all marginals permit every such pattern. The family contains exponentially many queries even though one query has a short description. A synopsis is therefore an efficiently evaluable representation, rather than a literal list of exponentially many answers.

Privacy and accuracy quantify different objects. The privacy guarantee compares the complete output distributions after changing one person’s row. Accuracy concerns all queries simultaneously on each fixed database. Once a successful synopsis has been released, its deterministic evaluation reveals no additional access to the original records. An algorithm answering only a prespecified small batch is not automatically an algorithm for this target.

Vadhan’s Open Problem 7.8 asks about polynomial-time private estimation of all higher-order marginals with vanishing error using only polynomially many rows in the dimension. The present card fixes approximate-DP parameters, replacement adjacency and a noninteractive evaluable synopsis. These choices state one concrete version of the proposal; they are not asserted to be equivalent to every interactive or fixed-order formulation.

Chandrasekaran, Thaler, Ullman and Wan give subexponential-time private algorithms for marginal queries on small databases. Their result illustrates useful progress between exponential and polynomial cost. The constant-accuracy, per-query statement in that paper does not provide the polynomial-time, vanishing-error synopsis required here.

Requiring synthetic records would impose an extra restriction. The benchmark permits any binary synopsis with an efficient evaluator, because hardness of synthetic-data generation need not rule out other ways of answering queries. The existing TCS-0506 concerns private PAC sample complexity, while TCS-6040 asks about strong approximation of coverage functions. Neither asks this computational query-release question.

An algorithm answering only a prespecified small batch is not automatically an algorithm for this target.

Vadhan’s Open Problem 7.8 asks about polynomial-time private estimation of all higher-order marginals with vanishing error using only polynomially many rows in the dimension. The present card fixes approximate-DP parameters, replacement adjacency and a noninteractive evaluable synopsis. These choices state one concrete version of the proposal; they are not asserted to be equivalent to every interactive or fixed-order formulation.

Chandrasekaran, Thaler, Ullman and Wan give subexponential-time private algorithms for marginal queries on small databases. Their result illustrates useful progress between exponential and polynomial cost. The constant-accuracy, per-query statement in that paper does not provide the polynomial-time, vanishing-error synopsis required here.

Requiring synthetic records would impose an extra restriction. The benchmark permits any binary synopsis with an efficient evaluator, because hardness of synthetic-data generation need not rule out other ways of answering queries. The existing TCS-0506 concerns private PAC sample complexity, while TCS-6040 asks about strong approximation of coverage functions. Neither asks this computational query-release question.

cards.title: Does every finite-template decision promise CSP have a P/NP-hard dichotomy?
cards.formal: For every pair of fixed finite relational structures A,B of the same finite signature, with a homomorphism A→B, is the decision promise problem of distinguishing I→A from I↛B either solvable in deterministic polynomial time or NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one promise reductions?
cards.definitions: A finite relational signature is a finite list of relation symbols R with fixed positive arities a_R. A structure A consists of a finite nonempty domain and, for each R, a relation R^A⊆A^{a_R}. A homomorphism h:I→A is a map on domains such that (v₁,…,v_a)∈R^I implies (h(v₁),…,h(v_a))∈R^A for every R and tuple. The templates A,B and their relations are fixed for each computational problem. Only I varies; its domain and relation tuples are explicitly listed in binary, of total length L. The algorithm must accept all I admitting a homomorphism to A and reject all I admitting no homomorphism to B. On I→B but I↛A, either answer is allowed. A→B makes the yes and no sets disjoint. Polynomial time means one deterministic algorithm for the fixed pair, halting on every input in O(L^c), with c and hidden constants allowed to depend on A,B. NP-hardness means a deterministic polynomial-time map from 3-SAT formulas φ to structures I_φ such that satisfiable φ yield I_φ→A and unsatisfiable φ yield I_φ↛B. The question is about deciding the promise, not producing a B-valued assignment. No uniform algorithm for classifying templates is required. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: The main classification question for constraint satisfaction with promises, encompassing approximate colouring and many local relaxation tasks. importance.reason: A broad structural question extending the finite CSP dichotomy into approximation and promise problems, with connections to algebra, topology, and optimization.
